THE TWO SOWERS. Death came to the earth, by his side was Spring, They came from God's own bowers, And the earth was full of their wandering, For they both were sowing flowers. "I sow," said Spring, "by the stream and the wood, And the village children know The gay glad time of my own sweet prime, And where my blossoms grow. "There Is not a spot in the quiet wood Bit hath heard the sound of my feet, And the violets come from their solitude When my tears hath mad 4 them sweet." "1 sow," saith Death, "where the hamlet stands, I sow in the churchyard drear ; I drop in the grave with gentle hands, My flowers from year to year. ".The young and the old go into their rest, To the sleep that waits them below; But I clasp the children unto ray breast, And kiss them before I go." "I sow," said Spring; "but my flowers decay When the year turns weak and old, When the breath of the bleak winds wears them away, And they wither and droop in the mould. "But they come again when the young earth feels The new blood leap in her veins, When the fountain of wonderful life unseals, And the earth is alive with the rains." "I sow," said Death; "but my flowers unseen Pass away from the land of men, Nor sighs nor tears through the long sad years Ever bring back their bloom again. "But I know they are Wondrous bright and fair In the fields of their high abode; Your flowers are the flowers that a child may wear, But mine are the blossoms of God." Death came to the earth, by his side was Spring; The two came from God's own bowers; - • One sow'd in night and the other in light, - Yet they both were sowing flowers. —Alexander Anderson, "Good Words" for April.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI-
CULTURE, &c.
Sir Thomas Munro, Bart., of Lindertis, has intimated to

his tenantry that the powers given by the Ground Game Act, 1880, may now be exercised irrespective of date of lease. LARGE LITTER OF PIGS.—Mr. Robert Dixon, of Preesall, has a sow of the large breed that gave birth to 23 living pigs on Sunday night last, 22 of which are at present living and doing well. It is stated that at Wisbeach there was not a single sheep for sale in the Cattle Market on Thursday week, a cifcum- stance which shows the scarcity of mutton at the present time, and which has not occurred there, it is said, for 72 years. Mr. J. E. Thor°ld Rogers, M.P., has just published an interesting little work containing the result of his observa- tions-on ensilage-in the United States. It embodies a large arrly of authentic facts and statistics, which will enable anTone to form a sound opinion upon this question which is just now engaging the attention of the agricultural world.

Circulars are being issued by the leading agricultural machinery manufacturers announcing important reductions. Sheaf binders, mowers, reapers, ploughs, and agricultural castings are all•dropped. Mowers and reapers are reduced 15 per cent., some ploughs 10 per cent., and castings quite 5 per cent. Among the chief firms for whom circulars are already delivered are Howard and Co. Samuelson and Co., and Ransomes, Head, and Jefferies.—Land. A paper on "Natural and Artificial Manuring," read by Mr. A. Smetham, F.C.S., on the 29th January last, before the members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, has just been pub- lished in cheap pamphlet form. It deals with the questions of concentrated foods as manures, farm-yard manures, pre- pared manures, the general functions of phosphates in agri- culture, the value of high farming, the utilisation of sew- age, and other matters, all of which cannot but be interest- ing to those who are interested in efficiently cultivating the land at the lowest possible cost. TiE RAPID GROWTH OF A TURNIP SEED.—It has been proved by the experiments of Dr. Desaguliers that in an average condition a turnip seed may increase its own weight 15 times in a minute. Turnips sown in peat ground have been found to increase by growth 16,000 times the weight of their seeds daily. The most minute of turnip seed is that of the "globe" variety; it only measures one-twentieth part of an inch in diameter, yet in a few months it will in- crease its bulk to 27 millions of times the size of the on-

ginal seed, with many leaves in addition. The number of turnip seeds in the weight of one grain is 30, and one pint of them weighs 14 ounces, the mean germinative power extending over five years, and sometimes over ten years. FARMERS AND RAILWAY GATES.—A case affecting far- mers who hold land contiguous to a railway was tried the other day at the Ipswich County Court. A farmer sued the Great Eastern Railway Company for the value of some pigs which had been killed by an engine on the line. A gate led from the field in which they were placed across the line to some of the farmer's land on the other side. The gate was made and maintained by the company for the farmer's use, and the pigs had evidently got between the bars. Since the accident the company had altered it. The Judge ruled that the company were bound to put up suffi- cient protection, as a man had a right to put any stock into his field without anyone to watch them. He would not grant a case for a superior court, as he did not like to en- courage litigation. The magistrates of the St. Asaph Bench appear to need a little rudimentary education in the laws which they ad- minister. The other day four men were charged before them for trespassing in pursuit of rabbits, the only weapon among the four being a catapult. One of the accused did ' not appear, and _another was discharged. In delivering judgment upon the other two, the Chairman first said that the magistrates had given the case their best consideration, and found that the prisoners were not guilty of poaching. They should have been summoned for trespass, for whichl they would be fined Is. and 7s. 6d. costs. The Clerk in- formed the Chairman that he could not fine the defendants for an offence they had not been summoned to answer for; whereupon the learned justice informed the culprits that they could not. be fined for trespassing, but would be fined is. and 7s. 6d. costs each for "a mild case of poaching," al- though he had just declared them innocent of that offence. THE " DUCHESS " TRIBE.—In the American exchanges for February two notices occur of the fortunes of the famous Duchess tribe. Thefirst is the intimation that, in the Flat Creek herd, Kentucky, of Messrs. Hamilton, Airdrie Duchess' sth, calved October 12, 1874. has died, having produced in the hands of her present owner a roan heifer. The other is that the heifer Duchess of Overlak-e, by Duke of Hillhurst , 7th from Duchess of Hillhurst 7th, has produced a red bull', calf. The owner of Duchess of Overlake (conveying the ' intelligence of this birth) thus breaks out:—" Duchess of Airdrie 10th is now a great-great-grandmother, with twenty- six living descendants, a female line in America, and, if we , are not mistaken, there are almost as many Mord in Eng- land. Can any other cow now living and breeding show a better record ?" To this we reply :—" Thomdale Rose 2nd, at Audley End, has had (and is still alive herself) sixty. descendants in the female line, of which fourteen are re- corded in the last catalogue as 'dead.'" It should, how- ever, be acknowledged that Thorndale Rose 2nd, calved in 1867, is the older cow by a year. MILKING UNRULY Cows.—Messrs. Haggin and Carr, the

great ranchers of California, have a novel-ay of managing unruly cows at their dairy near Bakersfield, Kern County. A corral is made triangular in shape, and in one corner is an opening which leads into a long passage way, about 112 feet in length, two and a half feet wide, and high enough to I admit the tallest animal. The passage way, or hall has a gate at either end, and is divided off into sixteen stalls of 7ft. each by inserting bars across it. The cows are driven from the triangular corral into this hall, the bars having, of course, been removed, and when full the bars are inserted in their proper places, each cow being confined in a separate Each stall has a separate door, about two feet square, directly under the animal's udder. The milker opens this door, seats himself, and milks; after which he closes the door, and proceeds to the next until all have been milked.

The 'front -gate leading into the pasture is then opened, the bars removed, and the cows allowed to pass on into the pas- ture; after which the gate is closed and the stalls again filled from the corral, and so on until all have been milked. Mr. Brown, who is in charge of the diary, says the plan worki to perfection. PRUNING AN APPLE TREE.—Upon the upper slopes of this Eden apple trees of choice sorts are planted here and there, which require the unremitting attention of pater- fanzilias to keep in proper shape. Let us approach him at work,' and try to learn something of the way an apple tree should grow from watching his actions and listening to the words of wisdom which fall from his lips. "See," he says, 'the first principle is that the tree should be trained to grow into the shape of a bell with its mouth upwards towards the sky, all the branches tending outwards so as to allow the light to penetrate freely, the internal parts not being shaded by the external. No branch or shoot which appears superfluous or useless should be allowed to remain, like those, for instance, which cross and touch each other, each impeding the other's growth by fraying and bruising their tender bark as they sway in the breezes." To one of these the sharp edge of the chisel is applied as close to the parent stem as possible, then strong taps at the end of the long handle with a heavy mallet sever it from its intrusive

I position, leaving a clean c-ut scar level with the bark, which offers no obstruction that might check the rain as it runs down, causing it to soak in and form a rotten spot. "Every superfluous shoot," our instructor adds, "is a tap by which the sap runs to waste, and by cutting off such shoots the life-blood of the tree is kept in its principal channel, and concentrated for the nourishment of the useful branches."— Land.

How BUTTER MAY BE SPOILED.—Good butter may be spoiled in churning. Qver-churning ruins the texture and changes the proper waxiness to a disagreeable, sickly greasi- ness. This is the more easily done in a churn with dashes, which will press the butter against the sides of the churn and squeeze it and rub until it is spoiled. Too long churn- ing spoils the quality by the oxidation of the butter and the premature formation of strong flavoured acids in it, the full presence of which we call rancidity. It may be spoiled at too high a temperature, by which it is made soft and oily, and of greasy texture and flavour. No subsequent treatment can remedy this error. It may be spoiled before the cream reaches the churn by keeping it too long, or, what is practically the same, by keeping it in too warm a place; fifty degrets is about the right temperature if the cream is kept a week; if it is kept at 62 degrees three days is long enough. White specks are produced in butter by over-churning, or by having the cream too sour. Either of these faults produces curd in the milk, and the small flakes of this cannot be washed out of the butter. Milk from a cow in ill health, and that is acid when drawn, will produce specky butter. So will the use of salt containing specks of lime, which unite with the butter and form insoluble lime soap. White specks are covered up to a great extent by using good colouring, which is made of oil as the solvent. But this use of colouring to disguise a fault and to add an undeserved virtue is worthy of denunciation.—American Dairyman.

Mr. C-, the faithful pastor of a church in New Jersey, was one day addressing the Sabbath School. He chose the subject of the miraculous feeding of the five thousand with five loaves and two fishes, twelve basketsfull of fragments being gathered up after they had eaten. Ques- tion after question was asked and answered, and all went on smoothly until the pastor, aiming mentally at the twelve baskets of fragments, said, "Children, when all these people had eaten of the loaves and the fishes, what was left?" "The bones!" shouted an eager little boy. GOOD-NATURED PEOPLE.—Be good-natured, if you can; for there is no attraction so great, no charm so admirable. A face that is full of the expression of amiability is always beautiful. It needs no paint and no powders. Cosmetics are superfluous for it. Rouge cannot improve tis cheeks, nor lily-white mend its complexion. Its loveliness lies be- yondwhen it all this. It is not the beauty that is but skin deep. einsthoaptheeoffactheeoffeaa features h ble -the:trtedyou see, nor yet the tint of the cheek, the hue of the lip, or the man nlleyr brilliance of the eye; you see the nameless something which animates all these, and leaves for your instinct a sense of grateful fascination; you see an indescribable embodiment of a heutfelt goodness within, which wins your regard in spite of external appearances. div.head: Tratettes,
div.p: Tratettes,

--,fones tTainks a man I s fortunate who has his will con- tested after his death only. He says his will has been con- tested ever since he married Mrs. Jones. "Do you realise—have you reflected over it—Angelina?" whispered Clarence to his betrothed. "Only two weeks more and we shall be one! But remember, darling, lam to be that one." A Scottish laird surprised his friends at dinner by affirm- ing that the finest grapes he had ever eaten were grown in the open air in Fifeshire. Their surprise was moderated, however, when he returned to the subject and added, " But I maim premise that I prefer them Boor." An Irish officer had the misfortune to be dreadfully wounded in one of the battles in Holland. As he lay on the ground an unfortunate soldier, who was near him, and was also severely wounded, made a terrible howling, when the officer exclaimed, "Hold your row, will ye? Do you think there is nobody killed but yourself ?" A little school girl asked her teacher what was meant by "Mrs. Grundy." The teacher replied that it meant "the world." Some time afterwards the teacher asked the geo- graphy clam, to which this little bud of promise belonged, "Whet is a zone ?" After some hesitation this girl bright- ened up and replied, "I know! it's a belt round Mrs. Grunly's waist !' A little four-year-old remarked to her mamma on going to bed, "I am not afraid of the dark." "No, of course you are not," replied her mamma, "for it can't hurt you." "But, mamma, I was a little afraid once when I went into the pantry in the dark to get a eookey." "What were you afraid of ?" asked her mamma. "I was afraid I couldn't find the cookies." The Rev. Doctor B—, of Dublin, while introducing to an audience the Rev. Dr. S—, a famous missionary from India (his home by biith), concluded his remarks with the following left-handed compliment :—" He comes to you from that land where every prospect pleases, and only man is rile?' The modest missionary arose, and blushingly rendered his thanks, amidst the irrepressible mirth of the audience. An old gentleman who had provoked the hostility of a fashionablelady whom he had known in boyhood, was asked by his wife what he had done to incur the lady's displeasure. "Nothing at all," replied the innocent old man; "on the contrary, I was cordial to her, and spoke of the time when I used to draw her to school in a go-cart, nearly half a cen- tury ago !" His wife threw up her hands and murmured, "How stupid men are." A celebrated naturalist had certain odd ways. One morn- ing his wife got up as usual, and was about to put on her shoes and stockings, when she suddenly uttered a scream which somewhat disturbed the serenity of the grave profes- sor. Rising in his bed he propped himself on his elbow, and inquired what was the matter. "Oh dear! there's a little serpent just crept out of my boot," she said in a trembling voice. "Only one, love ?" replied the husband, much dis- appointed, "there ought to have been three !" He had put them there himself to keep them warm. A SINGULAR LIBRARY.—A curious collection of books is contained in the library of Warstenstein, near Cassel, in Germany. These books appear at first sight to be logs of wood, but each volume is really a complete history of the tree it represents. The back shows the bark, in which a small place is cut to write the scientific and the common name as a title. One side shows the tree trunk in its natu- ral state, and the other is polished and varnished. Inside are shown the leaves, fruit, fibre, and insect parasites, to which is added a full description of the tree and its pro- ducts.

TACITURNITY OF Gxacius.—ln conversation Dante was taciturn or satirical; Butler was silent or caustic; Gray , and Alfieri seldom talked or smiled. Descartes, whose avo- cations formed him for mediation and solitude, was silent; Rousseau was remarkably trite in conversation—not a word of fancy or eloquenee warmed him. -Milton was unsocial and even irritable, when much pressed by the talk of others. -Addison and Molliere were only observers in society; and Dryden has very honestly told us, "My conversation is dull and slow, nfy humor saturnine and reserved; in short, I am not one of those who endeavour to break jests in company, or to make repartees. George 111. once ordered Mr. S., a tradesman of some eminence in London, to wait upon him at Windsor Castle at eight o'clock in the morning of a day appointed. Mr. S. was half an hour behind time, and upon being announced, his Majesty said, "Desire him to come at eight to-morrow morning." Mr. S. appeared the next day after the time, and received the same command. On the third morning he contrived to be punctual. Upon his entrance, the Bing said, "Oh ! the great Mr. S.! What sleep do you take, Mr. S.?" "Why, please your Majesty, lam a man of regular habits; I usually take eight hours." "Eight hours ?" said the King; that's too much; six hours' sleep is enough for a men, seven for a woman, and eight for a fool, Mr. S., eight for a fool." The late Lord R—, with many good qualities, and even learning and parts, had a strong desire of being thought skilful in physic, and was very expert in bleeding. Lord Chesterfield, who knew his foible, and on a particular occa- sion Nnished to have his vote, came to him one morning, and, after having conversed upon different matters, com- plained of the headache, and desired his Lordship to feel his pulse. It was found to beat high, and a hint of losing blood g,ive.n. "I have no objection; and as I hear your Lordship has a masterly hand, will you favour me with try- ing your lancet upon use?"—" Apropos," said Lord Chester- field, after the operation, "do you go to the House to-day ?" Lord R— answered, "I did not intend to go, not being sufficiently informed of the question which is to be debated; but you, who have considered it, which side will you be of ?" The Earl, having gained 1113 confidence, easily directed his judgment: he carried him to the House, and got him to vote as pleased. He used afterwards to say "that none of his friends had done as much as he, having literally bled for the good of his country." . OUR SOLDIERS IN THE PAST AND Now.—Few things are more remarkable than the contrast between soldiers past and present in respect to temperance. Although drunken- ness is still the curse of our army as of our nation, our men do not now glory in their shame, and one out of every ten abstains. Nearly all the men who had joined the Institute Temperance Society proved faithful during the Egyptian campaign, despite the torments of thirst suffered and the bad water. One Marine told me that, in the descent on the Ganal, he was in action from four o'clock on Sunday after- noon to ten o'clock on Monday morning without a drop of water or a morsel of food passing his lips. On landing, the first object that met him was a comrade offering him a bottle of rum. It was a moment of agonising temptation, but he dashed it away from him, and soon after found some water. As the native spirit is graphically described by a soldier as "enough to poison a dead horse, let alone the liv- ing jackass who pours it down his throat," he might have paid dearly but for that heroic resistance.—Enums HOE- XINS, in Good Words. A &ERR fl Scitoon.—Two boys were in a schoolroom alone together, when some fireworks, contrary to the master's express prohibition, exploded. One boy denied it; the tither, Ben Christie, *Ould neither admit nor deny it, and was severely flogged for the obstinacy. When the boys got alone again, "Why didn't you deny it ?" asked the real offender. "Because there were only we two, and one of us mast have lied," said Ben. "Then why not say I did it ?" "Because you said you didn't, and I would spare the liar." The boy's heart melted. Ben's moral gallantry subdued ' him. When school reassembled the young culprit marched up to the master's desk, and said, "Please, sir, I can't bear to be a liar. /let off the squibs ;" and he burst into tears. 'Me master's eye glistened on the self-accuser, and the un- deaerved punishment he had inflicted on the other boy smote his conscience. Before the whole school, hand-in- hand with the culprit, as if he and the other boy were joined in the confession, the master walked down to where young Christie sat, and said aloud—" Ben, Ben, lad, he and I beg your pardon; we were both to blame !" The school was hushed and still, as older schools are apt to be when something true and noble is beingdone ; so still they might almost have heard Ben's big-boy tears dropping on his book, as he sat enjoying the moral triumph which subdued him- self as well as the rest. And when from want of anything else to say he gently cried, "Master for ever!" the loud shout of the scholars filled the old man's eyes with some- thing behind his spectacles which made him wipe them before he sat down again. KAY'S °COMPOUND, for coughs and Colds, is equally ser- vice/o,le for Horses and Cattle.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 31, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 31, 1883.
SCIENTIFIC NOTES,

TELE STAR Or BETHLESEM.—A Berlin correspendent says the re-appearance of the Star of Bethlehem is predicted by astronomers for this year or the next. On November 11, 1572, Tycho von Brahe discovered a star in Cassiopeia which equalled Sirius, and everkVenu.s in brightness Or a month, and then fell back into its former insignificance. Conjecture has sought to establish a connection between this ephemeral phenomenon and two similar apparitions in 1264 and 945. A not unnatural inference was that the same increase in volume of this remarkable star occurred before 945, which would bring us to about 630 and 310 and to the date of the Nativity. This star is now again due. A REMARKABLE FIND OF BA.TITRAI, GAS.—Boring opera- tions for a supply of natural gas have been in progress at Hills Station, Western Pennsylvania Railroad, some nine- teen miles from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, on the line of ' the Alleghany River. A plate-glass manufactory is under construction at that point, and on February 13, when the drillers had reached a depth of 1,170 feet, a powerful vein of gas was struck. The vapour immediately ignited, burning down the shanty and derrick. The borers barely escaped with their lives. -The strike caused great excitement, and the parties interested in the works are naturally delighted, as it will, they think, make them independent with respect te fuel for melting and annealing purposes.—lron. AN ARTIFICIAL AIIRORA.—M. Lemstroem, the well- known professor of Helsingfors, who makes a study of auroral phenomena, has recently succeeded in producing' what may be considered as an aurora on a small scale. During the past winter he chose a station in Finland, just within the Arctic circle, where there are two conical hills, one about 2,000 ft. and the other about 3,000 ft. high. He connected the tops of these hills to the earth at their bases with a network of copper wire, and one evening was re- warded by observing a luminous circle proceeding from the summit of one of the hills, and reaching an estimated alti- tude of 360 ft. This terrestrial discharge into the atmos- phere was electrical, the electricity being of positive sign. —Engineering. PRE-HISTORIC REMAINS IN GERMANY.—A discovery, which is expected to throw some light on pre-historic times in what is now Germany, has been made near Andernach, on the Rhine. Remains of pre-historic animals have been found in a pumice-stone. pit, and Prof. Schaaffhausen, of Bonn has investigated the spot closely. A lava stream underlying the pumice-stone was laid bare, showing a width of only two metres. The crevices between the blocks of lava were filled with pumice-stone to a depth of one-half to one metre; below this, however, there was pure loam and clay,-and in this were found numerous animal bones, ap- parently broken by man, as well as many stone implements. It is supposed that there was a- settlement there, of which the food remains fell into the lava crevices before the whole was covered with pumioe-stone. HEATING RAILWAY TRAlNS.—Various means have from time to time been suggested for heating railway trains, in place of the primitive one of hot water. But Mr. W. H. Matson, of North Pownal, Vermont, has patented an inven- tion for warming railway carriages in which he even dis- penses with steam or stoves. By a special arrangement of the locomotive, the cold air is taken in by the momentum of the train furnishing the necessary clgaught through the fire-box, and is distributed to the cars by air pipes. A register under each seat, under the control of the passenger, regulates the admission of heat as required. This reads very well; but we are afraid the locomotive engineer will have to say something on the matter, and we should be very much surprised if that important personage were to approve of Mr. Malson's invention.—lron. A NOVEL VESSEL.—The now icebreaker which the city of Gothenburg has had built,"in order to keep their harbour open in the winter, has already rendered excellent service. Her construction deserves special notice. This vessel, which is the first of its kind constructed in Sweden, was built by the Lindholmen Mekaniska Verkstad, near Gothenburg. Her dimensions are :—Length over all, 135 feet; greatest width, 35 feet; depth in the hold, under deck, 19i feet; while she draws aft, when loaded and with coals for twenty- four hours, 12-4 feet of water. The vessel's keel, stem, rud- der, and rudderpart are of best Swedish iron; but spent' and knees-are of Bessemer steel, containing 0.15 to 0-20 per cent. of carbon; all made at Motala. At her trial the ves- sel attained a continuous speed of six knots per hour, and broke with the greatest ease ice from five to six inches in thickness, and infirm ice from eight to nine inches thick, in many places having accumulated in layers up to 15 inches. The vessel is provided with a series of iron tanks, which may be filled and emptied as required, in order to give her the trim and draught demanded by the various thicknesses of the ice. She has steering apparatuses both for steam and hand. These are found to work admirably. The cost sf the vessel is £25,000.—/ron. Loss OF HEAT FROM BEILDINGS.—One great cause of expense of fuel in English houses, and of the inconvenience experienced from draughts, arises from the loss of heat which takes place in consequence of thin walls, lightly-con- structed roofs, thin glue windows and skylights. The same carelessness In edonontising heat prevails in railway carri- ages, and they afford a ready illustration of what takes place, because the effects are so striking in cold weather. The floor and roof of a railway carriage, instead of being double, with air-spaces. between, are single; conse- quently the radiation of heat from them is very rapid. In cold weather the heat generated by the persons present and by the foot-warmers is insufficient to keep up the tem- perature. If the roof and sides of a railway carriage and the floor were made double, with an air-space between, the loss of heat by radiation would not much exceed half that , with the present roots and floors; and in stunner the carri- ages would suffer proportionately less from sun-heat. The same is true of houses. If houses were constructed with thick walls with closed air-spaces in the centre, with double windows, and with the slates of the roof laid on close board- ing.covered with felt, they would retain the heat in winter' far better than most houses do now. London houses with thin party walls also illustrate this question. When a per- son occupies a house, and the neighbouring houses are un- occupied, the heat generated in the house is so rapidly radi- ated through the walls into the neighbouring houses that it becomes very difficult to keep the house warm; whereas, when the houses on both sides are occupied, the warmth of the house is considerably increased. The loss of heat from glazed roofs and ceilings, from skylights, and from metal roofs, such as are used in railway stations, is very consider- able.—Our Homes, and How to make them Healthy. HYGIENE OF WRITING IN SCHOOLS.—An interesting paper has recently been published .by Berlin on the influ- ence upon the eyes and the spines of school children which so simple a matter as the position of the copy book, in writ- ing may exert. It is based upon the report of a commis- sion appointed to investigate the effect of slanting writing in the schools of Wurtemberg. In writing or drawing with straight lines the visual axes move, by preference, in two general directions, vertical and horizontal, because in look- ing upwards or downwards, or to either side, their paths are straight, while in diagonal movements they describe a curve. It was discovered that 93 per cent, of the children who were under observation made the down-strokes in a direction nearly at right angles with that. of the base line—i.e., the line connecting the centres of rotation of the two eyes' and forming a triangle with the visual axis in convergence. This is done with the least strain when the copy book is tilted towards the left; when the child is compelled to write with the book parallel to the edge of the desk, he brings the base line perpendicular to the down-strokes by turning his head towards the right and twisting his spine. This contortion brings the eyes nearer to the page, and the left eye nearer to itAhan the right. In a discussion on this subject at the mWting of the Ophthalmic Society, at Heidelberg, Laqueur and Manz favoured the slanting system of writing with an oblique position of the book on the ground that it throws the work more on the flexor muscles of the forearm, which are naturally stronger than the extensors, and Berlin dwelt upon the fact that this system admits of greater rapidity of execution. The surface of the common slate being shiny, and presenting an insufficient contrast with the letters, necessitates a nearer approach of the eyes and consequent excessive accommodation and: convergence—the most im- portant factors in the development of myopia—and Cohn has therefore caused artificial white slates and special pencils to be manufactured, which offer the conveniences which have given the old articles universal currency among former generations of children without their hygienic defect.—The Lancet.

FRANKLIN'S KIM EXPERINENL—The many points of resemblance between lightning and electricity were noticed by early experimentalists. The flash of the electric spark resembles faintly a flash of lightning. A loud sound ac- companies each, and both have the power of setting on fire inflammable bodies. Lightning destroys animal life, rends bad or insufficient conductors, and is attracted by the pointed tops of trees or buildings; and all these effects may be produced on a small scale by the agency of electricity. We easily see, then, the great resemblance. It was left, however, for the celebrated Franklin to prove their identity, and, by drawing down the lightning from the clouds, to render his name for ever famous in the annals of electrical science. About the commencement of the year 1752 he be- gan to investigate the subject, and formed the idea of erect- ing, on a convenient building, a tall insulated conductor, terminating in a point, by which he expected to be able to collect the electricity from passing clouds. He was unable just at the time to carry out his purpose; he had, however, given a full explanation of his ideas in a letter to a friend, and acting upon this a French electrician succeeded in ob- taining sparks from an apparatus he had prepared in ac- cordance with these plans. Franklin was now tired of waiting for the erection of a building suitable for his pur- pose, and the idea occurred to him of trying his experiment with.a kite. He accordingly made a framework of two this laths crossing one another, and fixed the four corners of a silk handkerchief to their extremities.. A tail was affixed in the usual way, and a loop for the string to be fastened to. In order to collect the electricity he fixed a pointed wire to the upper end of one of the laths, and connected it with the string of the, kite. The other end of the string he fastened to the ring of a door-key, and fixed to this a piece of silk ribbon, so that he might hold it without the electri- city escaping, and ould draw sparks from the key. Thus equipped he went out one stormy day, accompanied only by his son, and having raised the kite on a common near Phila- delphia, awaited with almost breathless anxiety the result. Eor some time no effects whatever were seen—there was not the slightest appearance of any electrical disturbance; after a while, however, he obAerved some of the fibres of the cord bristling up; and on applying his knuckle to the key, to his intense delight he drew from it a spark. Soon after- wards a heavy shower6of rain fell, and the cord having thus become wetted, its conducting power was much increased, and, a rapid succession of sparks was given off from the key, by which a Leyden jar was charged, and other experi- ments performed which proved beyond doubt the absolute identity of lightning and electricity.—Cassell's .Popular Educator.
"OUR OLD NOBILITY." {l3:Wislied by Mr. B. J. Kibilewhite, 31, Tavistock-street London, WC., and reprinted by permission]. THE HAMILTONS.

The Hamiltons, like the Braces are of Norman extraction, and, like many great Scotch families, they owe almost every- thing to the direct favour of the Crown. The present Duke of Hamilton Bgures in the new Domesday Book as the owner in—
Bute 102,210 acres. . Lanark , 45,731 „ Suffolk Linlithgow 3,694 „ Stirling ... BlO. „

Total 157,a84 The gross rental is £140,526. Heaven and Mr. Padwick alone know what it is net. The estates are in the hands of trustees, and the Duke has an allowance. As the Duke is richer in titles than a Royal baby in Christian names, I will not recount them all. Suffice it to say that he is not only the Premier Peer of Scotland, but also Duke of Brandon in the Peerage of England, and that his peerages are sixteen in number.

Almost every acre of his vast domains in Scotland are derived directly by grants from the Crown. His pro- prietary rights are, of coarse, no more affected by this fact than by his unwise use of his enormous income. But we may well echo Oxenstiern's excjamation as to the little wisdom with which the world Is governed, when we reflect that our ancestors placed it within the power of their monarchs to grant to their favoured 'followers the powers for themselves and their descendants through all time to take tithe and toll of the produce of the soil of great tracts of land which have constantly grown in value owing to the industry of the whole population. The grantors, of course, could not foresee that the posterity of the grantee's would ultimately Aerive such immense revenues for doing nothing at all; but when I hear people lamenting that rents over a large part of Scotland have gone down about 25 per cent., I cannot greatly pity the ' people whose ancestors obtained everything for nothing. The chief seats of the Duke of Hamilton in Scotland are Hamilton Palace, Lanarkshire; Kinnell House, Linlithgow; Brodrick Castle, Isle of Arran, Buteshire. They form con- venient landmarks in tracing the history of the family. The Lanark and Linlithgow estate, have been, with short interruptions, in the possession of the Hamiltons ever since the days of King Robert Bruce. A. certain Sir Walter Hamilton having attached himself to that monarch, although be had previously sworn fealty to Edward 1., was rewarded with extensive grants of lands, particularly of the barony df Cadzow and the estate of Kinnell. On the former estate is now erected Hamilton Palace (called a palace because Mary, Queen of Scots, once resided there), one of the moat magnificent mansions in the kingdom. The Kinnell estate has in modern times %Nuked greatly increased value from its collieries. Kinnell House was for a time the residence of Dugald Stewart, at which place he died.

The greater part of the Hamilton estates are situated in Arran, the larger of the two islands which form the county of Bute. Arran was anciently a domain of the Scottish Crown, but in the fifteenth century it was given as a dowry to the Princess Mary on her marriage with Boyd, who was created Earl of Arran. During one of thefrequent domestic convulsions of the time Boyd had to flee for his life, and his estates, as well as those of his brother, were confiscated about 1408. Of the lands in question, Mr. Burton says : "These domains were all forfeited to the Crown, but were not, in the usual manner, put at the disposal of the Crown to give away at pleasure. The Act of Forfeiture rendered it incompetent for the Crown to alienate any of them with- out the consent of Parliament, and assigned the greater portion of them as. a principality for the heir of the Crown." This Act, however, did not long prevent the Hamiltons from obtaining possession of Arran. Boyd soon died in exile, and the head of the house of Hamilton married his widow, the Princess Mary. In 1503 —less than forty years after the Act had been passed—the eldest son of this marriage obtained a grant of the island from King James IV., and since that time it has been held by his descendants.

As if the Scottish Monarchs had not already done enough for the Hamiltons, I find that James VI. of Scotland, in the yea.r 1606, granted to the head of the family the lands of the rich Abbey of Aberbrothock, in Forfarshire, a proceed- ing which moved Archbishop Abbot to an humble remon- strance, in which, after expressing his disappointment that the property had not been devoted to ecclesiastical uses, he ventured to hope "that two out of the poor clergy would receive small holdings out of this great domain." The lands in,question, I believe, are not now in the possession of the Duke.of Hamilton.

The Suffolk estates are a modern acquisition. Easton in Suffolk was purchased by a Dutch officer, who was illegiti• mately descended from one of the Princes of Orange. He appears to have been a great favourite with William 111., by whore he was created Earl of Rochford. The last Earl of Rochford bequeathed these estates to a Duke of Hamilton, who was his half-brother. _ _

The history of the house of Hamilton is so constantly interwoven with the history of Scotland that it would be impossible for me to give even a brief epitome thereof. My business, however, is with the lands rather than with the men. The second Earl of Arran was created Duke of Chatelherault in France, with a French pension, in order to induce him to consent to the marriage of Queen Mary with the Dauphin. At one time they seemed likely to lose possession altogether in favour of a certain Captain Stewart, but the fourth Earl, uniting with other nobles in a military demonstration, obtained possession of the King, regained his lands, and was created Marquis of Hamilton. The third Marquis, an ardent Royalist, WAS created a Duke after the outbreak of the Civil War between Charles I. and his Par- Mamma, and was beheaded in Old Palace Yard in 1749. His son, the second Duke, was mortally wounded at the Battle of Worcester, and, leaving only daughters, the estates fell to his sister, Lady Anne Hamilton, who married Lord William Douglas. From that time the Dukes of Hamilton have been Douglas-Hamiltons. On the failure of the elder male line of the great house of Douglas, the Douglas- Hamiltons laid claim to the great Douglas estate, but after prolonged litigation they were finally defeated. Since the death of the fourth Duke, who was a leading statesman at the time of the Hanoverian settlement, the Hamiltons have I not been distinguished except as house builders, art collectors, and pat Alts of the turf. The male line of-the Hamilton family is represented by the Duke of Abercorn, who was a few-years ago created a Duke by the grace of our Sovereign Lord, Benjamin I. This branch of the Hamiltons, like the other, owes everything it possesses to the direct favour of the Crown, or to what it has saved out of its extensive grants. The Duke of Abercorn , owns in—
Tyrone M,919 acres. Donegal 15,860 „ Edinburgh • 1,500 „ Renfrew Sussex 8 IP

div.head: HOUSEHOLD PETS.
div.p: HOUSEHOLD PETS.

• Doas.—CARB or Prrrirs.—Owners 'ef puppies should, take care that each one gets its share of food, for a puppy at all out of sorts soon gets pushed aside. For a puppy that feeds badly there is nothing better than the remains of a roast leg of mutton from one's own table, as it will gnaw off the meat, and then amuse itself with the bone for a long time. It must be separated from any of its com- panions while it is busy with the bone. Lime water and bone meal should be given in every meal puppies have, as these help to build up the frames of the growing dogs. On cold nights a warm feed should always be given the last thing, both before the puppies are born and afterwards to the puppies. The following will be found a useful mix- ture :—Boiled rice, soaked bread, some coarse brown sugar mixed with milk, but if the latter is skim milk it should be well boiled first. A small quantity of linseed oil given con- stantly in the food will now do puppies much good, as it tends to rid them of worms, and its fattening properties will warm them. It will also be found useful for full-grown dogs that are low in condition, or at all mangy. Oil or grease are both to a certain extent necessary to resist cold. ;When dogs are the least out of sorts it is better to give them a dose of physic in order to clear the system, and as soon as puppies get to a fair size they should be brushed gently as well as the older dogs. Brushing cleans off any adhesive particles of their food, and also gets the scurf out of their coats, which is generally more or less present. After use the brushes should be cleaned by a few drops of spirits of turpedtine being init on teem, and than rubbed backwards and forward. Good bleached cabbage is a wry useful food for puppies, and if their blood is kept pure by vegetables they vill grow all the faster. _

gNAFFS--FITTINGS OF THE CAGE.—If Our plan for keep- ing the cage warm be too elaborate, the heat may be kept up by hot water tins or bottles placed inside the cage proper. They must be wrapped up in flannel or any similar material, to conserve the heat and prevent the snakes burn- ing themselves. A thick layer of non-conducting material should be placed below the tins 80 as to send the heat up- wards. It is always well to have a forked branch of a tree inside the cage, upon which the snakes can twist themselves, ,and this requires to be strong. The bottom part should be fitted into a hole of the perforated floor, and the upper part secured to the zinc at an angle of the top with a rivet or wire. An open pan of water will also be necessary for the snakes to bathe in, and this should always consist of tepid water. To the outside of the cage a cover must be fitted, , and this should be made so that any of the sides can be lifted up without disturbing the others. The way to do it is to make the pieces the same sizes as the top, sides, and ends of the cage, the upper side of each being fastened to the top piece. This will make a perfect cover, and any side or sides can be thrown on to the top instantly. The object of the cover is to keep in the warmth, and thus it is better to make it of thick flannel or felt. It may be taken off during the day if this is thought advisable, but should always be on at night, except in the warmest of weather. Sometimes thin and thick covers are used, in accordance with the season.

CATS.—BLINDxsisti,---An interesting account of a cat which became quite blind rather suddenly from cataract, when about four years old, is given by Mr. Hovey in The Scientific American. At first the cat would sit and mew most piteously; and when he tried to move about he met with all conceivable mishaps—ran against walls, fell down- stairs' stumbled over sticks, (Ix. If placed on the top rail of a fence, he would traverse its whole length, seeking vainly for a safe place to jump off. On being called lie would run about in a bewildered way. Ere long, however, Dido (so-called irrespective of gender) showed a power of adaptation to altered conditions. He became able to run downstairs at full speed, turning into the hall after the last step. In this process he went to one side on the top step till he felt the banisters touch his whiskers, and by these he was guided. One by one he made each familiar path a study, noted the location of each door, dm, and with such success that it often seemed as if sight had been restored ; but if any unexpected obstacle was placed in his way he showed, by running against it, that he was still quite blind. Dido seems as eager for war as he formerly was, and he even goes abroad in quest of adventures. His value as a mouser does not seem to be in the least diminished. Put into a closet where rats were suspected, he'ras found in the morn- ing mounting guard over a large rat he had killed. Dido's sense of smell is by no means acute, yet he uniformly chooses the shortest rOad home without reference to the path he may have taken in leaving the house. Once, when the grOund was thickly covered with snow, Mr. Hovey took Dido out a considerable distance, and, after taking a number of turns to bewilder him, tossed him on a drift, and awaited results. The animal turned his head in various directions , and mewed piteously I but, finding he was left to his own resources, he stood motionless for about a minute, and then, to the author's surprise, made his way directly through the untrodden snow to the house door, RABBITS.—CARE OF THE LITTER.—Doe rabbits that have been kept in vigorous health rarely suffer much at the birth of their young ones. They should be kept perfectly quiet then, and not be disturbed in any way. After the birth it may be necessary to look at the young ones; and even to touch them, but neither should be done except in cases of actual necessity. During the second day the sliding door into the living-room should be shut, and a peep .taken into the nest, in order to count the litter. Care must be used in handling, and any dead ones removed gently. If there are more than six young ones, two or three shoula be removed, and ether killed or given to a foster doe, leaving the largest and strongest with the mother herself. .For lops, and the higher bred varieties, four are quite enough for one doe, but five, or even six, may be allowed to the hardier breeds. The yowlg rabbits are bon witliout hair and quite blind, but in a Few days a silky fur begins to appear, and then they commence to grow with very great rapidity. When about a fortnight old they begin to crawl about the nest, and will ' come to the feeding trough soon after. Great care is needed in rearing the young rabbits, as much loss is experienced owing to accident and other ways. Ground oats should be given as soon as they begin to eat. Too much green-sluff should be avoided, and if what is given is placed in the rack the youngsters will not come in for much. As soon as the young rabbits begin to come out of the nest the whole may be removed, and a fresh supply of bedding, in the shape of dry hay and straw, substituted. A very important matter is also the feeding of the doe. When there is a large litter the tax upon her strength is enormous, and she should be fed accordingly. Corn should be given to any extent, and also as much succulent green-stuff as she will eat, such things as bread and meal, boiled potatoes mixed with meal or ground oats, all are beneficial, and the food must be very generous.

MICE.—TEACRING TRICKS.—The teaching of tricks to any animal is a question of time and patience, but there are some animals quicker than others in learning. The first thing to overcome is fear, both in the animal and teacher, and until this is done no success can reasonably be expected. Constant acquaintance is neapssary for this, handling care- fully, but firmly, and, above all things, feeding the subjects immediately after they have received their lesson, which is better short than long. When the animals are tamed the lessons should be commenced, and, as all of them partake of the same nature, it is only necessary to describe one, viz., bringing a flag down from the top of a pole. For this pur- pose a round stick, about 18 inches in length, is required, and a small paper flag or two—the stick made of a match, and the flag half an inch square. The pole should be roughened with some course sand paper, and the handle of the flag scented with a drop of oil of aniseed before placing it in position on the top of the pole. The mouse must be allowed to smell the flag before it is placed in position, and in nine cases out of ten it will at once ascend to the flag and bring it down. If it does not do so the same process should be gone through again, and, it not effective, a flag that has tallow on the stick should be substituted. Each time the flag is brought down a grain or two of canary seed should be given the animal, and if these lessons are per- sisted in for a week or two that trick will be effectually learned, and another can be taken in hand. Always give lessons before feeding, and every time the mouse is success- ful give a reward, but never give sugar, as that induces liver disease. White, lavender, and fawn coloured mice are easiest to train.

NOTE.—In order to help readers of The Examiner over any difficulties they may meet with, the writer of the above notes will be pleased to answer any questions relating to Dogs, Pigeons, Cage Birds, Rabbits, and Pets, their management or disease', that may be put to him. These must be concise, yet contain all impori ant particulars, and be addressed to Alva," Eramv,er Office, Warrington, and contain the name and address of the correspondents, not necessarily for publication, but as a :uarantee of good faith.

A busy doctor sent in a certificate of death the other day, and accidentally signed his name in the space for "Cause of Death." The registrar says he wishes the profession would be as accurate generally. A medical student at Bowdoin College once asked the late Professor Parker Cleaveland if there were not some more recent works on anatomy than those in the College library. "Young man," said the Professor, "there have been very few new bones added to the human body during the last ten years."

A countryman stepped into a fruit shop and invested in two pennyworth of ckastnuts. In half an hour he returned and handed the proprietor one of the nuts. "What does this mean ?" asked the dealer. "Well," remarked the cus- tomer, "that is the only sound chestnut I found in the pint, and so thought you put it in by mistake. I am an honest man, and don't want to take a mean advantage of a fellow."

"CAVALRY" BOOTS.—A soldier of an infantry regiment at Nashville, being in need of a pair of boots, and not being able to draw them from the Quartermaster, went into the shop of a Jew dealer, and asked the price of some that were lying on the counter. " Dese poots ish nine dollars," said the deal\er. "Can't give it; they are too dear," said the soldier. "My grashus !" said the Jew, " dey costs me shust eight dollar and seventy-five cents in New York. You must let a potty make a little sometings. Here Shon (to a boy) pring de invoice of dese fine poots, and I show de shentle- mans de price." The invoice was produced, and after some higgling, which brought down the price considerably, the soldier bought a pair and started off. He had walked only the length of the street, however, when the soles came off., Of course, he at once returned to the Jew and branded him in strong military language as a swindler and imposter. The Jew looked up in amazement at his customer, and, putting on an air of well-feigned astonishment, replied :- "Oh, dem ish not infantry poots; I thought you was a cavalry man."

Claud, fourth son of the Hamilton who was created Duke of Chatelheriult, obtained from James VI. a grant of the barony of Paisley. The Hamiltons, by the way, also obtained possession of the rich Abbey of Paisley, which they subsequently sold. I presume that the lands they still hold in Renfrew are a remnant of these grants. The eldest eon of Lord Paisley was created Earl of Abercorn—a place with which, I believe, the Hamiltons have now no local con- nection—by the same monarch. But James had:nor come into possession of the Crown of England and Ireland, and he made to the Earl of Abercorn extensive grants of land in the barony of Strabane. A younger brother of this Earl was made Constable of Toome Castje, Antrim for life, and had a grant of 400 acres in Longford and 2,000 acres in the barony of Strabane. Another younger son also had grants of lands in Tyrone and Tipperary, and, after the Restoration, of other lands in Cork, besides several lucrative offices. The eldest son of this last, who was one of the favourite courtiers of Charles 11., obtained a grant of an estate in Meath, and £9OO per annum out of the firstfruits and tenths of the dioceses of St. David's, Hereford, Oxford, and Worcester. His eldest son, who was one of the Privy Councillors of James 11., went over to the side of the Prince of Orange, and assisted in the relief of Londonderry. By this time the eldest line had died out, and the Earldom of Abercorn was held by a descendant of the third son of the Duke of Chatel- herault. He held fast to James 11., fought for him at the Boyne, and was soon after killed. He was attainted, but his brother obtained a reversal of the attainder. The latter leaving no issue, the lands and titles passed to the Captain Hamilton who had assisted in relieving Londonderry. I have not space to mention the various civil, military, and ecclesiastical offices subsequently held by this branch of the Hamilton family. One of them, by the way, held no less than six rectories and vicarages in the diocese of Armagh. About the year 1745, the Earl ,of Abercorn purchased the estate of Dnddingston, in the county of Edinburgh, which had passed by marriage from the Lauderdale to the Argyll family, and erected a mansion thereon at a cost of £30,000. In 1790, the ninth Earl was created a Marquis, and his grandson was, in 1868, created a Duke. In addition to the above, there are ten other Hamiltons, who own between them about 140,000 acres more, chiefly in Ireland and Scotland, and of most of whose acquisitions I have no doubt an equally satisfactory account may be given. I shall certainly be quite safe in affirming that nearly the whole of the 367,000 acres possessed by this fortunate clan has been at some time or other obtained by lavish grants from the Crown.

div.p: An Irishman, bound over to keep the peace against all her Majesty's subjects, exclaimed, "Then heaven help the first foreigner I meet !" Morrow is a town of some importance, about forty miles from Cincinnatti. A new porter on the railway, who did not know the names of the stations, was approached by a stranger the other day, while standing by a train at the Cin- cinnati Station :—" Does this train go to Morrow to-day ?" "No," said the porter, who thought the stranger was mak- ing game of him; "it goes to-day yesterday week after next." "You don't understand me," persisted the stranger. , "I want to go to Morrow." "'Well, why don't you wait until to-morrow then, and not come bothering around to- day? You can go to-morrow or any other day you please:" "Won't you answer a civil question civilly? Will this train go to-day to Morrow ?" "Not exactly. It will go to- day and come back to-morrow." As the gentleman who wanted to go to Morrow was about to leave in disgust, another employe, who knew the station alluded to, came along, and gave him the required information. • THE STATE OF IRELAND. THE CROSSMAGLEN CONSPIRACY. The trial of the first batch of members of the" Patriotic Brotherhood" for conspiracy to murder was concluded at Belfast on Good Friday. In his summing up Mr. Justice Lawson directed the attention of the jury to the considera- tion of the question whether the evidence of the informer Duffy was corroborated by the" minute book" relating to the Crossmaglen branch of the Assassination Society. This book recorded speeches by the organiser Burns, who said he was an emissary of O'Donovan Rossa, and thA P. J. Sheri• dan was the organiser for county Mayo. His lordship pointed out among other entries in the book the following : —" At the request of the Land League, conveyed through Thomas Murphy, men have been sworn in specially to kill Mr. Brookes." After a consultation of about three hours and a half, the jury convicted all the prisoners. Sentence was deferred. The trials were resumed on Monday, before Mr. Justice Lawson. Six other men, alleged members of the "Patriotic Brotherhood," were indicted for conspiracy to murder orl the same charge as that upon which Nugent and others were convicted on the Friday previous. The prisoners' names are Peter Devlin, Patrick Finegan, Patrick Geogheghan, James Hanratty, Peter Coleman, and Bernard Smyth. There was a seventh name included in the indictment, that of John Donnelly, but in his case the Crown entered a wile prosepi. The prisoners all pleaded not guilty. The trial concluded on Tuesday, when the jury, after consulting for an hour and a half, returned a verdict of guilty on all the counts. Sentence in this, as in the previous case, was deferred.

The members of the Patriotic Brotherhood who have been convicted were on Wednesday sentenced by Mr. Justice Lawson. When the first batch had been placed in the dock the learned Judge, addressing them, said no more extraordinary case had ever been investigated in a court of justice, and the proceedings of a notorious association had been exhibited to public view by the discovery of a record, of which the prisoner Watters was the writer and custo- dian. His Lordship said he considered this prisoner the worst in the dock. He was the teacher in a National school, and it had been clearly proved that all the threatening notices were in his handwriting. He thought there could not possibly be a worse case than this; he should therefore pass the extreme sentence which the law assigned to the offence, viz., ten years' penal servitude upon Nugent, Daly Kelly, and Watters. He did not think M‘Bride was quite as active a member as the other four, and therefore he passed Ur )fl him a sentence of seven years' penal servitude. O'Hanlan, who at first gave information to the authorities, but afterward changed his mind and then attempted to escape from the country, received a sentence of five years' penal servitude. Six other prisoners, Peter Delvin, Patrick Finnegan, Patrick Geoghegan, James Hanratty, Peter Coleman, and Bernard Stnith, were then placed in the dock, and in addressing them Mr. Justice Lawson remarked that the object of the new society was to overthrow English rule. Now that the veil had been thrown aside he wondered if the people would learn sense. The elements out of which the country was to be regenerated by the process of murder and assassination were a few small farmers, tailors, labourers, and National schoolmasters. He wondered if the people of Ireland would ever learn the futility, the vice, and tho folly of assassina- tion. The six prisoners were then sentenced each to ten years' penal servitude. As they were being removed one called out, " O'Hanion did it all." THE ROYAL IRISH CONSTABULARY. The Dublin Freeman's Journal states that a number of important changes are about to be made in the organisa- tion of the Royal Irish Constabulary, and also in that of special resident magistrates. These latter will cease to exist, but there will be provincial inspectors-general with all the powers of the present specials, and far more besides. The Inspector-General in the Castle will cease to exist, and in his place there will be four provincial inspectors, in Ulster, Leinster, Munster, and Connaught respectively, who will have the same authority over the o%oers and men in their respective provinces as the Inspector-General has at present over the officers and rne.n in all Ireland. Among other changes county inspectors will cease to exist, so will head constables, though the latter will be retained under another designation.
The Countess Spencer arrived in Dublin, on Tuesday, from England. Special precautions were adopted by the police authorities at the station and along the route to the Viceregal residence.

• The Viceroy of Ireland has commuted the death sentence passed at Kildare on a woman named Keogh for the mur- der of two of her children to penal servitude for life. The crime was a very horrible one, but everyone will rejoice that the sentence is not to be carried out. In the case of Michael P. Boyton, who was arrested at Kildare on Tuesday, under the Crimes Act, it may be stated that, as on a former occasion it was decided by the Ameri- can Minister in London that the prisoner was not an American citizen, no action in the present instance will be taken on his behalf by the representative of the United States Government.

It is stated that nearly 950,000 persons in Ireland now speak the Irish language against 81,800 in 1871, though in the meantime the population has decreased by a quarter of a million. The Society for the Preservation of the Irish Language' which last year distributed 62,000 elementary Irish books, claims to be largely instrumental in reviving a knowledge of the language. The legality of the late Tipperary election is,it is stated,about to be tested. It will be remembered that the High Sheriff decided the nomination papers of Mr. Richard Bagwell and Mr. Stephen Moore were informal because they were signed by the same assenting electors, and he therefore declared Mr. Mayne duly elected. A petition is about to. be lodged against the return of Mr. Mayne, it being the opinion of counsel that the paper of Mr. Bagwell, the first handed in to the sub-sheriff, was perfectly valid, and that its rejection by the returning officer was illegal. We are informed that the description of the mysterious "No 1" has been substantiated by a message from New York, where the affidavits for his extradition are said to have arrived. The person in question was said to have been in Dublin a few weeks ago, where he was under police 'surveillance, but escaped, and passing to Havre, embarked from that port in, a French steamer to New York, where he arrived on the 7th inst. He is now stated to be safely quartered in a populous part of Mexico, where he has many friends, and among them a brother who holds a high posi- tion in the Church in an adjacent State. A correspondent, who gives the name of the mysterious individual as Mr. P—r T—n, says many persons will know who is re- ferred to, and will remember the highly respectable firm of ! stationers he represented. The "National Testimonial" to Mr. Parnell now amounts to a considerable sum. One of the latest and most important °contributors is Dr. Butler, Bishop of Limerick, who sends, together with a cheque for £lO, a very bitter denunciation of England and Englishthen. The right rev, prelate says that Mr. Parnell "has won for himself the bitter hatred of Ireland's enemies poured out upon him in the House of Commons and in the English press." Herein, he adds, lies for Ireland the crowning proof of Mr. Parnell's patriotism, "for the instinct by which the tiger knows and springs upon its prey is not truer or more ferocious than that which actuates the Parliament of England and her press when an Irish patriot of the genuine stamp is to be hunted down !" And yet this same tigerish Parliament and press has, it seems, even according to Dr. Butler, consented to "an in- stalment of justice—such as it is—conveyed to us in the Land Act of '81."

Further information is given by a New York correspond- ent respecting the extradition warrants that have been for- warded to America in connection with the Phoonix Park as- sassinations and the conspiracies in Ireland. Papers have been sent out with a view to the arrest of four persons—Ed- ward Fabey, P. J. Tynan, P. J. Sheridan, and Regan, the three first named being charged with complicity in the Phoenix Park murders, and Regan with an agrarian murder. Tynan has already been described as "Number One," and his family reached New York on Wednesday. Mr. Frank Byrne and his wife and family have also landed at New York, but as their arrival had not been anticipated, they drove quietly to their lodgings. In New York, the corre- spondent remarks, the informations against the men whose extradition is desired are considered insufficient- and in especial need of corroboration by independent witnesses. In Tynan's case the affidavits are sworn by the two Careys, Mullett, and WElroy.

div.head: RAINHILIT ASYLUM.
div.p: RAINHILIT ASYLUM.

The adjourned annual session of county justices was held at Preston on Thursday. Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P., presided, and there were 29 other magistrates present.—Mr. BLECKLY proposed that for the purpose of carrying out the neces- sary work in connection with the annexe of the Rainhill Asylum, and the completion of such works, a sum not ex- ceeding X,46,000 be granted, to be raised under the provisions of the -Lunatic Asylums Act, 1853, on mortgage of the county rates. In March, 1881, an application was made to the court for a sum of £120,000, in respect of a contract made for the purpose of erecting an annexe to Rainhill, un- der a resolution of the court passed in 1877, and at that time plans were preduced and passed by the court. Under that contract, however, the water supply, the gas works, the erection of boundary walls and several other matters were not provided for, and it was to do these works that the money was required. The cost of furnishing also was not included in the contract, nor in the present , amount.—The motion being seconded, Mr. RALPH ASSHETON (Clitheroe) said he had a considerable objection to it. Per- haps it was too late to make any alterations in regard to that particular annexe, but it struck him as being rather unsatisfactory that the original estimate and vote . for a building of that kind should not contain estimates for work which it was perfectly clear must be done and paid for. It was almost as absurd to leave the works mentioned out of the estimate, as it would be to leave out the roof or the flooring.—ln reply to questions, Mr. BLECKLY said the number of additional patients that the annexe would accom- modate was 1,040, and the coat per head on the building, including furniture, clothing and other necessaries, would be under £2oo.—The motion was carried.

MISCELLANEOUS.

A prize fight, in which there were 67 roundee, is reported from the Alfreton police division. The sale of the Sunderlansl library lealised a total of fe56,581. A boiler in a .weaving shed at Chorley, belonging to Alderman Savill, exploded on Monday, killing two persons and severely injuring eight others. P. De Civry, the French champion, won the 50-mile bicycle championship race at Leicester on Saturday, J. Mac, of Birmingham, being second. There were 10 competitort. It is reported at Poitsmouth that Rear Admiral Herbert, Director of Naval Ordnance, will be anointed to succeed the late Admiral M'Crea, as superintendent of Portsmouth Dockyard. It is stated that as a consequence of the notice given by the employers in the Huddersfied eiistrict to introduce a new Scale, there are now over 4,000 persons in the weaving trade out on strike, and that there is no prospect of a settlement of the dispute. 'Pour sea captains belonging to Montrose and two other left their ships in the Firth of Forth to come ashore. I.llieY did not reach land, and the body of one of them "aving been washed ashore, it is concluded that all perished in the storm which prevailed. The vestry meeting at Holy Trinity Church, Bordesley. Was held on Monday, and gave rise to a scandalous scene, The Rev. R. W. Enraght took part in the proceedings, which Were so disorderly'that the police were compelled to clear the church. The explosion of a fog signal which some mischievous Person had placed in one of the streets of Bolton is said to have caused an extraordinary "scare" in the immediate oeighbourhood, it being at first supposed that Fenians were at work in the town. It is stated on good authority that the Government has decided to add to the Criminal Investigation Department of Scotland Yard a section of police whose duty will be to Watch the movements of suspected agents of secret political organisations. rho Right Hon. Earl Fitzwilliam opened a bazaar at Dewsbury, on Monday, in aid of the funds of the new infir- teary. The cost of the building is £17,000, of which £12,000 has been raised. The present effort is to realise the remaining £4,000, and the bazaar will remain open during the rest of the week. The river Blvth, near Southwold, in. Suffolk, is now dammed at its mouth by nature. The easterly gale of the last few days has so lashed the waves on that coast that banks of shingle three yards thick, a score or two wide, and hundreds long, may be seen between Southwold and ancient Dunwich." One such has closed the Blyth. The Easter vestry meeting in connection with St. Jude's, Liverpool, was on Monday the scene of somewhat stormy Proceedings. The vicar, the Rev. E. J. A. Fitzroy, war Much hissed and interrupted, and when he was leaving the building at the conclusion of the business of the meeting he Was physically assailed and subjected to some rough osuage. For smashing the altar fittings and otherwise disturbing the congregation at St. Paul's Cathedral, on Saturday, an inventor and patentee named George Campian, who refused to give his address was on Monday fined £5 and costs at the Mansion House Police Court. The prisoner made a long, rambling and incoherent statement, bristling with Bible (Notations, in answer to the charge. In accordance with arrangements made on Saturday, a small number of the colliers of Messrs. Crawley Brothers, in the Forest of Dean, resumed work on Monday morning. Threats have been employed to intimidate those who were disposed to resume work, and upon the gates leading to the colliery has been written, "Blood, blood, blood. If you go in to work you had better make your wills." COCKFIGHTING IN THE BLACK COUNTRY.—On Monday aeveral pairs of cocks were fought for heavy stakes in several districts of the Black Country, but owing to the secrecy Ilene by the promoters of these brutal sports the police have been unable to detect any of the offenders. On Monday Morning the police discovered in a van travelling between Blackheath and HaAesowen a large number of cocks which had been specially trained for fighting. The carter would not divulge the names of the owners. The examination of the books of 12 selected bar iron firms fa South Staffordshire under the new sliding scale arrange- ments for the regulation of wages concluded on Saturday. The result is that puddlers' wages will be fixed for the next three months, April 2nd to June 30th, at the rate of 7s 9d Per ton, and millmen's wages in proportion, which is.equal to a reduction of 6d per ton to puddlers and 5 per cent. to mill- Men. This declaration will regulate ironworkers' wages throughout the whole of England, with the exception of Middlesborough district and South Wales. THE MINISTERIAL CHANGES.—The Daily Hews says : "The most important of recent Ministerial changes will lead to an increased charge in the estimates for the coming onancial year. As combining the offices of the First Lord of the Treasury and the Chancellor of the Exchequer Mr. Gladstone drew £7,500 a year. The salaries of the two offices now separated will be at the rate of £lO,OOO a year. The department of the Treasury remains relieved of pay- ment of £l,OOO a year, as Mr. Herbert Gladstone continues to hold the office and do the work of a junior Lord without salary." At Glasgow, Mr. Rothery, Wreck Commissioner, has can- celled the certificate of James Burns, master of the ship Falcon, of Arundel, which was burned after leaving the Clyde. The evidence showed that the utmost want of dis- cipline had prevailed on board, and that the vessel was allowed to drift about with no one irt charge. She was at _ length observed from the coast to be on fire, and when coast- guardsmen boarded her several of the crew were drunk, and the master himself was the worse for liquor. " The rum Cask had been emptied into a bucket, out of which the crew were supplied with the liquor in jngfuls." A correspondent says an important step has been taken at a largely-attended meeting of the committee of the Congre- gational College, Brecon, which may initiate a revolution in the theological colleges of Wales. By it the subscribers of the college are recommended at their next yearly meeting to consent to the students being henceforth sent to the Univer- sity College at Aberystwitle for their arts course, and for them later to return to Brecen for their theological course 91113'. The establishment of the proposed university colleges in North and South Wales will probably lead to the adoption (If a similar course by most of the Nonconformist colleges in the principality. TERRIBLE TRAGEDY. Another terrible tragedy is re- Ported from the New Cut, a district of Southern London 'which has long had an unenviable notoriety. After being out all day with his friends, a bricklayer named Smith went home and found his wife kind two children asleep. He awoke his wife, and irolne,d her to give him money, with Which he went out to buy brandy. The woman then appears tO have got up and, with one of her husband's razors, to have killed her eldest daughter and inflicted a terrible Wound upon her baby's throat. Then she was smitten with the thought of what she had done, and, taking up the child, she ran into a neighbour's house and told what had occurred. The woman has been arrested for the murder of the elder girl, the younger being still alive. NINE MILE RACE BETWEEN BLIND MEN.—On Saturday afternoon two blind men, John Thomas Hindle, aged 23 Years, and Edward Burnes, aged 35, started to walk a match for £lO a side, from the lamp at the bottom of Preston New- lead, Blackburn, to the Shooter's Arms Inn, Park-read, . rreston. The two men set off at five minutes past three, and went on pretty well together until they were about three miles on the road, when Burnes fell heavily, Hindle teing then a good bit ahead. When Burnes was taken up e was knocked out of both wind and time, and as he 'seemed so much distressed, he was placed in the vehicle ,Which was accompanying the competitors and conveyed to leresten, where Hindle arrived at the goal at two minutes Past five, three minutes under two hours, the.distance Walked being about nine miles. Hindle, of course,Zwon the stake, LOsS OF A SCOTCH PILOT BOAT AND FIVE LIVES.— buring the gale last Thursday week, a distressing occur- ,rence happened off the coast of Aberdeenshire. The pilot coat Christian left Fraserburgh that evening, in company with another pilot boat, for the purpose of meeting a vessel b°llnd from Peterhead for Fraserburgh. There was a con- test between the two boats as to which should reach the !hip first. The Christian lost, and the other boat returned Praserburgh in safety with the ship. The Christian, in rounding Scotston Head on her way home, was caught by a Null and swamped. All the occupants. five in number, Were drowned. They consisted of Alexander Noble, the Pilot and owner of the boat, and his two sons; Alexander Slaehan, an apprentice cooper, and John Buchan, seaman. With the exception of the pilot Noble, all the unfortunate °sew were young men and unmarried. MußnEnous ATTACK ON A LADY.—On -Saturday after- roo, a desperate attempt to murder a married lady named ene Strangeways was made at Scarborough by a Leeds Rentleman of independent means, named Joseph Gill. Mr. eeill seems to have been on intimate terms with his victim's feruilY, but for some reason had been denied the house. On taturday, lie went to Mr. Fox Strangeways's residence, in eigrave-crescent, and in the absence of that gentleman was refused an interview with Mrs. Fox Strangeways. There- Von he forced his way into the lady's presence, attacked and inflicted two dangerous cuts and a stab in her throat. ee'eue lady with difficulty summoned her servant to her '4lBi, stance, and Mr. Gill tlien made off. He was, however, tansequently apprehended at the Pavilion Hotel, where he _ad been staying, and lodged in prison. He effected his ier:.!alee from the police station on Monday morning. He was icaptured two hours afterwards, taken before the magis- ates, and remanded for a week. ISt l4 po,irt• —RIGHT AT GLASGOW.—Mr. Bright was on Good at e`Ley Presented with the freedom of the city of Glasgow great meeting held in tne City Hall. There was a large t"ioTher of influential gentlemen on the platform to greet the hon. gentleman, who on his appearance was received ,vfe-eee mach enthusiasm, the whole audience cheering and aril:lg handkerchiefs for two cr three minutes, and the earn Pealing forth "See the conquering hero comes."
