The Great Harwood Colliery ts stopped through the mine being flooded with water. On Tuesday night the Sktm yacht Eagle, 30 tons register, belonging to Mr. Kellen Johnstone, was lost off St. Abb's Head. The crew of th:ree men were drowned. At a meeting of Braackowners, held in Hull on Wednesday to organise a relief fund, it was stated that in the recent storms 180 liven had been lost, and property valued at £50,000. In the week ending March 24, 1883, the failures gazetted numbered 218,an increase of 12; the totals for portion of year to March 24, 1883, are 2,706, a decrease of 9.—Stubs' Mercantile Gazette. John Woods, driver of the Edinburgh train which collided with another train near Eglinton station, Glasgow, when four rersons were killed and many injured, was on Monday committed for trial on a charge of culpable and reckless driVing. Lord Rosebery has purchased, for the sum of £250, the reservoir and water supply of the town of Queensferry, which was put up for sale in consequence of the bankruptcy of the burgh, and has banded it over to the Town Courfcil as a gift to the community. Alarm has again been excited in Skye. The agents of MacLeod's trustees have received information that the crofters of Glendale have resolved to pay no rent till they get possession of Waterstein, and, further, it is stated they have resolved not to surrender the fourth man wanted for the breach of interdict. Sir Wilfrid Lawson replying to a correspondent, who ex- pressed regret tat Christmas Day and Good Friday had not been brought within the provisions of the Welsh Sunday Closing Act, writes :—" I agree with you in regretting the legal decision to which you refer. I shall be very glad if anything can be done to make the law more satisfactory.''' SHORT TIME IN- THE ENGINEERING TRADES.—The operatives at the Wolverhampton engine works of the Great Western Railway, numbering some 800, on Wednesday received intimation that they will quickly be put upon short time. The works will be closed from Friday evening each week until after breakfast on the following Monday morning. MARRIAGE Or MR. WM. BRIGHT. Mr. WM. Leatham Bright, second son of Mr. John Bright, M.P., was married on Wednesday' at Carshalton Parish Church, to Miss Isabella M'lvor Tylor, third daughter of Mr. Alfred Tylor, of Shep- ley House, Carshalton, in the presence of a large number of Mends both of the bride and bridegroom. Canon Farrar,D.D., of St. Margaret's, Westminster, officiated. The 'question of what is a bona-fide travaler was before the magistrates at Llangollen, on Wednesday. Since the passing of the Sunday Closing Act, it has been held by the police that a person who had travelled three miles for the purpose of obtaining drink was not a bona-fide traveller, the contention on the other hand being, that travelling that distance whether on business or pleasure, entitled a person to be served with refreshment. The Bench took the latter view.

Mr. Batt, Q.C., MT., whose appointment to succeed Sir Robert Phillimore was prematurely announced, has been offered and has accepted the vacant judgeship. Mr. Charles Parker Butt was born in 1830, and was called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1854, and was made a Queen's counsel in 1868. He was a member of the Northern Circuit, and has been leader in the Admiralty Court for several years past, and has been engaged in most of the leading mercantile cases heard at the Guildhall. His appointment causes a vacancy in the representation of Southampton. LORD GREY ON THE TRANSVAAL BUSINESS.—Lord Grey has occupied more than a column and a half of the leading journal in expatiating upon the wickedness of the Govern- ment in entering into a Convention with the Boers of the Transvaal, under which this country is pledged to perform certain duties to certain natives within the Transvaal borders, and then failing to carry out the Convention on the ground that to do so would be expensive. Stated in this way the Government's conduct is, of course, very re- prehensible; but Lord Grey has assumed all through his long letter the only point in dispute. The Government deny that they are under any obligation to defend the Bechuanas from the freebooters by whom they have been molested, and the Government may be supposed to under- stand the terms of their own Convention at least as well as Lord Grey. Until Lord Grey, therefore, can prove his pre- mises, his whole argument and denunciations go for nothing. ALLEGED ITOLEGAL DETENTION OF A WIFE. -- At Hammersmith, London, on Tuesday' Mr. William Mathias Lancaster, of Richmond-row, Earl's Court, and Mr. Thomas Durant, jun., solicitor, Guildhall-chambers, were summoned for conspiring together to deprive Gertrude Lancaster, wife of the former, of her liberty, alleging that she was of un- sound mind. From the evidence of Mrs. Lancaster it appeared that on the 6th instant, at the request of her husband, she went to Aylesbury and remained the night at a house in Walton-street. There were two women in the house, who tried to prevent her leaving next day, saying they had orders from Mr. Lancaster and Mr. Durant to keep her there. Witness, however, managed to escape, and sent a telegram to a friend, who came to her aid. For the defence there was an allegation of improper conduct on the part of complainant with a gentleman at Brussels. Mr. Shiel, the magistrate, thought the case was one for the Divorce Court, • but eventually, granted an adjournment. THE OUTPUT OF COAL FOR THE YEAR.—A return recently issued shows that the output of coal in the United Kingdom during the last year amounted to 156,499,977 tons, which, compared with the output in 1881, shows an increase of 2,315,677 tons; Scotland, 20,515,134 tons; and Ireland, 127,777 tons. Taking Lancashire, north and east, we find it set down for 9,749,363 tons; West Lancashire for 10,031,282 tons. For Derbyshire the output is set down for 1,586,554 tons; Flintshire for 834,577 tons; and Cheshire 755,000 tons. There were 503,987 persons employed in and about the mines under the Coal Mines Act. Of these 406,192 were employed under ground, and 97,795 above ground; of the latter number 4,652 were females. As com- pared with the respective numbers employed in the year 1881, this shows an increase of -8,510 persons. The fatal accidents during last year numbered 876, and the deaths occasioned thereby were 1,126, showing an increase on this head, as compared with 1881, of 32 in the number of lives lost, although there were 8,510 persons employed last year more than in 1881. The return shows a diminution of 33 mines abwork. Lancashire, North and East, employed 31,607 persons of both sexes, West Lancashire 30,397, Denbighshire 6,740, Flintshire 3,358,- and Cheshire 2,659 persons in the various coal mines last year. • THE " GREA.T SEER OF ENGLAND" SENT TO GAOL.— At the Birmingham Quarter Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. Stratford Dugdale, Q C., James Hartwell, alias Meth- tattoo, "the Great Seer of England," alias Anna Ross, "the Seeress of New York," was charged with defrauding numer- ous girls and women throughout the kingdom by selling " Love Charms," " Spells," "Seven Years' Future Life, and "Marriage, and other Particulars," with intent to de- fraud.—The Counsel for the Prosecution characterised the case as the most extraordinary fortune-telling imposture ever discovered, hundreds of women and girls in all parts of the kingdom, believing, as was shown by their letters, that the prisoner was really a "dealer in magic and spells," and possessed the talismearic art.—Miss Elizabeth Grant, a young lady of Leicester, testified to paying prisoner different sums of money in order to gain "a wealthy. Adonis, and live happy ever afterwards." The police proved three previous con4eictions against the prisoner for carrying on the business of a sybil twice in London and once at Daventry.—The prisoner, in the course of a long address, contended that he was not aware he was breaking the law by-selling talismanic charms. That was the opinion of a learned counsel -whom he consulted on the matter some time since, and to whom he paid five guineas for the advice. He further stated that he was descended from Lord Lovel, as jewellery in his house in London, which was left to his mother, and an "old oak chest," bearing family inscriptions, would testify. If he were allowed to leave the court he would at once go abroad.—The Recorder said he thoroughly believed that the prisoner did not know he was breaking the law, but only sailing as near as he could do. Tie sen- tence would be nine months' imprisonment as a rogue and vagabond. THE HOME SECRETARY AND Mn. W. H. SMITH, M.P. —Mr. W. H. Smith is not usually a thoughtless or reckless speaker, but at a recent Tory meeting in Westminster he launched out against Liberal Administrations and Liberalism in general in terms which were curiously inaccurate and audacious. One of his remarks was that the Government had brought matters to such a pass that it was unsafe to walk the streets of London or to go to bed except under police protection, and ke further declared that " this state of disturbance, of repression, of anxiety, of alarm, and of destruction of property is all connected—apparently insepar- ably connected—with a Liberal Government." Very many ignorant Tories will endorse every word that Mr. Smith said, and as they know no better they are perhaps excusable; but Mr. W. H. Smith does know, or should know' that his charges are as baseless as they are ridiculous. This Sir William Harcourt, in reply to Mr. Hugh Shield, who has questioned him on the subject, very clearly proves. Taking up the average Tory idea, which was championed by Mr. W. H. Smith, that all the present ills of Ireland and the disorder to which they have led have resulted from the Liberal policy, of which the Irish Church Act was the starting point, the Home Secretary goes back to 1867, and shows that in that yew.. under a Tory adminis- tration, a more alarming state of things existed with regard to Leland than at, this present moment. In that year there occurred in succession the Fenian raid on Chester Castle, the Fenian rising in Ireland, the murder of the policeman in Manchester, and the Clerkenwell explosion; and in December of the same year the London police force was increased by 1,000 men, which was relatively four times as large an increase as has now been thought neces- sary. And in addition to this, vestries and other bodies were invited to promote the swearing In of special con- stables, of whom before March, 1868.—while Lord Beacons- field was still in power more than 113,000 had been en- rolled. These facts pretty effectually dispose of Mr. W. H. Smith's assertion that Irish disorders are "inseparably con- nected" with Liberal Administrations. Mr. W. 11. Smith has published a " reply "to Sir W. Harcourt's letter. The right bon. member for Westminster makes a point of the alleged fact that the Conservative Government found Fenianism in existence when they came into power. He omits all mention of the equally important fact that, after being six years in office Lord Beaconsfield, in the famous letter to the Duke of Marlborough, painted the condition of Ireland in the most gloomy colours, and referred to the operation of the disloyal societies as threatening to bring about a state of things "worse than pestilence and famine." •

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH Bl 1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH Bl 1883

Mr. Li"ley, Surveyer,General of Her Majesty's Customs, is about to retire from the public service. The Xing and Queen of Holland are about to visit Eng- land, and remain in this country for a fortnight. William Rutherford Benn was charged before a magis- trate, at Derby, on Tuesday, with the murder of his father, the Rev. Julius Benn, Congregational minister, at Matlock Bridge, and was remanded for eight days. At Tuesday's meeting of the National Union of Elemen- tary Teachers a resolution was passed "condemning the sentimental objections raised by some people to the legiti- mate use of .corporal punishment" in schools. A man named Clere, who had attempted to commit suicide, and had been pronounced insane by doctors, on Tuesday, murdered his child, aged five years, by cutting its throat at Washfield, near Tiverton. At a meeting held in Dundee, on Tuesday, for the forma- tion of branches of the Scottish Farmers' Alliance in For- farshire and Fifeshire, a resolution was passed expressing the hope that the measure of the Government for giving , tenants legal compensation for improvements would be made applicable to existing leases. - The Glasgow Evening Citizen states that the Calton Spinning Company have suspended operations in their Broad-street mill. Six hundred persons have thereby been' thrown out of work. Another factory in the same district is expected to follow suit, the reasons in both cases being depression in the cotton trade, and the exorbitant premiums charged for fire insurance. The Church of st. Matthew, Sheffield, was on Tuesday the scene of considerable urkoar, on the occasion of the annual vestry meeting. The Ritualists and anti-Ritualists had a struggle over the election of parishieners' warden, but on a poll being taken "the Protestant champion," as the anti-Ritualist candidate was called, was found to have been elected by a large majority. THE COST OF THE NEW COURTS OF JITSTICE.—The ac- counts of the total expenditure in respect of the new Courts of Justice have been made up. They amount to £1,846,683. This is a considerable advance upon the ori- ginal estimate, which was for a little over a million and a half. A revised estimate, however, placed the cost at £1,933,000, or something over the actual expenditure. WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE.—On Saturday, Messrs. Smith and Son, Wolverhampton, accountants to the Iron Trade Wages Board, issued their return on the average sell- ing price of bar iron for the last three months. It shows the price to have been £6 19s 6d. According to this the puddlers' wages for the next three months will be 7s 9d per ton, a reduction of 6d. Mill men's wages will be 5 per cent. lower.

DEATH OF THE TOWN CLERK OF CHORLEY.—OR Good Friday Mr. Richard Jackson, the Town Clerk of the borough of Chorley, died very suddenly from aribplexy, aged 65. The deceased held several public appointments, and his loss will be greatly felt in the district. He had been town clerk since the incorporation of the town, and also held the offices of clerk to the county justices for the Chorley petty sessional division, clerk to the Leyland Hundred Highway Board, and was registrar of the county court.

DEATH ram KICKING.—An inquest was held at Sunder- land, on Tuesday, as to the death of Sarah Gibson which took place on Sunday. The husband of the deceased stated that on the 19th inst. their landlord, Walter Moffatt, who was talking with them asked deceased to get some beer. In her absence be knocked Gibson down and commenced to kick him, and on Mrs. Gibson's return treated her similarly. The medical evidence was that there were bruises. on the head and face, and several ribs were broken. The • jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against Moffatt, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. THE CLAIMANT AND THE PARAMATTA LUNATIC. Mr. Edmund Kimber, the claimant's solicitor, on Tuesday, re- ceived a telagram from Sydney announcing that Messrs. Charles .Orton and D. Smith, the delegates sent out to Australia last October by the London Tichborne Release Committee, for the purpose of identifying with Arthur Orton a patient named Cresswell, confined in the Paramatta Asylum, have started for England, and are bringing Cress- well with them. The party also includes Mr. Joseph Eck- ford, a member of the New South Wales Legislature, who has taken a very prominent part in the inquiries, and Peebles, one of the crew of the Osprey. As soon as they arrive the London Tichborne Committee will take immediate steps for bringing about a reconsideration of the Claimant's case.

• „„.. NEXT-OF-ItIN FRAUDS: DEATH • OF THE PRISONER SHAKESPEAR.—The death is announced, in Strangeways Gaol, Manchester, of J. H. Shakespear, who was sentenced to 21 months' imprisonment in June last in connection with the next-of-kin frauds. The deceased, with two other men, was charged last May with having obtained various sums of money from people under the pretence that they were en- titled as next-of-kin to estates in various parts of the country. Shakespear was taken seriously ill about 10 days ago,and his case became so serious that an operation had to be performed. His condition grew worse, and his mother was sent for and. remained with him up to the time of his death. An inquest was held on the body, which was afterwards remcvei from the gaol and interred in the neighbourhood of Manchester. The deceased was a young man, well educated and well connected.

ENGLISH PATENTS. - The following patents amongst others published in the Commissioners' of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending:March 24th, 1883 : John Musgrave and Robert Gregory, junior, Bolton, im- proved safety gear for starting or turning engines; George Alfred Sheers and Abraham Wright, Oldham, improvements in the construction of looms for weaving; John Hutchings, Warrington, improvements in, obtaining the extracts or soluble portion from tanning material, and in apparatus therefor; Francis James Odling, Derby, improvements in gas motor engines; Henry Lomax, Darwen, machinist, im- provements in looms for weaving; Edward WilliarnParnell, Widnes, improvements in the manufacture of alkalies; Robert Howarth, Wolverhampton, improvements in bolts land nuts, and in the method of fixing the same; Wm. Casper Kritch. Leeds, improvements in printing machinery.— List supplied by Mr. George Davies, CE., Patent Solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. A CHILD STARVED TO DEATH ON THE MANE HILLS.— Gteat sensation has been caused in the Isle of Man by the loss of a little child named Margaret Miller, daughter of a person residing in Liverpool, who some time ago was sent to Mr. Corlett, of the Clypse, her uncle. The child, who was only three years of age, has been missing since the 14th of the present month. Mr. Corlett lives on the banks of the Clypse reservoir, an enormous dam holding about 30 million of gallons of water, which affords the main supply to the town of Douglas. It was feared that the child had fallen into the reservoir, and a proposal was made to run all the water off. This step, however, was not taken, it being feared that it would interfere with the water supply of Douglas during the coming season. At the suggestion of the directors of -the Douglas Waterworks Company, tke police, under Colonel Paul, head constable, instituted a search of the mountains surrounding the reservpir. This search has been prosecuted for some days. On Sunday twenty policemen were thus engaged, and the body of the child was ultimately found three miles from the reservoir on the mountain called Glenroy. The child was much scatched about the legs by briars, and had lost her shoes' arid stockings, and she had evidently died a most agonising death.

LORD WOLSELEY IN MANCHESTER.—On Wednesday I Lord Wolseley arrived in Manchester on a brief visit. The chief object of the gallant General's presence was to attend the condecration of a Masonic lodge, to be conducted upon temperance principles. His Lordship reached Manchester at half-past twelve o'clock, and received a hearty greeting from a large concourse of persons assembled at the London- road station, and along the line of route to the Town Hall, where hetook luncheon with the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Hopkinson). Upwards of 400 members of the Masonic or- der, many of them holding high rank, assembled at the Memorial Hall, where the new lodge was consecrated, and on Lord Wolseley entering the hall, in company with Col- onel Le Gendre N. Starkie, Provincial Grand Master of Freemasons in East Lancashire, be was loudly cheered. In I response to a vote of thanks at the conclusion of the cere- mony, Lord Wolseley said that during his military career it , had been his lot to visit various parts of the globe, and he I could say with the utmost confidence that wherever he went he had always found the greatest possible benefit and ad- vantage in the fact that he was a Mason. He could give many instances in which it had assisted him in the most material Manner in the performance of his duties to the public and to Her Majesty. In the evening Lord Wolseley was present at a Masonic banquet in the Free Trade Hall. Lord Wolseley's visit was brought to a close on Thursday evening, when he returned to London. During the course of the day his Lordship, in company with the Mayor Atli others, visited the works of Sir Joseph Whitworth and Co., 1 at Openshaw, the Royal Exchange, tbc Free Library, and 1 the Fire Station. In the evening be was present at a con- ' versazione given by the Mayor and Mayoress to the Vice- Chancellor and the members of the Victoria University Court. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADE.—There was , only a dull market on Tuesday, with less than an average ' attendance. Inquiries of any kind were very few, but with no pressure on the part of makers to sell prices were un- changed. Lancashire makers of pig iron at their present prices are altogether out of the market, but with large de- liveries going away against old contracts they are kept fully going, and hold for 47s 6d and 48s per ton, less 21, as their quotations for delivery equal to Manchester. Some of the district brands are to be bought at about 2s per ton under local iron, but in these there is also very little business do- ing. The manufactured iron trade remains without change. Makers are still booking new orders only to a very limited extent, and although for some of the Staffordshire brands rather more money is being asked, Lancashire bars are to be bought at £6 5s per ton delivered into the Manchester dis- trict, with sellers in one or two exceptional cases upon to take even slightly under this to secure orders.—A fairly good de- mand for all classes of fuel is being maintained generally throughout this district. The continued severe weather causes the better classes of round coal to move off.freely for house fire purposes ;- common classes of .round coal are in moderate demand for ironmaking and steam purposes, and there is no pressure of supplies upon the market; engine classes of fuel meet generally with a good inquiry, and with slack already scarce at many of the collieries there is every probability that supplies of this class of fuel will be very short during the summer. Prices all round are well main- tained at late rates. At the pit month prices average about as under :—Best coal 9s 6d to 10s, seconds 78 al to Sc, com- mon house fire coal 68 6d to 7s, steam and forge coal 5s 9d to 68 3d, burgy 4s 9d to 58, good ordinary slack 3s 6d to 4s, with some of the best qualities fetching 4s 6d per ton. In the shipping trade there has been only a very limited busi- ness doing. Delivered at the high level, Liverpool, or the Garston docks, ordinary Lancashire steam coal can be bought at about 78 ed per ton

Dr. Benson, whose arrival at Canterbury on Wednesday was the occasion of a great and enthusiastic demonstration of welcome, was on Thursday duly enthroned in Canterbury Cathedral as Primate of All England. Eleven hundred war medals were distributed by Sir Daniel Lysons to the troops lately engaged in Egypt at Aldershot, on Thursday. The troops afterwards marched past the commanding officer. The election of a judge to the Jersey Royal Court took place on Tuesday, amid great excitement. The contest was between town and country, and Mr. John Vaudin, represen- tative of the latter, was chosen. The arbitration to settle the amount to be paid to Mr. Clapperton, shipbroker, Greenock, in respect of the personal injuries sustained by him in the collision at Pennilee, on the Caledonian Railway, in September, 1880, has resulted in an award for the large sum of £8,250 and expenses. Enham House, Andover, one of the oldest family resi- dences in the district, NY as on Thursday morning destroyed by fire, and a nephew of the Rev. C. Cheales, the occupier, who had returned from Malta only on Wednesday, was burnt to death.

The failure has been announced at the London Bank- ruptcy Court of Messrs. Schutte and Kramer, merchants, of 4, Billiter-street, London, trading under the firm of "A. L. Schutte and Co." The liabilities are stated at £81,700. At a meeting, on Thursday, of the Board-of Arbitration in the northern iron trade, it was decided to diminish the pro- duction of finished iron by stopping work on Mondays for the rest of the year. Both employers and workmen are in accord on the question. A Renter's telegram from Rome states that Italy has ' joined the "defensive alliance " of Germany and Austria against France. The three Powers pledge themselves not to provoke France to war, but if the Republic should attack any one of them, the others will assist in repelling the attack. A building used as a store in connection with the exten- sive calico printing works of Messrs. Tod and Higginbotham on the south side of Glasgow was burned down on Thurs- day, causing damage to the extent of £l,OOO. The fire caused some alarm in consequence of the proximity of other valuable buildings. The temperance organisation of Bolton have had a suc- cessful canvas for signatures to a petition for Sunday closing. The Wesleyan petition numbers 6,620; British Women's, 9,068; and other organisations 15,836, the aggregate total being 21,500. The signatures to the petition of the British Women's Association and joint organisations make a roll 164 yards long. At Glossop, on Thursday morning, John Fisher Gibbons, of the Addfellows' Arms, Mellor, was fined 20s. and costs for keeping open his licensed premises during prohibited hours on the sth instant. Six of twelve men who were found in the house when the police visited it, at 25 n2inutes. past eleven were each fined half-a-crown and costs. The defendant said the main-spring of his watch was broken. At Wigan, on Thursday morning, four milk dealers were summoned for selling milk adulterated with water, vaiying from nine to nineteen per cent. In every instance the milk had been sent to the defendants from the country, and the plea was that they sold it as they received it. The Bench said the defendants supplied the working classes with the milk, and it was an injustice to have such stuff. One defendant was fined £5, and the others lesser amounts. While the steam yacht Eagle, lately purchased by a gentleman in Southampton. was on her way from Aberdeen to Southampton, on Tuesday, she foundered bf St. Abbs Head. Two of the crew were drowned. A third died from exposure in a boat, in which the only survivor arrived on Wednesday at Coldingham, Berwickshire, after being 13 hours afloat. Two fishermen were drowned on Wednesday by their boat upsetting in Loch Ryan.

The Central Police authorities have received a letter, pur- porting to issue from the Fenian Society, intimating that if their "brethern," the Phoenix Park murderers, are not forth- with released by the Government, " sweet revenge will be had by the blowing up of the Central Post and Telegraph Buildings, at St. Martin's-le-Grand, during the present week." Special vigilance has, accordingly, been enjoined upon the police patrols, who will keep a strict watch on all visitors.

A PLUM PeDDING FROM THE PREMIER —Mr. Heywood, of Newark, received on a bursday morning the following letter from the Premier:—" lam exceedingly pleased to' hear that a dinner is to be given to the remaining 10 of the scot and lot voters who were on the register when I had my first electoral campaign in Newark over 50 years ago. Had any hope of being free to attend I would have begged the favour of an invitation for myself. As this cannot be I ask that I may be allowed to direct my cook to supply a plum pudding for the occasion, and I beg to be informed of the day so that it may not arrive too soon or too late." A Lloyd's telegram just received states that the steamer Durham, from New York, has arrived in the Downs, and signalled that she has on board 25 men, forming the crews of two vessels which had been in collision off the entrance to the Channel on Saturday last. Lloyd's agent at once went on board for particulars, and it appears that the vessels in question were the iron barque Henry Swayne, of Liver- pool, 743 tons register, homeward bound from Peru to Queenstown, with a valuable cargo, and the Norwegian barque Anna, from the United States to France. The coin- ' sion was so serious that both vessels had _to be abandoned, ' and when left were fast sinking. MR. GLADSTONE AND DOMESTIC LEGISLATION.—The fol- lowing letter was on Tuesday received by the secretary of the East Staffordshire Liberal Association :—" 10, Down- ing-street, Whitehall, March 26th, 1883.—Dear Sir,—l am directed to acquaint you that Mr. Gladstone has received the resolutions of the East Staffordshire Liberal Association, of which you have favoured him with copies. In reply, I am to say that he appreciates in full the importance of the legislative measures which are mentioned, and that as re- gards the bill announced in the Queen's Speech for dealing with agricultural improvements of tenants, he wishes me to refer you to the answer relating to this subject which he re- cently gave to Mr. Heneage in the House of Commons. I am to add that his hopes for the full future efficiency of the House of Commons depend mainly on its succeeding in making satisfactory arrangements for what is termed delega- tion or devolution as to considerable portions of its business. —I am, sir, your obedient servant, E. W. HAMILTON."

_ DEATH OF MR. JOHN BROWN.—Mr. John Brown, the Queen's personal attendant, died at Windsor Castle at a quarter-past eleven o'clock, on Tuesday evening, of erysipelas. This melancholy event has caused "the deepest regret to the Queen, the. Royal family, and all the members of the Royal Household. To her Majesty the loss is irre- parable, and the death of this truly faithful and devoted servant has been a grievous shock to the Queen. In 1849 Mr. John. Brown entered the . Queen's service as one of the Balmoral gillies, and, by his careful attention, steadiness, and intelligence, he rose in 1858 to the position of the Queen's personal servant in Scotland, which in 1884 was extended to that of constant personal attendant on her Majesty on all occasions. During the last eighteen years and a half he served her Majesty constantly, and never once absented himself from his duty for a single day. • He has accompanied the Queen in her daily walks and drives, and all her journeys and expeditions, as well as personally waiting on her at banquets, tfee. An honest, faithful, and devoted follower, a trustworthy, discreet, and straightfor- ward man, and possessed of strong sense, he filled a position of great and anxious responsibility, the duties of which he performed with such constant and unceasing care as to secure for himself the real friendship of the Queen. HOTTENTOT HERDSMEN.—The Kaffirs, who are still their untiring persecutors, and who were the first cause of their _ _

national ruin, the Hottentots hate with an undying hatred to which the history of tribal malignity shows no parallel. Silently and patiently they will'track their foes, singly or In small bodies, until, in the darkness of-the night and safely, they can glut their dire vengeance. In a pitched battle, undisciplined and unaccustomed to fight under leaders in bodies, they have no chance with the more warlike Kaffirs, but in cunning and insidiousness they make up for what they lose in military skill. When Hottentot sights Kaffir, then comes the tug of war. This hatred of their conquerors .is intuitive, for the civilised Hottentots have the same lively feeling towards them as the most savage, whose fero- city is continually stimulated by the sight of acts of cruelty and oppression heaped upon their devoted race by the Kaffirs in their vicinity. The result of this hatred was utilised by-the British in the last Kaffir war,by the employ- ment of the Hottentots as scouts and guides, and to this day the " Totties," with a quick eye for a Kaffir cow-steal- ing thief, make the best herdsmen in the colony, just as the London pickpockets, with their senses acutely trained in early life by unlawful predatory pursuit in quest of snuff- boxes and pocket-handkerchiefs, were found, when in an evil day their ill-fortune landed them at the Antipodes, to be able to turn their quick ears and sharp eyes to good pur- pose as shepherds, in which calling their reputation for skill stood high among the Australian squatters.—The Peoples of the World. THE LABOUR MARKET.— The Easter holidays have ' caused the labour market to be somewhat depressed, although the building trade and railway construction con- tinue brisk, and many large jobs are in hand, where good navvies are in brisk demand: In Londori. there is great dis- tress amongst the dock operatives of all deseriptions, while skilled workmen in most trades find plenty of work. In the mining districts, trade disputes cause much interference with labour. The workers in most branches connected with iron are fairly employed. At Barnsley, foundries and ironworks are busy, and pig-iron makers„ae steadily employed. At Birmiogharn, the bicycle and ttrYcle makers and.machine- made watchmakers are busy, brass founders are fairly employed, and hardware makers have plenty of work. At Darlington, the plate mills continue closed, and steel makers are actively employed. There is an increasing demand for labour at Newcastle•on-Tyne. At Sheffield, ironfounders and engineers are very busy, and cutlery makers are well employed. The dispute amongst the file makers is assum- ing .a critical stage. At Sunderland, rolling mills and and foundries are working full time, and marine engineers and shipbuilders are busy! The bottle-makers who are on strike have decided to stand to their original demands. At Wolverhampton, finished ironworkers are busy. In the tex- tile trades labour is rather quiet. At Bradford and Halifax spinners are not busy. At Kidderminster, worsted-yarn machinery is fully employed. At Huddersfield, about 4,000 weavers are idle owing to the strike. At Leeds, weavers of printed coating q and rneltons are fairly employed. At Man- chester, spinners are not doing much. At Nottingham, lace and curtain makers are moderately employed, but hosiery weavers are barely making regular time. At Leicester, both fancy and boys' hosiery weavers ate busy, and the boot and shoe makers are moderately employed. The straw platters at Luton are busy. At Northampton, Stafford, and Norwich shoemakers have full work. Emigration is active, and pro- mises to continue so, the colonial demand for all classes of good workpeople being large.—Labour News.
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
LETTERS FROM THE EGYPTIAN EXILES.

The Central News has received copies of foar letters which have been addressed by the leaders of the late rebel- lion in Egypt to Mr. A. M. Broadley, their counsel. Arabi, writing on January 24th, says they all arrived in good health at Colombo, Ceylon, on January 10th, after a sea voyage of fourteen days. They were cordially received by the authorities of the island, who had secured houses for their accommodation, and who furnished them with nourish- ing food sufficient for the wants of their families for several days. They all join in offering their warmest thanks to the English authorities for the respect and kindness with which they have treated them. The town, the climate, and the face of the country itself suits them perfectly. They purpose sending their children to the local schools, and learning the English language themselves. Once the question of the confiscation of their property is settled they will lead a happy life. Toulba Ismet writes on the same date saying the British Government has treated them with every honour. Well-furnished and spacious houses had been set apart for their accommodation, and they were all pleased with this generous act. Yacoub Sami, writing on February 4th, en- closes two photographs, one recently taken, and the other wearing the uniform and decoration won in the Crimea. Yacoub protests against the unjust deprivation of their rank. Toulba Ismet, writing on February 19th. says he has been confined to his bed by sickness, an illness which he con- tracted in the Daira Sanieh having increased.

News from Sicily would appear to indicate that the eruption of Mount Etna has exhausted itself. A further despatch from Braidwood, Illinois, received at New York, on Tuesday, announced that 22 bodies had been received from the Diamond coal mine, which was flooded on February 7th. Despatches from Constantinople state that several villages at the foot of Mount Ararat have been destroyed by snow avalanches. One version gives the number killed at 59, and that of injured at about 100, Another account puts down the number of killed alone at 150. Amongst the places that have suffered most is the town of Schadogo, which, it is said, has been reduced to a heap of ruins. The Tripoli apology has scarcely been made when it has become necessary for the Porte again to submit to an Italian demand for reparation. The interpreter of the Italian Consulate at Aleppo has been arrested without cause. The Porte; apologised, but the terms are not thought to be sufficiently ample, and the Italian Charge d' .4faires has "drawn up a fresh form," which the Porte is now endeavour- ing to digest. Rumours of pending trouble in the East are again cur- rent, but no new cause for them can be found. Turkey professes alarm at the discovery that Bulgaria is calling out 45,000 men, and reports from Erzeroum declare that the military activity of Russia on the Armenian frontier of Asiatic Turkey is very suggestive of war. Much depends upon the source of such rumours; and an accurate and calm opinion upon Russia's military movements in the neigh- bourhood of Kars, Batoum, and the Caucasus generally is not likely to come from Erzeroum. SERIOUS FIRE AT BUENOS AYRES.—The most destructive fire ever known at Buenos Ayres broke out on the night of the 25th inst., at the corner of the Calles de Europa and Chacabnco, and ended in the total destruction of nine houses , and a boot shop, where the fire commenced through the explosion of a kerosene lamp. The total loss is estimated at 3,000,000 Mexican dollars. Altheugh some of the houses destroyed were old wooden ones and the flames spread very rapidly, no lives were lost. Several accidents occurred, however, amongst the firemen and police. Some comment has been provoked in New York by the publication of a statement to the effect that the British Ambassador had informed the Secretary of State that the violent language of professed American citizens towards England might disturb the amicable relations of the countries. The only ground for this rumour is that Mr. West has addressed a note to Mr. Frelinghuysen respecting the character of the men in America who are advocating the dynamite policy in this country. The friendly relations of England and America are in no way disturbed by these events. THE BERLIN TRAGEDY.—The German Police have cap- tured at Magdeburg the man who about a fortnight ago cruelly murdered a money-ordar messenger at Berlin, and whose crime caused a sensation in Berlin similar to that produced in London by the Lefroy tragedy. He turns out to be a young man named Sobbe, who has served as a non- commissioned officer in the Cuirassier Regiment to which Prince Ilismark is attached. It was by the merest accident that he was discovered, the police having been on the track of quite a different person. He was taken in fetters to the Central Prison at Berlin, where he is said to have confessed his crime, even before being confronted with the witnesses against him. -

EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDES IN PARIS—Two suicides were committed in Paris on Wednesday under the strangest circumstances, At No. 27, Rue Notre Dame de Nazareth, have lived for many years one Madame Chretien, a widow of 60, who kept a jeweller's shop, and M. Demanchy, her nephew, a rnantof 33, employed as copying clerk at the Lyon and Allemand Bank. On Friday morning, as neither aunt nor nephew appeared, their apartments were entered by the workpeople. M. Demanchy was first discovered lying on his bed with his brains blown out. The workpeople then went to the room of their mistress, expecting to have to break to her the sad news, when they found her also dead, with a revolver in her hand. Both aunt and nephew had left directions in their own handwriting respecting their funerals and other details. It has transpired that M. De- manchy had lately embezzled money of his employers to the amount of 40,000 f. To repay it, they had pressed him to get his aunt to sell up her shop and business. This he refused to do, proposing to pay something every month out of his salary. His employers did not accept this, but took stops to prosecute, and this, it would seem, proved too much for both aunt and nephew, who had lived together from his infancy.

div.head: EASTER MONDAY REVIEW.
div.p: THE EASTER MONDAY REVIEW.

The Easter review and sham fight at Brighton is an established institution of great importance among Volun, teers in the southern districts of England. Though Easter has this year occurred considerably earlier in the season than usual, the volunteers were exceptionally fortunate on Monday in respect of the magnificent weather which favoured the interesting proceedings in which they took part, albeit the day was ushered in 'by a sharp snowstorm of half an hour's duration, and again closed under similar wintry conditions. Conforming to previous practice, the review was led ug, so to speak, by a series of manceuvres on Friday and Saturday, with the view of affording a con- siderable section of the volunteers some instruction in arduous duties which fall to the lot of soldiers in actual campaigning. This year these preliminary manceuvres took a shape which was doubtless highly calculated to attain that end. According to the general idea of the operations, an invasion was threatened, and the part of the coast most likely to be attacked, was that between Newhaven and Brighton. A force was accordingly despatched from London to keep watch on that part of the sea-board. The British force, consisting of several crack Volunteer regiments, was at Three Bridges on Friday, and frJm thence they pushed for- r ward in five columns by parallel roads. On Saturday the commanding officer (Colonel the Hon. Paul Methuen) was 'supposed to receive intelligence that a small force of the enemy had landed at Rottingdean and were preparing to de- stroy the railway at Peacombe. The object of the advancing columns was then to defeat this intention, and the carrying of it out led to some brilliant skirmishing and fighting with the imaginary enemy. This contest, from the place where it happened, will henceforth be known by the name of the "Battle of Clayton," and when it was over and the enemy driven back the volunteers marched into quarters at Brighton. In the meantime a division of the in- vaders, numbering about 8,000 men, was understood to have effected a landing. and taking up a position on Newmarket Heights „ to cover the disembarkation of the whole force, and this landing of the enemy furnished the make-believe occasion for the fighting which occurred on Monday. Bri- gade after brigade of volunteers and an immense crowd of spectators collected on the low spur of the Downs, which is occupied by the town end of "The Bottom." The troops were in their appointed stations in good time, and the spec- tators stretching away in two long lines on the Higher Downs. Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar was riding about superintending the final preparations soon after 11 o'clock, and at twenty minutes to twelve the Duke of Cambridge took his place at the saluting point, and the march past began. Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar, as the com- mander of the whole army corps, was the first general officer to pass the saluting point, and among the well-known officers who followed, in various positions of command, were Colonel Goodenough, who commanded the. artillery of the Egyptian expedition; Colonel Methuen, who conducted Friday's march and Saturday's sham fight; Colonel Clive, who managed the marching column last year; and Lord Ranelagh, the veteran of the Easter Monday reviews. His ' colleague—or perhaps he should be.styled his rival—Lord Bury, was unfortunately prevented by illness from appear- ing at the head of a brigade. The volunteer artillery made an unusually good saw. First came the Honourable Artillery Company, as smart as ever, then in succession the let Hampshire, Ist, Sussex, and the 3rd Kent, all looking well drilled and well disciplined. They were all in column of division, two guns abreast, and occasionally there was weakness of dressing, both of guns and.of gun detachments,' but they were much better handled than they were last year at Portsmouth. With the artillery of the defence there were only the twelve 20-pounders of the 3rd Middlesex, but both this regiment and the 2nd, which had no guns on Monday, marched past in very good style. The rifle volunteers made by no means so good a show. The distances between the companies were properly kept by scarcely a single bat- talion. The supernumerary ranks were badly dressed, and too often the dressing of the leading companies was dis- turbed by the hanging back of the field officers in front. Of the corps generally considered entitled to be called crack regiments none but the London Scottish marched past at all well. The Surrey corps and the two West Kent battalions, the 17th Middlesex, and the Lancashire battalion all went past fairly well, and the Ist Sussex, which made a really splendid march past, seemed to be the best corps on the ground, at any rate at this parade exei cise. The last battalion passed the Royal Standard at about half-past twelve o'clock. The attacking forte then proceeded in an easterly direction across the Downs to a point called Falmer Hill, and there took up position pre- paratory to delivering the attack which was to rid the dis- trict of the supposed invaders. The defending force; repre- senting the enemy, marched to a point nearer the sea, seek- ing the shelter of what is kqown as Newmarket Heights. These operations presented a number of very inieresting manceuvres, and,took some considerable time, but by about

half-past two o'clock all were in their allotted places, and the battle opened with a heavy artillery fire from the at- tacking force, and briskly replied to by the defending forces. It will not be necessary to describe how this big gun firing was kept up for about two hours; how skir- mishers were thrown out by both forees, supported by large bodies of men; or how the attacking troops, after warm work at close quarters, succeeded in driving the enemy from point to point. Suffice it to say that the attack was con- ducted with much spirit and dash, and that it was success- ful in defeating the invaders, even to the extent of sur- roanding and capturing their General. "Cease fire" was then sounded, and the divisions having Fe-formed, marched back to the rendezvous enclosures at Brighton.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AND MR. GIBSON AT BIRMINGHAM.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AND MR. GIBSON AT BIRMINGHAM.

The Marquis of Salisbury and Mr. Gibson were enter- tained at dinner by the Birmingham Conservative Associa- tion on Wednesday evening. The Marquis of Salisbury, in responding to the toast of his health, expressed the pleasure he felt in seeing such evidences of strong Conservative feel- ing in Birmingham, whence the Liberal party had derived so much of their strength, inspiration, and ability. Comment- ing on Mr. Bright's criticism at Glasgow last week on our - past war expenditure, his lordship said Mr. Bright's idea was that this vast sum which had been expended on war would be represented by an England in which Protestant succession had not been maintained, a Canada that had not been won, an India with no portion under British rule, and that Eng- land would have been overrun by Napoleon's legions and would have followed the fortunes not of her own people but those of France. Mr. Bright, amongst other things, had pro- phesied that the advent of Mr. Gladstone to power would be followed by great calm. But what about Egypt and the Transvaal? His policy of peace at any price had led to the Egyptian campaign when stronger measures at the outset would have prevented it. Again, in the Transvaal peace was made after English blood had been spilt and our honour trailed in the dust, just at the moment when one blow would have achieved all the objects of our policy. It was the peace party that induced Russia to dare England to mortal combat, and that same party had been responsible for many wars. He strongly criticised the policy of the Uovernment in Ireland, and said experience had taught them the necessity of a recurrence to the old and tried method of English government.—Mr. Gibson, in respond- ing for the House of Commons, 'briefly criticised the pro- gramme of the Government for the present session, and said that while it was one that did not impress the nation favourably, it did not even awake enthusiasm amongst the supporters of the Government. He denied that there was any intention on the part of the Opposition to obstruct the business of Parliament, and challenged assertion to that effect. Now that the Government had reformed the rules of procedure, and were masters-of the situation, the Opp.- sition were entitled to expect that something would be done, but up to the present only one Government measure had been read a second time, and the outlook was not promising. The Marquis of Salisbury on Thursday opened a Junior Conservative Club, in Birmingham. At a luncheon at ter- wards he delivered an address, which was meant to excite the local Conservatives to organisation and future action. Whilst counselling organisation, however, he condemned the Caucus. Later in the day the noble lord received addresses at the Conservative Club from the local Conser- vative Association and other bodies; and in the evening he was the principal speaker at a great Conservative gathering in the Town Hall. Replying to a resolution of confidence in Her Majesty's Opposition, he again referred to the Caucus —the special creation of the Birmingham Liberals —and pointed out various ways in which, as he believed, it operated injuriously. He unsparingly condemned the cloture, and said that its action, so far from facilitating business in the House of Commons, had been to remove the proceedings of the Ministry, to a very great extent, from the constitutional control of the House, which, in former times, was the great security of the country. Its effect was seen in the action of the Government both with reference to the IPlmainham business and the Transvaal. Lord Salisbury referred to the housing of the working classes in our great cities as one of the most pressing questions of the day; and claimed for Sir Richard Cross the credit of having made, by his Act of 1875, the only serious attempt to deal with that question. The late Government, he said, was the only one which had made any substantial effort towards reducing local taxa- tion. He mentioned these and other matters as indicating the spirit which had animated Conservative policy in the past. If asked for a wider definition of that policy he would say that it was eminently; national, in contrast to the senti- mental, or cosmopolitan, or philanthropic theories upon which Radicals were too apt to rely. The noble lord re- ferred to the question of Free Trade and the extension of the suffrage in counties, and expressed his belief that any extension of political liberty in Ireland, in the present temper of the Irish people, would have the effect of strengthening the element which was opposed to the Eng- lish connection.—Mr. Gibson, M.P., also spoke in reply to I the resolution.

div.head: lAIPORtANT FENIAN ARREST IN LIVERPOOL. DISCOVERY OF INFERNAL MACHINES.
div.p: lAIPORtANT FENIAN ARREST IN LIVERPOOL. DISCOVERY OF INFERNAL MACHINES.

We (Liverpool Mercury) understand that the Liverpool detective police have succeeded in making an apprehension which has probably saved many lives and much valuable property. For some time past, in consequence of what has taken place in Ireland, London, and elsewhere, the Govern- ment authorities and the police generally have been very much on the alert, and, from what we can gather, Captain ! Nott-Bower, head-constable, and Mr. Willia ns, chief of the ' detective depaament in this city, have been on the look-out with the view of apprehending anyone suspected of com- plicity in the widespread plots. As we have already hinted, extra police supervision Has been exercised in condection with all our public buildings; and the arrest which has been made amply justifies the wise measures of precaution which has been adopted. The steamers coming from Ireland for some time have been care- fully watched; and upon the arrival of a steamer from Cork at the landing-stage a man was seen to come on shore with , a box si hich appeared to be exceedingly heavy. The per- ! son was watched for some distance, but before he had pro- ceeded far the suspicions of the police were aroused and he was taken into custody. The box in his care was of the ! ordinary clothes type, made of wood, with a patent lock, the key of which was found in the prisoner's possession. We have reason to believe that the box contains chemicals of a most dangerous and highly explosive nature, and several pieces of mechan- ism which are more popularly known as " infern-74 machines." We understand that the result of an analysis will disclose the fact that the compounds and the machines are of the most modern manufacture, and highly destruc- tive in their construction and composition. Although the police are naturally very reticent, there is good ground for believing that the man arrested is one of a band of Irish , conspirators whose object is to destroy public buildings in this immediate neighbourhood, and the importance of the 1 arrest cannot, therefore, be over-estimated. The police authorities have in this instance shown the greatest amount of vigilance in the matter, and their well-directed efforts are worthy of the highest praise, whatever the result may be.

div.head: LATER DETAILS.
div.p: LATER DETAILS.

The Cork boat, it transpires, was being watched by no less flan four Liverpool and two Irish detectives as well as several constables in plain clothes. The man arrested was dressed like a labourer, and he is described by the police as being undoubtedly a Fenian. He seemed taken by surprise and offered no resistance, but walked quietly to the detective office. The contents of the box have not yet been analysed, but the police say there is no doubt as to them being explosives of a dangerous kind. The Government has been communicated with, and the local authorities are awaiting instructions before taking any further steps in the matter. The steamers arriving from Ireland have been closely watched for some time, par- ticularly the Cork boats. A young Irish porter was arrested at Sutton, near St. Helens, on Thursday morning, by the Liverpool detectives, on a charge of being concerned with the man who came by the Cork boat in receiving explo- sives and infernal machines. ha his possession was found a bag, the contents of which have been sent to the public analyst. There is, it is said, strong evidence of guilt, but at present the police are not in a position to reveal anything further.

div.p: FOOTBALL

WIDNES V. BARROW VOLITNTEERS.—This mafch was played at Widnes on Saturday; the home team winning a plessant game by 3 goals, 1 try, and 9 minor poh ts, to Barrow 2 tries and 1 minor point. St. Eidhin's decided to play with the wind in their favour. WARRINGTON V. MOSS SIDE (MANCHESTER). The match betweers these clubs attracted a little attention In Manchester on Saturday, and the home team, after a fairly exciting and Interesting match, beat their opponents by one goal, four touchdowns, and one dead ball, to Warringzon one touchdown and one dead ball. Osmium CHALLENGE CUD (Sinai. Tie.) Northwich Victoria v. Crewe Alexandra: This important match was played at Hartford on Saturday, in the presence of 4,000 spectators. Both teams were in good condition, and a splendid game ended in favour of the Victorians by one goal to nil. This is the fourth time that No: thwich have won the cup. WIDNES (ISt TEAM) V. The winners were composed of ten of the Wasps F. 0., four of the True Blues F. 0., and one of the Litherland F.O. The goals were obtained—one from a try by T laws, W Kiddir convert- ing it into a goal, and the other goal being spleadidly dropped from the field of play by 11 Wright. .

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY—w."'". THE ALLEGED ATTACH ON LADY DIXIE.—The House of Commons reassembled after the Easter recess.—Capt. O'SERA put his interesting question as to the alleged murderous at- tack upon Lady Florence Dixie, and inquired if the Hone Secretary had been able to come to any definite conclusion. - in the matter.—Sir W. HARCOURT replied that the case rested mainly on the statement of Lady F. Dixie, and that the he. vestigations of the police into the matter had not resulted in discovering any further circumstances in confirmation of it. SEIZURE OF EXPLOSIVES AT LIVERPROL. —The Hoxn SECRETARY informed Sir S. NORTHCOTE that he had heard of a seizure of explosives and an arrest at Liverpool, but as the matter was in the hands of the police he would rather not say anything more about it at present. SIXPENNY TELEGRAMS.—On the motion to go into Coin. mittee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, Dr. CAMERON moved that the time had arrived when the mini- mum charge for inland postal telegrams should be reduced to sixpence.—Mr. PULESTON seconded the motion.—The POSTMASTER GENERAL replied that nothing would give hi* greater pleasure than to be told by the Chancellor of the Exchequer that the time had arrived when the financial position of the country was such that they could afford te sacrifice the temporary loss of revenue which the reduction in the price of telegrams would involve. That was a ques. tion which could not be determined by a motion. When the day arrived the annou'ncement would be hailed by the great mass of the people of the country with satisfaction. He admitted there were some striking anomalies in our pre. sent system of telegraphing. The minimum charges in this country wus much highier than in most countries on the Continent, and we were now in the poSition that we could send a telegram from any part of England to Belgium fer Bd., while we could not send a telegram from even one part of London to another for less than a shilling. He was, how- ever, unwilling to give up the principle of uniformity, and instead of introducing changes by driblets he preferred to wait until they could have' the 'reform completely and effectually brought forward. --The -Clam- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER Said he was strongly in favour of reducing the telegraph rate, and he would undertake that the question should be thoroughly investigated between now i and next year, but he did not think it would be wise te adopt a change in the year when they were about to carry out the system of postal parcels.—A division was called in a small House, and Dr. Cameron's motion was carried by 68 to 50. After a discussion on the management of the Crown lands, , raised by Mr. A. Arnold, the House went into Committee of I Supply on the Civil Service Estimates.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
*SATURDAY, MARCH 31, 1883.

The member for Westminster, Mr. W. H. SMITH, is one of the most cautious of speakers on the Opposition benches of the House of Commons, and for that reason whatever he has to say is always listened to with respect, but even he, poor man, in his anxiety to damage the Government has been led into an indiscretion of which by this time he has, we hope thoroughly repented. The ther evening he addressed the West- minster Constitutional Association, and in the course of his observations remarked that the members of the present Liberal Ad- ministration had "brought matters to such a pass that they could harldly walk the streets of London or sleep in their beds without the most vigilant attention on the part of the police," and he went on to add that "this state of disturbance, of repression, of anxiety, of alarm, and of destruction of property is all connected—apparently inseparably connected —with a Liberal Government." These ex- travagant and, we will add, untruthful state- ments, seem to have been too much for a Mr. HUGH SHIELD, who straightway Com- municated with the Home Secretary, Sir W. V. HARCOURT, inquiring whether in 1867, when a Conservative Administration was in power, a state of things prevailed not less grave than the present as regards the danger to which the Queen's Ministers were believed to be exposed and the precautions adopted for their protection. This is a matter, it will be no'Liced, involving a question of fact alone, about which there need be no dispute; and that Mr. SMITH should be so utterly ignorant of the facts, or what is much worse, should for party purposes deliberately close his eyes to them or distort them—because we do not believe he can be so blind to the truth—is unpaTdonable in an ex-Minister of the Crown. And what are the facts? Sir Wm. HARCOURT, in his reply to Mr. SHIELD, points them out very clearly, and we commend his historical narrative to the careful perusal of Conserva- tive politicians more especially. in the early part of 1867—in which year the DERBY- DISRAELI Administration was in power— occurred the Fenian raid on Chester Castle, in the spring of that year took place the abortive Fenian rising in Ireland, in Sep- tember the murder of the policeman in Man- chester was recorded, followed by the Clerkenwell explosion in December. It is generally believed by our Conservative friends that it was this _explosion which led to the disestablishment of the Irish Church, from which, it is often said, all our recent troubles in Ireland have sprung; but we would re- mind those who are of this opinion that two years previously Mr. DILLWYN had moved a resolution in the House of Commons affirm- ing that the Irish Church was in an unsatis- factory condition, and that in the debate which followed Mr. GLADSTONE delivered a remarkable speech which segmed to fore- tell a time when the disestablishment question would have to be dealt with. The Clerkenwell explosion was the means undoubtedly of calling public attention to Irish grievances, and, at the same time, it was the means of opening the nation's eyes to the disgraceful neglect of Irish in- terests by a Conservative Government. Mr. SMITH tries to make a point of the protection that it is necessary to give to Ministers at the present time, but the HOME SECRETARY shows that in 1867 Conservative Minis- ters had also to be protected; further, that it was necessary to increase the metropolitan police force by 1,000 men, vastly in excess of the actual augmentation now judged neces- sary, whilst, in addition, thousands of special constables were sworn in to assist in the pre- servation of the peace, and in affording pro- tection to life and property. All this took place towards the close of Mr. DISRAELI'S first Administration; and it is within the recollection of all of us that at the close of his second Administration he warned the country of the dangers brewing in Ireland as something worse than 'pestilence and famine." How, then, can it be said that a state of disturbance, of repression, of anxiety, of alarm, and of destruction of property is all inseparably con- nected with a Liberal Government ? The two Liberal Governments which preceded the DERBY-DISRAELI Administration of 1866 did not provoke by their legislation any dis- order in Ireland, or, indeed, anywhere else ; and the first Administration of Mr. GLAD- STONE, which remained in office from 1868 to 87k, was not marked by any outbreak

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCT 3L1883,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCT 3L1883,

lagainst law and order in the Emerald Isle, nor any necessity for the police precautions which are so essential at the present time. 'We are inclined to think that they would not be requisite now had the late (.3oN;elnment liste/;ed to the legitimate demands of the Irish pepple, instead of turning a drsaf ear to their entrt:aties and ruling them wi' h, as it were, a rod of iron. We are not =u prised that the HOME SECRETARY should show no little degree of warmth in his communica- tion, or that he should administer a well- deserved castigation to Mr. SMITH for so glaring a manifestation of crass ignorance, if ignorance it be, all the more reprehensible in a gentleman of the position of Mr. SMITH. who ought really to be above making party capital out of so grave a crisis. The SI. James's Gazette, ever ready to assist the Con- servative party, or the members thereof, might be expected to support Mr. SMITH, but that organ of light and leading cannot defend him, and is bound to candidly confess " Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT has no difficulty in showing that in 1867 ' it might have been ' said with equal truth, or want of truth, that a state of disturbance and alarm was inseparably con- ' nected with a Conservative Government." Mr. SMITH, evidently writhing under the Home Secretary's drubbing, has returned to the charge, but we fail to see that he has in any way improved his position. He says that Mr. HARDY, the Home Secretary in the Ad- ministration of 1867, was the only Minister whose "life was threatened," and this may be quite true, but it does not alter the fact that all the members of the Cabinet had to be more or less protected. He tries to make a point by asserting that the present Govern- ment disregarded the warning of Lord Beaconsfield in 1880. We presume Mr. Smith here alludes to the fact that the Peace Preservation Act was allowed to expire, but in this the hon. member is again at fault, for the late, not the present, Government are to blame for that, if blame can be reasonably cast upon either Administration. Mr. SMITH says there were not wanting indications a few months ago that some of the most devoted partizans of the Government, and some even of the members of the Government them- selves, were prepared to throw Lord SPENCER and Mr. TREVELYAN overboard in their desire to make terms with the agitators, and to give them a fresh triumph. This statement will be new to most pople, and it would be in- teresting to know to what indications Mr. SMITH alludes. It seems to us that if there be one point more than another. one which all parties—Conservatives, Liberals, and Radicals alike—are agreed, it is that Lord SPENCER and Mr. TREVELYAN should be per- mitted to carry out the Irish policy of the Government with the courage and firmness which have characterised their rule, and which have been productive of such good results in so short a time. This statement, for which there is not a shadow of founda- tion, has originated only in the fertile imagination of Mr. Smini, in whose case silence certainly would have been golden. It is a misfortune Tory orators should be so regardless of facts in their utterances. A cause which requires bolstering up by mis- representation cannot possibly be a good one

A CUTE ImrosTEst Kr RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Capt. C. W. Hazlehurst, Thomas Gibson, who stated he was a native of Flintshire, was charged with obtaining money by false pretences.—P.S. Whalley said about eleven o'clock on Saturday morning he saw the prisoner in Bridge-street. He was lying on the side of the footway, pretending to be ill, and people were giving him brandy tea and money. After- wards the prisoner went to another street, where he behaved in a similar manner. Witness followed him to a lodging. house, where be found him with a pint of porter before him, and heard him declare that "he was as good as any- body in the house." Witness took him into custody.—Mr. Rogerson, draper, Bridge-street; said on Friday afternoon he was in Lugsdale - road, Widnes, when he saw the prisoner leaning against a door, apparently very ill. A crowd of people round him was giving him coffee, and when he (Mr. Rogerson) left they were knocking at the door of a public-house in order to obtain some stimulants for the prisoner. At Runcorn, on Saturday morning, he saw the prisoner go through the same performance, and suspect- ing that he was an impostor, he gave the police information of the occurrence.—Dr. MacDougall stated that on Saturday afternoon he was requested to examine the prisoner, and was taken to a house in Mersey-street, where he was. He found the prisoner sitting in what he supposed he must call the kitchen with a quantity of porter before him. He asked him whether he was drinking porter, but he replied in the negative, and referred him (witness) to some woman in the house, to whom he alleged it belonged. The woman, in answer to his inquiry, said it belonged to the prisoner. Wit- ness then examined the prisoner very carefully, but could see in him nothing that would cause him to fall in the street and act in the manner described. He was not very strong-chested, but there was nothing to account for him having a seizure.—P.S. Whalley observed that the prisoner at first gave his name as Donovan. On searching the prisoner he found 7P. upon him.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to a month's imprisonment, with hard labour, MEDICINES, ELASTIC STOCKINGS, CITILMICALS, Bce., per poet (or rail delivered free, under lib in Great Britain ed.) RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT WIDNES.—Whilst Dennis Murphy, a boy, 14 years of age, was attempting to pull a small boat named " Coffin " out of the canal on Good Friday, he slipped into the water. Another boy who was playing on the bank ran to his rescue, and seized him by the hair. In this way he prevented him from sinking, and a man arriving on the scene in a few moments pulled Murphy, who has not suffered through his immersion, out of the canal.

Preston, M.A., Rev. Llewelyn, and the Rev. J. Lockwood. MR. E. K. MCSPRATT AND THE " TIMES."—Mr. E. K. Muspratt, president of the Financial Reform Association, replies through tke Times to some comments made by that journal on the recent deputation from the Association by the Chancellor of the Exchequer in favour of a free breakfast , table. Mr. Muspratt clears up some prevalent misconceptions ;as to the objects of the Financial Reform Association, pointing out in particular that what it aims at is not the taxation of the rich to the unjest relief of the poor, but a system of taxation which imposes a burden upon each citizen duly proportioned to the advantages he enjoys from State protection of person and property, and not unneces- sarily increased by a needlessly costly system of collection. This necessarily implies as large a" resort to direct taxation as possible and the abolition of exemptions from taxation. Mr. Muspratt strongly insists upon the fact that taxation restricts trade, and demonstrates that the carrying out of the policy advocated by the Buancial reformers would necessarily have beneficial results upon the volume of both exports and imports. A WIDNES PUBLICAN FINED.—John Cregg, landlord of the Cricketers' Arms, Milton-road, was summoned to Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises, and also with•Bupplying beer to a drunken person named Thomas Burns.—P.S. Strickland stated that at twenty minutes past eight on Sunday night, the 13th inst., he visited the defen- dant's house, and in the taproom he found three men sitting. One named Thomas Burns, who was very drunk, had a half pint glass of beer in his hand, and a quart jugful of beer on the table before him. Witness drew the landlord's attention to the drunken state of Burns, when he admitted that he had served the latter with the beer, but he did not know that he was drank.—P.C.'s Almond and Snowden corrob- orated this statement.—Defendant said Burns went into the taproom whilst he was in another part of the house. He was sitting so quietly that he did not notice that he was drunk.—Superintendent Barker said the defendant had only been in charge of the house two montbs.—Mr. Brock (the chairman) said this was a serious offence with a heavy penalty attached to it, but as the defendant was new to the business the Bench did not wish to he hard upon him. The police withdrew the summons for permitting drunken- ness, but on the other summons the defendant would be fined £2 and costs 155., or in default a month's imprison- ment.
