A REFRACTORY PAUE.tR AT VIITTON WortrifOrsE.—At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesdays before Mr, Charles Reynolds and Mr. John Brundrit, Thomas Jarnee Lloyd, 19 years of age, but who appearei about 12; was charged with being a refractory pauper. It was stated that the prisoner was thoroughly unmanageable, andthad been an endless source of trouble at Ditton workhouse, of which he is an inmate. He has several times suffered imprisonment for his unruly conduct, but his punishment seems to have had no effect upon him, and a few days ago he was given a new suit of clothes. He tore to shreds his vest, neckerchief, and shirt, and smashed crockery and tinplate utenoils in abundance.—The Bench :sentenced him to six weekr7 im- prisonment with hard labour.

WIFE BEATING AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Ashton was charged with assault- ing his wife Christina.—From the prosecutrix's statement it seemed that on Saturday the prisoner knocked her down to the ground with his fists, blacking both her eyes. He had behaved to her in a similar way previously. She gave him no provocation. In answer to Mr. Pilkington witness ac- knowledged that she had drank three gills of beer with the prisoner the same afternoon.—Prisoner stated that he was wrestling with his wife for a glass of beer.—Mr. Brock said Mrs. Ashton bore upon her face the marks of severe punishment, which were a disgrace to the prisoner.—The prisoner was hound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties in .E 5 each. FARNWORTII GRAMMAR SCHOOL: IMPORTANT BRO- POSALS.—It has been decided to re-open, in September or October next, this school, which has been for several years in abeyance. The governors have purchased land near the Cheshire Lines Railway bridge, Locket's-lane, Farnworth, and have decided to erect thereon a school building capable of accommodating fifty boys, at a cost, iNluding furnishing, of £2,000. The contract has been let to Messrs. Brown Ji Pack - house, of Wavertree ; and we understand that the work will be commenced-at once. A headmaster has been advertised for. The foundation is a very ancient one, dating back to the fifteenth century, when the first donation was given by Bishop Smythe, a native of Farnworth or one of the ad- jacent townships. It may be intereeting to state that among the pupils educated at Farnworth School was Richard Ban- croft, who became Archbishop of Canterbury, and was created a Privy Councillor and Chancellor of the University of Oxford. Owing to the want of a suitable school build- ing, the institution was in 1879 discontinued. A new scheme was subsequently drawn up by the Charity Commissioners, and reeeived the assent of the Queen. The school will now be opened under its provisions, and will give instruction in the higher branches of education, and be of an entirely no- sectarian character.

AN INCIDENT OF THE MID-CHESHIRE ELECTION.—With reference to the statement made by Mr. J. C. Lawrance, M.P., at a meeting at Runcorn during the course of the Mid- Cheshire election, that Mr. Chamberlain had obstructed legislation and had divided the House of Commons 22 times in one night on the Army Discipline Bill, the right hoc. gentleman was communicated with on the subject, and has written the following letter :—" 40, Prince's Gardens, S.W., March 14th, 1883. Dear sir,—l have been so busy that I jia%e been unable to reply before to your letter of the 10th inst. The statements which you report as having been made by Tory speakers are, as you may suppose, entirely untrue. I never divided the House 22 times in one night on the Army Bill, and I deny altogether that I ever obstructed that or any other measure. I offered strong opposition to one or two of the clauses relating to flogging, and on another occa- sion I opposed with some pertinacity a Bill fOr altering the conditions of Public Works Loans, which was brought in at the end of the session by Sir Stafford Northcote. In both cases my opposition was justified by the concessions which were obtained from the Goverament, and in no instance was it pushed beyond fair limits. The nature of the opposition to Government business which has shown itself during the present session may be best appreciated by stating the fact that at the commencement of the session to the present time the Government have not had .one single minute open to them for the purpose of promoting their legislative proposals. The whole time of the House has been taken up in the neces- sary and routine business of supply, in attacks upon the Government, and in discussions raised by private members. —Yours obediently, J. CHAMBERLAIN. F. J. Norman, Esq."

ROBBERIES OF LEAD AT WIDNES. On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, John Connolly, a respectable-looking working man, was charged, in custody, with stealing 161hs of lead, worth 2s' from Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons' chemical works, Anne-street East, Widnes.—On Monday evening P.C. Almond was on duty in Anne-street West, when he saw the prisoner coming from the direction of Messrs. Muspratts' works. His pockets were very bulky, and the officer detained him and searched hint, when he found the lead produced. The prisoner stated that a man for whom he had been working had given it to him, but he afterwards said he had got the lead from under a railway arch in Moss Bank. He was taken to the police station where he was charged with stealing the lead, when he re- plied, "It has been stolen, but I didn't steal it."—Jobn Conley, labourer, at Messrs. Muspratt's works, and living in Moon-street, said he saw the prisoner in the works on Mon- day evening, He was standing near the boilers warming himself.—Wm. Turton, foreman plumber, at Messrs. Mus- pratt's, and living in Vine-street, deposed that on Monday a quantity of old lead was put into the melting pot. The lead produced corresponded with the lead in the pot.—Pri- soner now pleaded guilty, and he was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment.—Robert Knight and John Tobin, boys, were charged with stealing 291bs of lead and 71bs of indiarubber, of the value of ss, from Messrs. James Mus- pratts and Sons' chemical works.—Wm. Flannigan, vitriol foreman, at the prosecutors' works, stated th it about half- past twelve, on the previous day, he saw the prisoners and another boy in the works. Their clothes were bulky, and becoming suspicions, he went to them. One of the prisoners dropped the piece of indiarubber tubinc, produced. The prisoners had no business in the work;.—Superintendent Barker, on this evidence, asked for a remand for a week, which was granted. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY LECTURES. Oa Thursday evening a lecture on "Bees, their habits and homes," was delivered in Bethesda Schoolroom, by Mr. A. Bathgate, of Liverpool. It was the fifth of the series instituted by the .Free Library Committee, and was very well attended, many young folks having been attracted by the magic lantern illustrations of the subject, which were given by Mr. J. R Frith. Mr. G. Rhodes presided, and introduced the lecturer, who described how the keeping of bees had extended in the United States of America, until at the present time it had reached the dimensions of a separate and profitable industry. An immense quantity of honey was exported from that country. During the season of 1881 about a million and a half pounds of honey were produced, being an average of (39 pounds per hive. Illustrations of bee ranches were thrown on the screen and described, as well as capital drawings of the flowering plants from which the busy worker extracted its honey. The lecturer was of opinion that bee keeping could not be carried on in England as a profitable and separate industry, but he observed that tenant farmers and people living in the country could make bee cultivation a pursuit from which considerable profit could be realised. It would, besides be a most pleasurable occupation, affording a healthful relaxation from the worry and cares of business. The construction and habits of the drone, the worker, and the queen bee; the structure and interior economy of the hive; were described in a most interesting way, which frequently called forth demonstrations of interest and appreciation from the audience. From the busy and un- tiring, though abort lives of the bees, their extreme loyalty and devotion to their queen, Mr. Bathgate extracted some apposite lessons for the human family, observing that if the lives of men bore in their own degree more resemblance to the lives of bees, the millenium would not be far distant. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. F. A. Lake.
WIDNES SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION.

The annual gathering of the scholars attending the school comprised in this union was held in Lacey-street schoolroom on Sunday aitcrrtoon. Mr. B. Brown, the presi- dent, occupied the chair. Mr. 8e1E.7., of Rochester, gave a most interesting and instructive lesson on the subject of "Abraham's sacrifice," which he illustrated by means of the black-board. Several teachers and friends from the various schools made a few observations, and the thanks of the meeting were accorded to Mr. Belsey. The following schools were represented at the meeting :—Lacey-street V;resleyan, Zion United Methodist Free Church, Simm's Croa Primitive Methodist, Albert-road Wesleyan, Hutchin- son-street Primitive Methodist,Simm's Cross Congregational, and the Welsh Congregational. A tea party was held on Monday ,afternoon, when there were about 100 persons pre- sent,

The awing meeting was held in the Lecture Room of Lacey-street Weblvan School on Monday evening. Mr. B. Brown, the presidenf, occupied the chair, and there was a large audience. Devotional exercise having been engaged in, Mr. J. Peet read the rules of the Union..

Mr. T. J. PEYERS read the first annual report, which, after relerring to the formation of the union, went on to say that the committee had from time to time met to consider by what means they could best carry out the objects of the union. They thought benefit had been derived by schools from the union. At the same time they would sub Tait that the establishment in full activity of a Sunday school union was a matter of a progressive rather than an instantaneous nature, and they would remind the schools that the more interest they took in the union the greater would be its vitality and real usefulness. In September last Mr. S. B. Stringer, at the request of the committee, gave a most ex- cellent paper at a teachers' conference on the subject "Discipline in the class." There was a good attendance, the subject was thoroughly discussed, and the conference must have been helpful to those present. The teachers' examination was held in February Jest, all the candidates having entered under the head of scripture, the subject of the examination being "The history of the Early Christian Chtirch, as recorded in the first eight chapters of the Acts of the Apostles." The number of papers sent up was only four, but the committee, in hope of a larger list next year, would urge upon the teachers the importance of going through a course of study, and proving themselves in respect of knowledge, at all events for their work. The result of the examination was not yet known. With regard to the scholars' examinations, the committee, desiring to encourage a system which has been found useful in aiding in grounding the scholars well in Scripture knowledge, had made very liberal offers of prizes and certificates to success- ful candidates with the view of inducing them to study the subject for examination, namely the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and sth Chapters of Acts. Having made these offers it was thought desirable that the minimum number of entries should be 50 to secure a proper number of competitors. But the com- mittee were much disappointed to find that so far the num- ber of entries had net quite reached 50. They admitted, however, that in some quarters considerable inttre6t was manifested, and they were hopeful of the result after thus prominently bringing the matter before the teachers. The committee had previously hinted that they hardly had time to develop as fully as provided by the rules the capacity of the union. In the coming year they hoped this would be more completely carried out, and that they might receive the cordial support of the teachers. In concluding their report, the committee desired to acknowledge their great obligations to the parent union, an institution which, uniting as it did, irrespective of denomination, Sunday school workers throughout the kingdom, had been of un- told benefit to the Sunday school cause.
Mr. F. LAWRINSON, the treasurer, presented his financial statement, which was regarded as favourable.

The CILAIIIMAN moved the adoption of the report. He thought that they would agree with him that it was a very respectable one. Although not twelve months in existence they had been able to present to them a very fair amount of work, and what was always a satisfaction, there was a bal- ance against the treasurer. (Hear, hear, and laughter). The committee would like the teachers to interest them- selves and their scholars in the examinations which they in- tended to bring before the schools again. Mr. DROUGHT seconded the motion.which was carried un- animously. The Rev. T. PATERS proposed that the following gentle- men be the officers for the coming year :—President, Mr. B. Brown; vice-president, Mr. Thomas Marshall; chairman of committee, Mr. Samuel Drought; treasurer, Mr. F. Lawrin- son ; visitor, Mr. Roger Fogg; and secretaries, Messrs. T. J. Peters and Joseph Peet.

Mr. S. ROBINSON seconded the motion, observing that the gentlemen proposed were all eminent in Sunday school work. He congratulated them' upon the good step they had taken in establishing the Sunday School Union, which, be thought, would bring about a good state of feeling amongst the Nonconformist societies in the town. The motion was carried.
On the motion of Mr. S. B. STRINGER, seconded by Mr. S. ROBINSON, a vote of thanks was passed to the officers for their services 'during the past year.

The CHAIRMAN, in replying, said if he could be of any service during the next year he should be glad. (Hear, leer.) He took a great deal more interest in tbe union now than be did when he took office. He became president, not because he wanted the office, but because it was stated that there was no one else who would accept it. A union had already been tried among the schools of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, and considerable expense was gone to, but it failed; and there were a good many of the friends present—good Sunday school workers—who fought shy of the present union. He must say that he was one of those. He did not think the union would be of very great benefit to Sunday schools generally; he did not expect that there would he sufficlent interest taken in it to make it a benefit; but through the, way in which it had been worked, and the interest manifested in it, and especially through the inspiration which the members had received by the visit of their esteemed friend, Mr. Betsey, he believed the union would be of some benefit to Widnes. He hoped it would not be simply a name, but would make itself felt in every school throughout the town, and put them in the position they ought to occupy as Nonconformist Sunday school teachers. (Applause.) Mr. F. F. BELSEY, J.P. (ex-mayor of Rochester), atten- ding as a deputation from the parent union, then read his paper, which bore the title "In consideration of the present educational and religious circumstances of the country, how can we more perfectly adapt our Sunday school methods of organisation and instruction to the needs and sympathies of the young ? " Mr. Belsey expressed the great pleasure he had in attending the first annual meeting of the Widnes union, which he was pleased to find was making so good a start. The President was the right man in the right place, and he should earnestly look forward to seeing the Widnes union one of the best worked of their local Sunday school unions. (Applause.) Coming to his subject, Mr. Betsey said the educational condition of England was one of rapidly increasing development. The influence of recent Education Acts had not only brought their children within the day schools but by the force of the recognised obliga- tion regularly to attend to them, had led to a more punctual and steady attendance on the part of the younger scholars at the Sunday schools. The improved and improving character of the teaching power in the day schools was helping the child every day to more readily recognise not only a true and well qualified teacher, but to detect weakness and incapacity when such were visible in the Sunday school. How often in their Sunday schools did they see the man who could interest fifty children sitting besides the man who failed to interest five. Therefore, let them take care to ave,id teachers who had not what Mr. Schanffier, of New York, described as "scholar power" at all ; do not let them overweight those who had some but not much, and clo not let them waste the precious surplus of those running only part power. Referring to the general stampede of their young people from Sunday school, just at the age when they were most anxious to enfold them amidst Christian influence, Mr. Belsey said if teachers too busy to fulfil the important duty of yisiting the elder scholars, would appoint a class absentee -isitor, who would be the ready bearer of the loving message or note from teacher to the absent class-mate; if he was followed up where necessary by some kindly visitor appointed by the school itself, able to drop a winning word in the parents' ears, and in more pressing cases by the teacher himself, how much oftener would•their scholars be preserved from the teniptations charming them away from their care. Did their school organisation provide for reasonable prejudices, which although. largely overcome amidst favourable circumstances in many senior departments of their best schools, generally operated to the serious loss and injury of church and school? Had they been altogether wise in so long ignoring the re- monstrance of their departing senior scholars as they gave up Sunday school, "It is for children—we are no longer children ?" Mr. Betsey advocated the teaching of the seniors in a room distinct from the other scholars, a plan which had been found to work well in a church in which he was acquainted under the name of" Christian Institute," thus breaking off the juvenile associations con- nected with the word "school." Another weak point in school organisation was the very meagre opportunities for employment and respon- sibility in connection with church or school work which it afforded the young people, and which they were panting for. Alluding to method of instruction, Mr. Belsey observed that it was necessary that the teachers should be heart workers—men and women whose hearts the Lord has touched, and asked was the teachers' prayer meeting a languising institution in our schools? He spoke strongly in favour of a teachers' preparation class, remarking that the scholars should see as well as hear. Let the blackboard, the map, the diagram, to picture the object more than ever be brought to the assistance of the lips and tongue of the teacher, making the impression deeper and the memory more enduring.
A discussion, in which Mr. T. S. Swale, Rev. R. Harper, Messrs. S. B. Stringer, T. Reay, S. Drought, Kil- lingbeck, S. Robinson, C. Brown, and S. Owens took part, followed.
Mr. Belsey having replied, a vote of thanks was passed to him, on the motion of Mr. T. P. PETERS, seconded by Mr. S. ROBINSON.

The CHAIRMiN called upon Mr. Lawrinson to propose a vote of thanks to the gentleman and lady who had been Mr. Belsey's host and hostess during his visit, but Mr. BELSEY rose to his feet, and remarking that he was the person who ought to do that, made tthe proposition in a very appropriate speech. The motion was heartily carried, and a similar compli- ment having been paid the chairman for presiding, the meeting broke up.

LATEST NEWS.

---...,-...,-„,... FIFTY 'WHITE MEN MURDERED BY INDIANS. According to intelligence received from !New Mexico an Arizona, nearlY fifty white men have hem murdered by Apaches during the past four days. The Indians threaten to annihilate the white inhabitants in the thinly settled districts. Troops have been despatched in pursuit of the- marauders. ILLICIT WHISKY IN THE POTTE2IES. The police and excise officers of Hanley have, in conse— quence of the large quantity of illicit whisky wltich found its way lute the town and neighbocrhood, been recently making exhaustive inquiries, which have already resulted in the conviction of three people for making or dealing with illicit whiskY. On Thursday, another large still in full work, was discovered a few miles from the town. THE FENIAN ARRESTS AT LIVERPOOL. The Liverpool police have information that the arrest of the man Deasey, with the infernal machines in his posses- sion, and also of the railway porter Flanagan has prevented another outrage which had been fixed to be perpetrated on Thursday night, and which would have involved the demo- lition of a public building, and probably loss of life.. The police know the town in question but do not feel at liberty -to state it publicly. Experiznents have been made, which show the compound in the canisters to be possessed of enor- mous explosive power. Instructions are expected from the Home Secretary during the day as to the manner-in which the two men are to be dealt with.

Mr. Puleston will on Monday next ask the Government when they propose to give effect to the resolution in favour of sixpenny telegrams. Mr. Gladstone left Downing-street yesterday morning for Sandringham on a visit to the Prince of Wales. He will return to London on Monday. At a meeting at Carlisle, yesterday, of the creditors of the Mary-Port Hematite Iron Company, an offer of 2s in the £, by the debtors was accepted. A Privy Council order was gazetted last night;under date 28th March, prohibiting the landing in England, Wales, er Scotland of animals brought from France.. Thit order, will be in force from 6th April to 6th May next. The Good Templars' Grand Lodge, Sitting at Gloucester yesterday, passed a resolution strongly urging the Govern-- ment to rteal with the liquor question, and not attempt to give the drink traffic a new lease of life. A passage leading from Dowoing-streel to the Horse Guards, and above which are some of the rooms of Mr. Gladstoße's official residence, is from this date to be closed after six in the evening, a notice to that effect having been posted yesterday.

At a-meeting-of colliery representatives of South Wales and Monmouthshire, held at Cardiff yestPrday, it was re- solved to summon a conference of house and steam coal dele- gates to meet at Aberdare on the 23rd and 24th April to con— sider the c,xisting sliding scale arrangements. The ship Normanhursr, from Java to Greenock, which called at Queenstown for orders on Wednesday, and then gave information of having passed two derelicts, has herself been wrecked on the Welsh coast. It is feared Captain Mcßride and a crew of 22 men have all been drowned. An exciting scene was witnessed at Cefn Mawr, near Wrexham, on Thursday. A boy fell into the canal, and his cries attracted a large number of women who screamed for. assistance. Another boy, 10 years of age, fortunately hap- pened to come by, and the brave little fellow atonee plunged into the water and succeeded in rescuing the drowning boy. It is intended to bring this brave deed under the notice of the authorities.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. • HOUSE OF COMMONS. LOCAL OPTION,—Mr. CAINE, on behalf of Sir W. Law- son, gave notice that on that day four weeks he would move a resolution in favour of Local Option. THE CUBAN REFUGEES.—Lord G. FITZHAIIRICE made statement confirmatory of the report published in to-day's papers relative to the release of the Cuban refugees.--Sir R. CROSS said the answer of the noble lord not being satis- factory, he should proceed with his motion with regard to the release of all the refugees, and ask the Premier to fix a day to enable him to do so.
THE BECHT:JANA CHIEFS—Mr. ASTLEY said he was not yet in a position to give any information as to the course intended to be pursued with regard to the techuana chiefs.

UNIFORMITY OF FRANCIIISH.-Mr. ARNOLD called atten- tion to the representation of the people, and hioved a resolution in favour of uniformity of franchise through- out the United Kingdom by a franchise similar in principle to the present English borough franchise. He pointed out the necessity that existed for a redistri- bution of political power, and the advantage that would arise if the entire elections were conducted on one and the same day by the latter arrangement. Continued ex- citement would be avoided, and the expense to candidates greatly reduced. He expressed a hope that the Govern- ment would take the matter earnestly in hand, and thus make uniformity of franchise a reality.—Mr. A. ELLIOT seconded the resolution, and justified the bringing in of a large portion of the rural population in coun- ties to the privileges of the franchise.--Colonel ALEXANDER opposed the resolution both as mischievous and inoppor- tune.—Sir W. HARCOURT said the Government believed the subject one that the present Parliament was elected to accomplish, and with every word of the resolution he be- lieved he might say the Government agreed.—Mr. RAIKES, opposed the resolution, believing that if it was carried into effect old constituencies would be swamped by the new.— Mr. FORSTER said the present Parliament was elected to prevent the anomaly of county houvholders not having a. vote. They had got beyond the abstract resolutions on that subject, and were waiting for the Government Bill giving the county franchise to county householders.—The House was counted out at 7-40.

THE ST. HELENS MINERS AND THEIR GRIEYANCES.--The committee of the St. Helens Branch of the Miners' Federa- tion, on Wednesday, issued an announcement, of which the following is the text:—" Notice to St. Helens Miners. Your representatives have been insulted by the manager of a colliery in this district, who refused to meet them to dis- cuss a grievance. There will be a meeting on the Market- square on Thursday night to discuss the state of affairs at the colliery in question. Men, will you be sent home two or three days each week, and be deprived of work through upholding a good cause? The good time islcoming, if miners will only stand firm and be united." PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD ELECTIOX.—The triennial election of members of Prescot School Board takes place on Saturday. The following 10 gentlemen bare been nomina- ted for the seven seats :—W. L. Evans, J.P., Fazae- kerley House, Prescot; Henry Fogg, Middleton House. Whiston • William Goldsworth, Yew Tree Farm, Eccleston; James Turner Hall, Prescot Hall, Preseot ; T. P. Hewitt, Plumbs House, Whiston ; C. B. Johnson, Kemble-street, Prescot; James _Mawdsley, Market-place, Prescot; J. B. Sanders, Eccleston-street, Prescet ; Castle Spenceley, The Elms, Knowsley. Of these gentlemen three, viz., Messrs. Dyson, Mawdsley, and Johnson, have retired, so that there will be no contest.

- - - PIGEON MILK. Sir,—Kindly allow me space to remind the writer of the 4" Household pets" column that his pen moat have slipped, 4r his thoughts wandered, when he mentioned" pap" as the -substance parent pigeons feed their young with. . "Milk" as the correct term, not pap. The existence of pigeon milk is a fact. Has hef or she, never heard the story of the chil- dren who went into the wood to search for the birds that -made milk, and who, when they returned unsuccessful, were reproached by their own "pet doves." Again, just as " acineakers" fatten and thrive during the "sucking term," ao in the Indian and Kaffir folk-lore stories bird milk is -credited with possessing the virtue of making the bodies of those who drink it fat, and their skins shiny. The pigeon provides milk for its young, just as greyhounds can un emergency provide soup for their pupa, or an ingenious boy, when sent to fetch stirrup•oil, takes a rise out of his would-be tormentors by producing the veritable article.-1 am, Sir, &c., ANCiLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, S.E. •

POLICE INTELLIGENCE. WARRIN. GTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. BenritrAr.—Before Alderman Chandiey. There were several cases for disposal, but there being only magistrate present, they were adjourned until Wednesday. MoNDAT.—Before Alderman Davies, Major Cartwright, and Mr. John Fairclough, DRlJNYElninss.—Bethesda Knoatton, for having been drunk and disorderly, on Saturday evening, was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. BlTspiciOnS Fuery, 79, Lower Bank- street, and Martin Connelly, Dolman's-lane, persons of sus- picious characters, were each charged with having been found in Orford-street, on Saturday evening, for an unlawfnl pur- pose, and, on the evidence of P.C. ifonoghan, were remanded till Wednesday. WEDNESDAy.—Before Alderman Davies, Alderman Chandley,

and Mr. John Fakelough. DRUNINNNISS.—For this offence John Harris was fined ss. and costs, and John Bohan 103. and costs. VAGRANCT.—George Gerard, for having slept in a shed be- longing to Mr. John Welsby, Fennel-street, was sentenced to one month's Imprisonment with hard labour. ROUNDING ON I COMPANION.—Wm. Fuery and M. Connelly were charged with having been in Orford-street, on Saturday night last with intent to commit a felony. P.O. Monoghan was on duty in Orford-street, and found the prisoners, whom he suspected intended to commit a felony. He was approach- ing them when Fuery espied him and,walked away. Connelly, on being accosted by the officer, admitted that they were about to commit a theft. He had been with Fuery at an early part of the evening, and the latter told him that he intended to take some ropes tLat were on the sailway, near Coekhedge factory. At Fuery's request he accompanied him to Orford- street, but when Fuery saw the officer he walked away and left him (Connelly) who did rot see the officer, to shift for him- self.—Fuery was sentenced to one month's imprisonment with bard labour, and Connelly to 14 days'. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reyrolds, Mr. John White, and . _
Mr. Ziba -Armitage. The cases of interest will be found reported lo another eolumn.
DARESBITRY PETTY SESSIONS. TrZSDA.Y.—Before 3.1 r. dward G eenall and Ur. W. C. Jones. _ _ _

DRUNEENNESS.—Charies Saville was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk at Appleton. A FURIOUS DRIVER —Thos. Holcroft was fined 5s and costs for driving his horse and trap on the highway, at Stretton, to the danger of the pasrengers thereon. A WARNING co BREAD BAKERS.—James Strange, F. W. Hallwood, Thomas Carter, Samuel Davies, and John Roberts were each charged with haying carried out bread for sale and delivered it without having weights and scales for weighing it. —Each defendant was ordered to pay Is and costs. REMOVING A COW WITHOUT A LICENSE.—Edward Mflhing- ton and Frank Millington were charged—the first-named with having allowed to be, and the latter with having, removed a COW from Wartingi on to Stretton without having Previously ehtained & license for such removal. —The defendants stated that they had been informed no license was required.—A fineOf 2s 6d including costs was impozed. ENDANGERING THE PUBLIC SAFET7.—GOO. Dutton was fined 6s and costs for erecting and working a steam thrashing engine within 25 yards of the highway, on Mr. Beeches' farm, at Grappenhall, on the 2nd inst. A SLEEPY DPAYmAIs.--Wm. punt was fined Is and costs for haling been asleep whilst in charge of a dray, at Moore, on the 17th inst. FAILING TO REPORT CASES OF SWINE FEVER.—John Taylor, Appleton, was charged with hying two pigs suffering from swine fever, and not reporting the same to the authorit'es.—A police officer and Mr. Darwin, veterinary surgeon, went to de- fendant's premises and found that two of his pigs had been burled. Mr. Darwin had the pigs exhumed, and he examined them and found that they had died of swine fever.—The de- fendant, who is an old man and unable to read, pleaded ignorance.—The Bench said there seemed to have been no at- tempt at concealment, and they would deal leniently with the defendant, who would have to pay the costs, 12s 6d.—Thos. Moors, Antrobus, was charged with a similar offence. On the 18th ult. the defendant reported a case of swine fever on his premises, and the pig was slaughtered: On the 22nd ult. a police officer visited the defendant's premises, and found one of the pigs very bad with the fever. On coming away he met defendant and told him of this, and the defendant said he knew the day before tkat the pig was ill, and if it grew no better he intended to report it.—A fine csf 53 and costs was im- posed.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MoNDAY.—Before Messrs. henry Reynolds (chairman) and
. C. W. If az:eburst. • The eases of ilterest will be found reported in another column.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAT.—Before Mr. John Brock and -Ti. George Fl I kin gton INERRIATES.—The following persons were fined for drunken- ness :—James Henry Young, James Eustace, Thomas Welding, Michael Flannery, Joseph Worrell, Edward Connor. Mary Black, Bridget Barrett, Thomas Blinkhorn, Peter Tansey, John McGarry, Lawrence Keegan, Maria Keegan, John Mur- ray, and Catherine Owen. BREACH OF THE PACE.—Patrick Brophy and Alfred Kul- ham, young men, weie charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting together in Hale-rcad, Ditton, on the lath inst.—Brophy stated Kilham was the aggressor. and called witnesses who corroborated his statement.—He was ordered to pay the costs. A warrant was issued against Kit- ham, who did not appear. immix i CHARGE.—CLarIes Smithson was charged with having, on the 16th inst., been drunk whilst in zharge of a horse and lorry in T'etoria-road, Widnes.—P.O. Barker and P.S. Clarkson proved the case, and the defendant was fined 103 and costs. MAINTENANCE OF A 10N.—Jchn Bowe, who did not appear, was summoned for the arrears of an order made upon him at Et. Helens, on the 3rd April last year, to pay 2s per week to- wards the support of his son in an industrial school.—The arrears amounted to £3 12s, and Superintendent Barker and Inspector Barker hayjng stated the facts of the case, the Bench made an order for the amount to be paid in seven days. AN trEMANAGEAEL': Mobley, 16 years of ago, was charged with Oeeping cut —Superintendent Barker said the prisoner was unmanageable. Be had been fined fis for wilful damage, committed a month for theft, and fined 2s 8d for playing cards.—The Bencll sent him to gaol for 14 days' bard labour.

"Well, then, if a man is born in Bolland, is he a Hole ?" "Tut, tut; I'll answer no more of your silly questions." It was recorded as something remarkable that Gottschalk had composed a piece of music for thirty pianos. Upon reading which Mac declared it nothing wonderful, for he knew a man who had written several pieces for forte_

pianos! "Jeanie," said an old Cameronian to his daughter, who was asking his permission to marry, "Jeanie, it's a very solemn thing to get married." "I ken that, father," said the sensible lassie, "but it's a great deal solcinner to be single." SERVICE OF SONG AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCH*, EARLES- TOWN.—On Sunday afternoon last the Church of Sc. John the Baptist was crowded with an attentive congregation who assembled to hear a service of song entitled "The Sa- viour King" by the choir of the church. Mr. H. J. Duman efßciently conducted the singing and presided at the organ with his accustomed and well-known ability. The various selections were rendered with considerable skill, and the ser- vice from beginning to end was greatly enjoyed by all pre- sent. The connective readings, illustrative of the life and sufferings of Jesus Christ, were given by the vicar, Rev. T. B. Matthews. A collection was made in aid of the Sunday school fund.

div.head: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.

The Rev. J. G. Richards, vicar, presided at the annual vestry meeting of the above church held on Tuesday morn- ing. There were present Messrs. P. Calvert, Hewitt, Dagnall, and Woeds (vestry clerk.)—The VICAR thought they had every reason to congratulate themselves upon what had been accomplished during the past year. The church had been got out of debt, they had worked har- moniously together, they had had good congregations; and the only drawbacks that he could remember were that the churchwarden Mr. Calvert, was taken ill during his term of office and had not thoroughly recovered, and that Mr. Hemment was about to leave them. They had reason to regret Mr. Hemment's removal, as he thought that gentle- man and his family had been most useful in getting up the bazaar and making efforts to get the church out of debt. He thought they might say the same of Mr. Calvert and his family and others who had done much for the bazaar, and they deserved their best thanks for the manner in which they had helped the church out of its financial difficulties.— Mr. Thomas Brocklehurst was elected vicar's warden, and Mr. Richard Hewitt parishioners' warden.—Messrs. Peter Calvert, Wm. Richardson, Thomas Rigby, and Wm. Gleave were appointed sidesmen ; and Messrs. Stephen Looker Williams and Charles Calvert lay representatives.—A vote of thanks to the vicar for presiding concluded the meet- in.

The expenditure was £236 16;. 4d.,, which with £2lO 45. id. paid to the rector for distribution to sick and Poor, and charitable institu. tions, brought the total to £458 Os. 5d., leaving a balance of £6 ss. in hand.—The accounts were audited and passed.— The next businas was the appointment of parish warden, and the RECTOR, before the appointment was proceeded with, pointed out the peculiar position in which they were placed. There WAF, I groat responsibility attending the °Mee for the nod year. On account of the violent storm they had encountered, a great deal of damage had been done, and to put everything in a perfect state they would want £5OO. They wanted to save all the money they possibly could in the shape of architect's fees, and he sug- gesZed that it would be advisable to appoint a man to the office whO knew something of the work that required doing. —Mr. W. H. HAnnisos proposed the appointment of Mr. J. E. Wright, and Mr. Alderman WEBSTER seconded the proposition, which was carried.—The RECTOR then re-ap- pointed Mr. Wm. Dooley as his warden.—Mr. J. Dewhurst and Mr. T. Moores were nominated as sidesmen by Mr. Dooley and Mr. Wright, and in addition there were ap- pointed Messrs. Wm. Gill, James Morris, Stanley Higham, and N. B. Percival—On the motion of Mr. DOOLEY, seconded by Mr. PERCIVAL, it was decided to lay a voluntary rate of 31. in the .Z.—Mcssrs. Webster and Buckton were re-elected lay representatives, and Mr. James Nicholson, vestry clerk. —The RECTOR then produced the architect's report on the state of the church, and said he would be happy to take upon himself the whole of the expense of the repairs to the chancel amounting to £32.—Mr. WEES'TER remarked that the statement would give very great satisfaction to the parishioners.—Mr. BUCKTOII stated that the repair of the chancel was a duty which devolved upon the rector of the parish.—A conversation then ensued respecting the archi- tect's report, and it was agreed that it was not absolutely 1 necessary to carry out the whole of the work mentioned therein, but no resolution was come to on the matter.—A vote of thanks was accorded to the Rector, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: BANK 110LIDAY AT WARRINGTON,
div.p: BANK 110LIDAY AT WARRINGTON,

The Easter Monday bank holiday was generally regarded by the people of Warrington. The works throughout the town were stopped, and it was only here and there in the principal streets that the deserted appearance presented by the long lines of shuttered and barred establishments was broken by an open shop. However, even where the shutters had been taken down it was in the majority of cases as much with the view of supplying holiday-makers with creature comforts as of increasing the gains of the proprietor of the establishment. As to the weather, it was as fickle as that of an April day, and was a marked -uouirasi io the bright sun- shine of Good riLtAy. The morning opened with a dull leaden sky, which became more dense about 10 o'clock whenl there was a smart fall of snow. As the snow ceased, there were observable in the sky streaks of blue, which gradually extended, until the sun broke out and completely dispelled the leaden-hued clouds. The sun shone until the afternoon was well advanced, and then the dark clouds again gathered, and resulted in another downfall of snow. The gloomy morning doubtless deterred many from venturing upon a journey to one of the numerous pleasure resorts in the vici- nity, but a large number of persons, during the favourable change in the weather later on in the day' availed themselves of the opportunity of spending a few hours out of town. For those who remained at home there were the attractions ef the park, and also those afforded by the river, and a revival of the old Warrington sports. It is nearly thirty years since the sports were an institution of the town, but Monday last showed that it only wanted a little effort to I make the sports as popular as ever they were. The sports were held in Arpley, in a field known as the " Anglesea,' kindly lent by Mr. John Cross, where about five thousand people assembled to participate in the fun. There were donkey, sack, wheelbarrow, pony, and foot races, all of which went off satisfactorily. Indeed everything passed off , in a most orderly manner, and will doubtless encourage the ' committee to make the sports an annual affair.. On the river a series of boat races took place, and they were originated with the object of reviving the once popular War- rington regatta. The first event was a sailing match, the boats starting from Fiddler's Ferry, sailing round a buoy at Mandock Bay, and finishing at Mr. Capner's stage. It resulted as follows :—let prize, £3 17s. 6d., Deerfoot (captain, T. Skellhorn); 2nd prize, £2 17s. GI Spud (captain, W. Leigh) ; 3rd prize, £2 2s. 6d., Red Jack ' (captain J. Leigh); 4th prize, £1 7s& 1., Chuckho (captain, W. Welding); sth prize, 17s. 61, Lively (captain, G. Higham). There was a fair breeze' and the sailing on the whole was good. A four- oared race from Mandock Bay to Walton Arches and back was won by Skellhorn's crew, prize, £2 103. ; 2nd prize, 10s., Wild's crew. In a single-oar sculling race from Mandock Bay to Mr. Capner's stage, the first prize, £l, fell to John Edgar; the second, 103., being obtained by John Webb. Samuel and Laurence Spencer secured first prize,lllos., in a pair-oared race from Mandock Bay round a buoy at Wilderspoal and back; the second prize, 10s., being won by Thomas and John Skell- horn. Notwithstanding the thousands of persons who thronged the banks of the river there was only one immer- sion during the day, and it was that of a man apparently under the influence of drink, whose double "ducking" caused much amusement to the spectators. The holiday- makers were exceedingly well behaved, and no better proof of this can be given than that which is afforded by the records of the police court, where not a single charge was booked during the day.
PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The usual fortnightly muting of this Board was held on

div.head: BURIAL FESS.
div.p: BURIAL FESS.

The Master's report book contained the following entry: —"A Catholic inmate of the workhouse was buried on Monday, the 12th inst., at Prescot cemettiy. The master sent the usual request to the priest asking him to attend the funeral, but learned next morning that no religions cere- mony had taken place. The master at once waited upon the priest, and was informed by him that he required a fee for each pauper funeral before he could undertake to attend. To prevent another occurrence of this nature the Master arranged with the priest for his attendance at any funeral that might take place before the matter could be brought under the notice of the Board. Will the Board kindly con- sider the question."—At a meeting of the Visiting Com- mittee the Master bad read some correspondence with the Rev. R. Brindle, of Present, on the subject.—The CLERK said the matter should be referred to the Visiting Com- mittee, as it was one affecting the workhouse, and the Visit- ing Committee would hriag up a report as to the fees that ought to he paid, if any, and the practice of other unions similarly situated. —On the motion of the Rev. T. CHAMBERS, the ,subject was referred to the Vibiting Com- mittee.

The annual meeting of the ratepayers of Ashton was held at the Local Board Offices, Bryn-street, on Wednesday. The proceedings were merely of a formal character, and the attendance very small. A vote of thanks to the retiring overseers (Messrs. Valiant and Clarke) was accorded on the motion of the Chairmanj seconded by Dr. Hannah. The statement of accounts showed that there was a balance of £879 in hand, and it was intimated that the ratepayers might reasonably expect a reduction in the rates for the ensuing year. It was moved by Dr. Hannah, and seconded by Mr. James Hill, that the names of Mr. William Valiant and Mr. C. F. Clark be at the head of the list of names to be submitted to the magistrates (who will select two as overseers), and that the following be added: Mr. William Richardson, Mr. Edward Burchall, Mr. Thomas Crompton, and Mr. John Wilkinson. This was the only business, and the meeting was brought to a close.
SERIOUS JEWEL ROBBERY AT ASHTON—EXTRAORDINARY CASE.—Thomas, Varty, an apprentice_ watchmaker, is in

_ . custody at Ashton on a charge Of breaking and entering the shop of Mr. Thomas Milner, Warrington-road, Ashton, and stealing therefrom a quantity of gold brooches, gold ear- rings, ctc., amounting in value to £22 ; and Elizabeth Shar- rington and Louisa Sharrington, mother and daughter, are also in custody for receiving the above-named property, well knowing it to have been stolen. The details of the case are of an extraordinary character. Sometime about the 16th inst. Narty effected an entrance into the premises by taking out a square of glass in the back kitchen window and afterwards unscrewing the lock from a door leading into the shop. He then secured the jewellery and returned as he had proceeded—replacing the lock on the door and again fixing the glass in the window. It is stated that several persons were asleep in the rooms upstairs at the time, and a dog was kept on the premises. The robbery was not dis- covered until some time afterwards—the thief being found out in a somewhat remarkable way. A young woman, named Williams, attempted to sell a gold bracelet for 6d. at a jeweller's shop in Wigan, but as it was seen to be worth about 18s. a constable was sent for. Enquiries were after- wards made, which resulted in the prisoners being appre- hended on the charges named. The two Sharrington's had disposed of some of the brooches and rings. The prisoners wdre brought up at the Wigan County Police Ccurt, on Tuesday, but were remanded until to-day (Friday), when the case will be fully gone into.

THE ASHTON LOCAL BOARD ELECTION—PROBABLE CON- TEST.—From present appearances the annual election of seven members of the Ashton Local Board will not be al- lowed to pass without a contest, which gives every promise that it will be a very spirited and closely-fought one. The ratepayers are manifesting considerable interest in the pre- liminary proceedings, and as eleven candidates for the seven vacant " chairs" appear in the field, the chances of each are being discussed with some eagerness. The re- tiring members are Messrs. T. Aspinall, Edward Burchall, Theodore Drayton Grimke, Adolphus Benedictus Moubert, Joseph Pimblett, Rev. Henry Siddall, and James Wright. The first named gentleman has not again been put forward, but the Right Hon. Lord Gerard, .of Garswood Hall, has nominated the remaining six, and also John Lyon, of Woreley Mesnes, near Wigan, gentleman. The other aspir- ing candidates are William Boardman, 76, Gerard-street, Ashton, provision dealer, nominated by William Latimer, of 74, Gerard-street, Ashton; Thomas Crompton, Downall Green, hinge manufacturer, nominated by William Latimer; John Fairhurst, Arch-lane, Ashton, farmer, nominated by Thomas Mather, 17, Liver- pool-road; and William France, 28, Bolton-road, cashier, nominated by Wm. Latimer. It may be remembered that at the election last year Mr. Boardman was one of the de- feated candidates, but he again puts forth his claims to a seat on the Board. The voting papers were delivered on Wednesday last, and each voter can vote for seven of the candidates. The papers must ba filled up before the 3rd of April (next Tuesday) when they will be called for, and the votes will be counted on the following Thursday. TEA MEETING AND BAZAAR AT ASHTON.—The Congre- gationalists of Ashton are making a praiseworthy effort to clear off the debt remaining on their chapel and schools, and there is every probability that within the next few weeks that object will be accomplished. The original debt was formerly £350, but by various efforts it was reduced to £9O, at which sum it at present stands. To reduce this amount, and if possible wipe it off altogether, a tea meeting and bazaar were held on Monday last; an entertainment was given on Wednesday, and in about a fortnight a concert will take place. The bazaar was held in the schoolroom in Gerard-street, Ashton, and though the affair was on a small scale, the room presented a cheering and inviting appear- ance. A stall had been erected on each side of the room, and these were well stocked with useful and ornamental articles. The stalls were in charge of Mrs. Wilson, Miss Latham, Mrs. Ashton, Mrs. Latimer, and Miss Wheeler. At one end of the room was a refreehment stall, which was looked after by Miss Wood. In addition to these were a number of other attractions, including a " museum " and " fine art gallery," ," fishing tank," and "astronomical telescope," while Mr. James Roberts exhibited, some really fine and artistic original views and drawings—to see which a small sum had to be paid. Before the bazaar was declared open a public tea meeting was held, and about 200 persons were present. The tea was a very substatial one, and was well served by the following ladies: Mrs. Wilson, Mrs. Fairless, Miss Stobie, Miss Ferguson, Mrs. France, Mrs. John Latham, Mrs. Winstanley, Mrs. Pomfret, Mrs. Bennett, and Mrs. Crompton. After tea the Rev. H. Wilson presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. Mr. Potts, of Crewe, Mr. R. Whittle, of Crewe, Dr. Latham, and Mr. C. Latham.—The Chairman explained the objects for which the bazaar was being held, to what the funds would be devoted, and introduced Mr. Whittle, who had kindly come to declare the bazaar open.— Mr. Whittle was warmly received. He referred to his early connection with the Ashton Congregational Church, and alluded to the great changes that had taken place, and the success the Congregational movement had met with during the time that had passed. He hoped that venture would be a success, and concluded by declaring the sale of work open.—The Rev. Mr. Potts then briefly addressed the meet- ing, after which Mr. C. Latham moved a hearty vote of thanks, which was seconded by Dr. Latham, and carried with acclamation.—The sales were then proceeded with. In the evening there was a crowded attendance, and the room presented a gay appearance. The Congregational temper- ance brass baud was present, and gave selections of music at intervals, while songs, ate., were also given by the mem- bers of the choir and friends. The receipts during the even- ing amounted to nearly £4O, but this sum was increased on the following day, when the bazaar was again opened. CADISHEAD.

CONGREGATIONALISM AT CADISILEAD.—A Congregationalist 1 School-Chapel for the neighbourhood of Cadishead was opened on Good Friday afternoon by the Rev. J. A. Mac- fadyen, who preached the sermon, the service being taken part in by the Revs. W. Reid and J. Yonge. For several years past a mission has been conducted in Cadishead by laymen under the management of Mr. Yong°, but the growth of the population of the district has recently made IL desirable that the temporary premises used for the pur- poses of the mission should be exchanged for larger and more commodious quarters. Accordingly the school- chapel opened on Good Friday has been erecttd at a cost of about .£6OO. Towards this sum the treasurer had re- ceived £250, and promises to the extent of £lOO more. The committee also have received promises for £lOO, conditional on the debt being cleared off before the end of the present year. This makes a total of £450 cash received and pro- mised, and it was hoped that the collections of Good Fri- day and Easter Sunday would greatly reduce the balance of £l5O.

div.head: bARESBUR'F.
div.p: bARESBUR'F.

A FEMALE POACHER AT DA.RESEURY.—On Tuesday, at Daresbury Petty Sessions, Eliza Powell, a married woman, was charged with having, on the 26th ultimo, trespassed on land in the occupation of Mr. Hayes, at Daresbury, and also with having taken game without having a license.—Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant.—One of the assistant gamekeepers to Sir Richard Brooke said that on the 25th ultimo he found several snares set on a field in the occupa- tion of Mr. Hayes, and he and George Rigby, another assis- tant gamekeeper, watched the place. The following morn- ing, about six o'clock, they saw the defendant enter the field. He saw her take up a rabbit, and on going to her found that she had a bag containing a hare, three rabbits, and six anares.—George Rigby corroborated.—The Bench fined defendant 10s. and costs in the first case, and ss. and onsts in the second case.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

GAMBLING AT OVERTON. On Saturday last, at the Oc- casional Court-house, Frodshatn, John Kewgh, who stated he belonged to Liverpool, was charged by the police with gambling on the public highway, near Overton hills, on the 23rd inst. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, an 3, in default of payment was committed for fourteen days' hard labour. .

On Sunday afternoon, while two men were sailing in a small boat in the river Mersey below Frodsham, they picked up the body of a man, which had apparently been in the water several days. The body was that of a sailor of foreign appearance, being about 35 years of age. He was wearing a blue pilot coat, striped woollen shirt, grey-worsted stock- ings, and low boots. In his pockets were found two spirit bottles and ten cents. The corpse was taken to the Queen's Head Hotel, Frodsham, and an inquest was held by Mr. Churton, coroner, on Tuesday, when the body was identified as that of George Hindley, of Barnton, a flatman, aged 42 years. It was stated in evidence that the deceased fell off the flat " Sarah " near Liverpool, at about one o'clock on the morning of the 13th February last, and it is supposed that the body must have been in a sand bank, as it was in a good state of preservation. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned." GOLBORNE. div.head: POOR LAW CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE POOR LAW CONFERENCE.

The CLY.mt read a letter from Mr. John Holgate, secretary of the N'orth Western Poor Law Conference, convening a meetir4 of representatives of Guardians, to be held in Man- ehe'ster on April 3rd, to consider the Poor Removal Bill Vireland), the Maintenance of Children Bill, and any other , bills introduced, or to be introduced into Parliament this session respecting poor-law administration; and also to make preliminary arrangements for bolding next year's con- ference.—The CHAIRMAN proposed that the letter lie on the table,—The CLERK : This is a case where you won't get anything allowed.—Mr. TYRER said that if he was a Guardian when the meeting was held he would attend at his own expense.—Mr. MEADOWS said that he also would gladly attend, because much valuable information was to be obtained at such meetings. They would have to pay their own expenses.—The CHAIRMAN: We will not pay them.—Mr. TYRER :We will not ask -you. In ibis case ' even the ss. will not be allowed.—The CHAIRMAN: Will our friend Mr. Hall go ?—Mr. HALL: Oh, yes, I will go.— The Rev. T. CHAMBERS : I move th9.t the three gentlemen go—at their own cost. (Laughter.)—The motion was seconded and agreed to. THE:AUDIT. The CLERIC announced that the audit had been ad- journed till April 14th.
A FEVER HOSPITAL FOR PRESCOT.
The Visiting Committee recommended that the attention
of the Prescot—Local Beard be called to the number of cases

of fever being admitted into the workhouse hospital from their district, and the necessity of their providing hospital accommodation for such cases.—Mr. LEATHEBBLEROW in- quired if the same thing would not apply to other local boards, and the Clerk replied that it would.—The recom- mendation was confirmed.

div.head: VAGRANT WARDS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: VAGRANT WARDS AT ST. HELENS.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, held on the 20th inst., the Clerk read a letter, dated 4th March, from the Town Clerk of St. Helens, replying to he resolu- tion adopted at the previous meeting of the committee with respect to the application of the Town Council for the pro- vision of vagrant wards in St. Helens. The committee re- solved that the subject be considered after the formation of the new Board.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS remarked that if it were possible he should like to have more than six hours' notice of the meeting of the committee, otherwise they might !ming upon themselves the accusation of treating the vagrant wards in a somewhat "casual " manner. He re- ceived only six hours' notice of the last meeting, and con- sequently he was unable to attend.—Mr. P. LONGTON said it would have been advisable if the committee had given the Clerk instructions to get up some information against the formation of the new Board because it was quite a new thing for them.—Mr. SADLER : It means a large expense to the Union because other people may apply for the same thing. Mr. MEADOWS said it was some tim since the St. Helens Corporation applied for the warde and he did not see why the present Board were not in as position to settle the matter. The matter should not be staved off because the Corporation were entitled to a definite reply.—Mr. TYRER said the Corporation did slot seem in a great hurry, because the committee did not receive their last letter till nearly a month after their meeting.— Mr. MEADOWS: If we are short of information, the sooner it is got the better. In common courtesy we should reply in one way or the other.—Mr. FIDLER remarked that the Guardians of the City of London had advertised for sale their vagrant wards in Fenchurch-street.—Mr. NEWSOME thought the committee were acting very wisely in post- poning the consideration of the matter. With regard to the information Mr. Longton 'asked for, he thought the present officers of the Union were quite able to give all the informa- tion the Guardians needed.—Mr. MEADOWS: We know very well they don't need vagrant wards in St. Helens.—Mr. HALL: We can see how vagrancy is dropping off.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS asked if the matter ought to be referred to the new Board if their minds were made up so thoroughly as they appeared to be.—Mr. FIDLER: But, pardon me, they are not made up.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said all the Guardians who had expressed an opinion were decided. The Vagrant Act was doing its work so well that there was a va- grant ward to be parted with in London. As their minds seemed to be made up that vagrant wards were not wanted in St. Helens at present, why put the question off to the new Board ?—Mr. FIDLER said the City of London Guardians having advertised their wards for sale.. had not altered his opinion, but his opinion had not been expressed.—The CLERK explained with regard to the six hours notice, that it was his fault a longer notice had not been given. It was not his intention at first to have a meeting of the Com- mittee, but he afterwards thought that as it was a subject the Guardians were not likely to take up for a month or two yet, and he did not wish the Corporation to supose they were slighting them, or not giving due consideration to their letter, he called the meeting in order to get the matter formaly adjourned till the new Board was formed.—Mr. NEWSOME said the Board had asked the clerk to apply ba the Corporation for statistics to show the necessity of the wards, and they had not got those statistics.—The CLERK said the Corporation were woiking, up their case.—The resolution of the Committee was con- firmed.

div.head: MASTER'S CLERK.
div.p: THE MASTER'S CLERK.

The Visiting Committee recommended, having regard to the infirm state of health of the master's clerk, that the clerk to the Guardians be empowered to engage a suitable person as master's clerk, at a salary of £3O per annum with rations, tic., in the Workhouse, and that the Local Govern- ment Board be asked if the Guardians could make a retiring allowance to Mr. Larimer.—The recommendation was approved.

div.head: REVALUATION Or TOWNSHIPS.
div.p: REVALUATION Or TOWNSHIPS.

Mr: MEADOWS stated that the overseers of a number of townships had made application to the Assessment Com- mittee for certain works and properties to be revalued. He moved that the Assessment Committee be authorised to employ Messrs. Raby and Sons to value such works and property in the Union as the committee thought fit. Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co. had appealed against a valuation made recently by Messrs. Raby and Sons, but the Assess- ment Committee had confirmed that valuation. He, there- fore, moved that the Assessment Committee appear as re- spondents in the name ef the Guardians in the appeal to the quarter sessions by Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., against the rating of their works in the township of Widnes.—The CLERIC, in answer to the CHAIRMAN, explained that the appointment of Messrs. Raby and Sons arose from the overseers of their large town- ships asking the committee to employ a professional firm to revalue the property in those townships.—Mr. FIDLER: And the new zeal of the overseers is entirely on payment by commission.—The CLERK said he had received a notice from Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s solicitors that they proposed prosecuting their appeal at the quarter sessions in April. and he therefore asked for authority to engage such legal assistance as might be necessary for resisting the appeal. He asked this to cover any quibble on the auditor's part, because the Assessment Committee could do it without any authority, but they had better have the consent of .the Board so as to get over that zealous official—On the motion of Mr. LEAMIERI3ARROW, seconded Isy Mr. SADLER, the resolutions moved by Mr. Meadows were agreed to, and the authority asked for by the clerk was given.

div.head: ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WINDLE.
div.p: THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WINDLE.

On the motion of Mr. FIDLER, seconded by Mr. JAc4sox, Mr. Twist was appointed for three months at a salary at the rate of £BO per annum to assist his father, the assistant overseer for Windle, who was to ill to attend to his duties.

div.head: UNION FINA.NCES.
div.p: THE UNION FINA.NCES.

Mr. NEWSOME read a return which had been prepared for him by the clerk showing the receipts and expenditure of the Union during the past three years. The total income dming that period was £150,170, or £51,000 a year. The expenditure was as follows :—Maintenance in workhouse, £17,359; outdoor relief, £34,727; maintenance in lunatic asylums, £10,190; loans and interest repaid on workhouse, £4,118; salaries and rations for officers, £7,586; other expenses connected with relief, £9,611 ' • law proceedings, £259; payments to county treasurer, £34,666; payments to treasurers of highway boards and rural sanitary authority, £12,896; payments to Widnes and Prescot school boards, £10,199; school attendance committee expenses, £531; payments on account of registration, £1,250; vaccination expenses, £1,535 • parliamentary registration of jury lists, £694; school fees for non-pauper children, £610; expenses under Union Assessment Act, £593; salaries, per- centage, and superannuation of parochial officers, £5,524. He moved that the return be printed and circulated for the information of the public.—The motion was seconded, and agreed to.

GOOD FRIDAY AND EASTER MONDAY AT EARLESTOWN. —As the Viaduct, Vulcan, and other works in the neigh- bourhood of Earlestown were stopped from the Thursday afterneon before Good Friday until Tuesday morning last, it will be readily understood that the days in the interim were very quiet, and wore a holiday aspect. Fortunately the weather was fine on Good Friday, though a cold wind greatly interfered with the comfort of pleasure seese,rs. A considerable number of persons left the town for popular places of resort—parties also proceeding to Frodsham and Warrington. All the shops were closed and business was at an entire standstill. During the day Newton was pretty largely patronised by visitors from neighbouring districts, and in the afternoon and evening, the usually quiet and unassuming village presented quite a gay and animated ap- pearance. The large and beautiful lake was one of the chief attractions, and numerous boats were constantly plying thereon. In a neighbouring field some hundreds of young men and women greatly enjoyed themselves in dancing to the strains of a concertina, in fact, the attendance was :0 large that it became very incorfvenient. As evening ap- proached, however, the pleasure-seekers left for home, and the place gradually assumed its wonted aspect. On Easter Monday many of the shops were closed, but evidently there was not the same pleasure and enjoyment as on the previous Friday. One drawback was the weather, which was not quite so favourable, and then there were not the same at- tractions in other respects. The town wore a holiday aspect, however, and very little business was done.

THE HOLlDAY.—Altbough Good Friday and Easter Mon- day were recognised as a general holiday at Lyrnm the town wore an unusually quiet- appearance. All the shops were closed on Good Friday, and this was the case, W th a few exceptions, on Monday. The only visitors were two pic-nic parties from Manchester who came in on Monday; and few of the inhabitants left the town.

RATEPAYERS' MEETING.—A ratepayers' meeting was held in the vestry of the parish church on Thursday week, and there was a fair attendance, the Rev. G. W. Guest pre- siding. For the office of guardians of the poor the Rev. J. Cullin, the Rev. G. W. Guest, Mr. J. Thomason, and Mr. R. Edmondson were nominated, but Mr. Guest has since withdrawn, and unless one of the other gentlemen with- draws a contest will be inevitable. Mr. H. T. Ste Hos and Mr. T. Richardson were nominated as overseers, and Mr. Ardern and Mr, F. Holt as collectors and assessors of taxes. A vote of thanks to the rev. chairman for presiding con- cluded the proceedings. VESTRY MEETING.—The vestry meeting in connection with St. Mary's Church was held on Tuesday evening, the rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest, presiding. The accounts, which showed a deficiency of £22, were read and passed. Votes of thanks were accorded Mr. T. P. Norris and Mr. A. W. Callender for their services as churchwardens during the past year, and they were re-elected for the ensuing year. Dr. Brabazon, Mr. C. Maclver, Mr. H. Pearson, and Mr. W. Bayley were elected to the office of sidesmen ; and Mr. Pearson and Mr. T. Ardern were chosen as lay delegates to attend the Chester conference. A vote of thanks was ac- corded to Dr. Fox for his services as organist and for a I donation of £l7 10s., his half-year's salary as organist. The meeting concluded in the usual way. CONCERT.—A concert under the auspices of the Lymm branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held in the National School, on Thursday evening, and the proceeds of the entertainment are to be devoted to the buy- ing of a number of new instruments for the drum and fife band in connection with the society. The attendance was very good, many of the elite of Lymni. ben?g. present. A pianoforte duet by Miss Pearson and Miss Williamson opened the proceedings :and was well rendered. A part song, en- titled " Sprirfg song," was given by members of the Parish ' Church choir, after which the well-known popular song " Sailing," was sung in good style by Mr. Todhunter. A violin solo was given with masterly skill by Miss Middle- ton, a very accomplished young lady, who is visiting at the 1 rectory. Miss Pearson did full justice to the song, " For- ' give, forget," with violin obligato, by Miss Middleton ; and the song, "Orpheus with his lute," afterwards given by the latter, received an encore to which she responded. Colonel Godfrey, who is a favourite with Lymm audiences, sAng, in his old characteristic fashion, "Mad girls song," and was accorded an enthusiastic encore. After a short interval Miss Middleton performed, with consummate skill, the ' pianoforte solo, " Valoe Caprice ;" and the members of the choir followed with the part-song, " Golden d1r..," which sas very nicely rendered. "The powder monkey " received a good interpretation at the hands of Mr. Todhunter, and he was loudly applauded. div.p: VESTRY MEETINGS. WIDNES. PARISH CHURCH. On Wedaesday evening the annual vestry meeting was held in the Waterloo-road schools. The Rev. J. Wright Williams presided, and there were present :—The Rev. W. H. Duggan; Messrs. W. Crabtree, T. Balmer, J. Beacham, ' T. Atherton, W. Chadwick, James White, W. Treacy, Ben., J. B. Imison, J. McCollom, J. Matthews, 'Whittle, J. Jones, liemmingwy, Watson, Barton, J. IL Pankhurst, Farrant, H. N. %Tifton, Dwerryhoute, T. Atherton, J. Williams, Lord, and T. Davies.—Mr. W. TREACY, senior, presented the statement of accounts. lie said last Easter there was a balance in the hands of the churchwardens to the amount of £33 5s 54d, but in accordance with a resolution which was passed, that sum Lad been transferred to the Repairs Fund Account, so that the churchwardens commenced the year, which had just closed, with " nil," The receipts for the past year had been—Offertories, al 1.9$ 10el net proceeds of tea party' £25 14, sd, kit £4 Bs, and ground rent £ll 488 91 The diehntlements had been, ordinary expenses, £73 58 04d, ex..t-caordinary ex- penses, repairs to bell, Ste., £32 ds 31, leaving a balance of £lB 11s 80 in the hands -et the. churchwardens. (Applause.) He might explain that the balance was not so large as last year in conseque'nce of the receipts from the tea party being £l4 less than the previous year. Mr. Treacy then read the accounts of the Repairs (No. 21 Fund. At the commence- ment of the year there was a balance against that account of £4558 Sid, and since then there had been a, contract en- tered into for the erection of a front wall to the churchyard for £6B, making a total against the account of £136 5s 84d. On the other side of the account there was to be placed £33 5s 54-d, transferred from the churchwardens' account, £69 3s Td, subscriptions, nett receipts from concert, SU. Ss 4d; leaving a balance of £22 14s 4d still owing on this account.—The CHAIRMAN acknow- ledged the readiness with which the members of the church had fallen in with the contributions, remarking that improvements OR the inside and on the outside of the church showed that the money had been judiciously spent.— A question was asked with regard to the new church gates, and the CHAIRMAN, in reply, said toat they were a standing wonder to the Iowa; but they had not been fixed without a great deal of remonstrance from the architect and church- wardens. The account with reference to them had not been paid.—Mr. ArtuartoN begged to give notice that at the next meeting of the vestry he should ha prepared to opposo the payment for the gates. (Laughter.)—The accounts were passed.—Mr. JAMES WHITE!, as auditor, referred to the amounts, and spoke in high terms of praise of the manner in which they had been kept. He moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Je B. Imison for his services as treasurer.—Mr. LOWEI seconded the motion which was unanimously carried.— The CHAIRMAN, alluding to the church officers, -observed that it used to be a reproach that the church was managed by the parson, and, perhaps, the clerk, but if ever that re- proach existed in the Widnes parish, it was growing beauti- fully less, and he had to acknowledge the very earnest help notokly of men who were officially in harness, but of men who were in harness unofficially.—On the motion of Mr. CHADWICK, seconded by Mr. CRABTREE, a vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to the churchwardens.—Mr. Lcrais Kilvross was appointed the parishioners' warden, on the proposal of Mr. W. TRRACY, SEN., seconded by Mr. IlAtacan.—The CHAIRMAN spoke in flattering terms of the cervices of his churchwarden, Mr. J. B. lmison, and re- marked that he could not do better than ail.- Mr. Imison to consider himself re-appointed. (Applause.) He also ap-1 poisted,the following gentlemen as his sidesnsen : Messrs, Bairaer, Chadwick, Treacy,sen., Charles Jones, Treacy. jun., Pankhurst, Atherton, and Warton.—On the motion of Mr. ZAL*2I32, seconded by Mr. DWERRYHOUSE, the following !were appointed parishioners' sidesmen : Messrs. 'Crabtree, Beecham, Lord, Whittle, ?arrant, Lowe, Meanie, and Cave.—Mr. J. White and Mr. J. Matthews .eath,made Slew remarks with reference to their visit to conference last year, and they were again unanimously Chosen the lay representatives for the ensuing year.—Mr. J. `Wmemets moved that .'fir. Chadwick be appointed the vestry- cleek.—Mr. KILCROSS seconded the motion, which was car- ried.—The CHAIRMAN said before he came to the meeting he heard that some people were under a misapprehension about tine appointment of a suecessor to their pool,lamented Mr. Jeseop. He wished it to be known that t6at appointment 4el4d. not remain in the hands of the vestry meeting, but of the vt'ear and churchwardens.—Mr. CRABTREE! asked if the chairman could inform the meeting of the exact date that 4the sod would be cut for the new church at Anderson's ccrner.—The CHAIRMAN replied that all he could, say was -that he would give them the date when he got it himself. A • contract had been entered into, and the plans had been ft:a- warded to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners.—The meeting then terminated.
RUNCORN. Pews H CHURCH.

The Aster vestry meeting was held in the chancel of the Parish Church on Monday morning. The Rev. Canon Barclay; vicar, presided, and there were also present Messrs. John Brundrit (vicar's warden), Peter Briscoe (sideaman), U. Summerfield, J. W. Lightburn, J. Toaks, J. Ward, and W. Heaton.—Mr. Jorna Bausoarr, in presenting the church- wardens' accounts, remarked that they commenced the year with a balance of £52 2s 9d in hand. The expenditure from 1881 to 1882 was £l4B 13 Bd, and the expenditure this year was £2oo' gs fid. This large increase of more than £5O was due to the fact that the church had been pravided with a new gas meter at a cost of £l5 14s 6d, three new coronas at a coat of. 49.5 lls 3d, cover for gas meter £3 3s, new bell ropes (an expense which only occurred once every 4 years) £5. Notwithstanding all this increased expenditure, the churchwardens had still a balance in hand of £l5 us 11d. During the past year there had only been 13 morning offertories, which produced the sum of £5l 19s 3d, or an average of £3 19s 11d. In the preceding year there were 14 morning offertories, which produced £62 5s 2d, or an average of £4 8s 11d. The eleven evening offertories of last year produced £2O 193 sd, or an average of £1 18s id; while in the preceding year 12 evening offertories produced £26 16s 4d, an average of £2 4s Bd. 'Thus while there was an increase in the expendithre, there was a de- crease in the receipts.—The vouchers having been produced and examined, the accounts were passed on the motion of Mr. LIGHTBURN, seconded by Mr. SUMMERFIELD.— The VICAR observed that it gave him great pleasure to again appoint Mr. Brundrit his warden for the ensuing year. He was glad to know that the appointment had given universal satisfaction in the past. Mr. Crosby was appointW. parishioners' warden. Mr. Brundrit appointed Mr. W. Whittaker his eidesman, while Mr. Peter Briscee was unani- mously chosen the parishioners' warden for the ensuing year. Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Whittaker were appointed the lay representatives of the parish at the ruri-decanal and diocesan conferences. It was resolved that the bell-ringers be engaged for the ensuing year at a salary of £B, with per- mission to collect the usual gratuities as heretofore.—A vote of thanks was uranimously accorded to the choirmaster and choir for their voluntary services during the past year. —Mr. LIGHTBURN proposed that the thanks of the vestry be I given to the churchwardens, the sidesmen, and the chair- man, and the motion having been seconded, was carried.— The CHAIRMAN and Mr. BRUNDRIT remarked, in reply, upon the harmonious feeling which pervaded the church. The latter, referring to the decrease in the the receipts, expressed the hope that the report in the news- papers wogld induce people to give more liberally, se that the churchwardens would have a larger balance in hand. —The CHAIRMAN said he did not think Mr. Brundrit had gone to the root of the niatter. It was not because people gave less money, but because there were fewer people to give. The chairman also referred to the rule adopted in 1875, to the effect that all seats unoccupied at 10-30 in the morning and 6.30 in the evening were free to any worship- pers going into the -church. He wondered why people bothered so much about seats when there were so many empty ones in the church. Service was not taken until five minutes after the bell stopped in order that people might have ..a chance to occupy the seats which were empty, so that really people had no grievance.—Mr. BRUNDRIT said the officials of the church tried to suit people as far as possible.—Mr. SUMMERFIRLD remarked that many people did not like seats to be occupied when they came into church.—Mr. LIGHTTSITRN was of opinion that the people ought to feel glad when they came late to find their seats occupied..—After some further conversation the meeting terminated.

The annual tea party and ball, in aid of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants' Orphans Fund, was held on Good Friday, in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes. Railway servants are exposed to many perils, and are frequently sent to a pre- mature grave through some unlooked-for accident. The fund in question is specially organised to provide a living for the orphans of such men; although the same provision is made in the case of death being the result of natural causes. It is consequently regarded with much favour, and the annual event is largely patronised. Last evening ablaut 300 sat down to tea, the tables being presided over by the female relatives of the men. The room had been decorated with bannerettes, flags, mottoes, dm., and imparted a rather bright appearance to the generally dingy room. After tea a ball was held. About 250 couples were present, and to the -strains of Mr. Powell's band danced until early morning.
