THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. PETHION AGAINST BY THE WARP...LNG TON CORPORATION.

We append a copy of the petition • v-,oloh has been pre- sented by the Warrington Corporati- ge against this Bill on its merits : - To the Honourable the Ce of Great Britain and - Anmons of the United Kingdom The humble petiti . Ireland, in Parliament assembled. se f the - .en of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Bur, gess o P aeerough of Warrington, under their common seal, shew-ath as follows :- I.—T Hot, oat a Bill is now pending in your hon.eurable - .se, intituled "A Bill to authorise the construeetion of a Aeip canal to Manchester, and for other purposes:" 2.—The preamble of the Bill, amongst other.. things, states that the construction of a canal from the river Mersey to Manchester, navigable for ocean steatoers and ships of large burthen, and of docks at Warrinr_ton and Manchester, would be of great public and loca', advantage, and that certain persons are willing at their own expense to con- struct the same, and that it is exrdedient that they for that ,purpose be incorporated into a 'company (hereinafter called "the company,") and that the powers of the company of proprietors of the Mersey o.nd Irwell navigation (hereinafter called "The Mersey Irwell Company ") so far as they relate to the said navigation, be transferred to the company. That it is expedient that the company be authorised to con- struct docks at W'arrington and Manchester, and that the company be eP.abled for the purposes of the canal, docks, and works to enter upon, take, and use the bed, channels, and banks 'of the rivers Mersey and Irwell, and of the cuts connecte:a therewith, and of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, where the same may be coincident.with or intersected by Vile line of the intended works. And that it is expedient tleat the municipal corporations and local boards of health in the counties of Lancaster and Chester should be empowered to subscribe to and to hold shares in the capital of the company. 3.—Your petitioners are the Local Authority for the high- ways and sewers, and the Sanitary Authority, who are responsible under "The Public Health Act, 1875," for the health of the borough, and at present are in the habit of using, as the Road Authority for the district, a portion of the river quays withia the borough for their road materials and otherwise, and they will be injuriously affected in the use of the same in manner hereinafter appearing. 4.—Your petitioners are the Local Authority hereinbefore mentioned,and as representing the ratepayers and inhabitants and trade of the borough, your petitioners allege that the Bill, if sanctioned by your honourable House in its present shape, will very seriously affect their property, rights, and interests, and they strongly object to the said Bill for the reasons hereinafter set forth. 5 —At the present time there is a free navigation exten- sively used from Liverpool to Warrington on the tidal river Mersey, which is capable of being improved at comparatively small cost. The improvement of the navigation has been for a long time contemplated by your petitioners, and the initiatory steps are now being taken prior to the introduction of a Bill into your honorable House for that purpose. With this object in view, in the year 1880, when the Corporation of Liverpool obtained an Act of Parliament for the purpose of bringing water from the river Vyrnwy to Liverpool, your petitioners appeared before your honorable House and ob- tained the insertion of a clause in the Act providing that the iryrnwy aqueduct was to be laid at such a depth under the bed of the river Mersey as the Board of Trade should pre- scribe, so as not to interfere with any proposed improvement of the navigation of that river. 6.—By the Bill (clause 3) the navigable waters of the rivers Mersey and Irwell between Garston and Manchester, and the canal, and all channels, canals, docks, and works of the company within those limits are constituted the harbour , and port of Manchester, and the company the harbour authority of that harbour and port, and (by clause 4) the limits of the Act are the harbour and port of Manchester. Thus the whole of the existing waterways and the power to control the navigation will vest in the company, and War- rington will virtually become part of the port of Manches- ter, and the navigation of the river Mersey between Run- corn and Warrington, which has hitherto been free, will be placed under the control of the company. This, your peti- tioners submit, is unnecessary for the purposes of the canal scheme, and will greatly prejudice the interests of your petitioners and the town of Warrington, and will prevent any independent improvement of that navigation. 7.—Clause 22 compels the existing Navigation Companies te sell all their rights and powers in and over to the rivers Mersey and Irwell, and the branch canals connected there- with respectively, and all their estate, rights (including the right to levy tolls), powers and privileges to the com- pany. Clause 26 gives powers to the company to dredge, scour, open, deepen, widen, straighten, cleanse and improve the beds, banks, shores, and channels of so much of the river Mersey as lies beween a point in the township and parish of Runcorn, in the county of Chester, on the left bank of that river, about 48 chains east of the western and of the north pier of the Old Quay Docks, measured along that bank, and the point of junction with that river of the River Irwell, and also so much of the river Irwell as lies between the said point of junction and Hunt's Bank, in the town- ship of Manchester, in the .parish of Manchester, and the cuts, canals, river., backwaters, streams, brooks, and water- courses connected with the said rivers Mersey and Irwell, or either of them within the limits aforesaid and within those limits, to remove, alter, lengtken, curtail, raise or lower all cuts, canals, weirs, banks, dams, sluices, locks, channels, and water-courses, bridges, arches, culverts, pipes, sewers, and drains, and do such other works as may be necessary or convenient in connection with or for the pur- poses of the works proposed to be authorised. B.—By Clause 28 it is proposed to authorist, among other things, the construction by the company of the following works:—" (a.) A new navigable canal or channel, com- mencing in the township of Runcorn, in and out of the river Mersey, at a point on the left bank of that river, about 48 chains east of the western end of the north pier of the Old Quay Jocks and terminating in the township and parish of Flixton, in the county of Lancaster; (b) a new navigable canal or channel, commencing at the termina- tion of the foregoing work and terminating in the parish .of Manchester, at a point situate about five chains west of the western, end of the northern abutment of the Trafford Bridge, measured along the right bank of the river Irwell." And it is provalea that in connection with the foregoing works the company may raise or lower the level of the waters of the said rivers . Mersey and Dwell, and of the cuts, canals, and channels connected therewith respec- tively, between the commencement of the first-mentioned work and Hunt's Bank aforesaid. "(j) A dock or basin, with an entrance from the canal, wholly in the townships of Warrington, Thelwall (detached number 2) and Latch- ford; (1) deviation railway number 1. The diversion of the main line of the London and North-Western Railway, where it crosses the river Mersey at the Walton viaduct near Warrington by the construction of a deviation railway, commencing in the township of Moore by a junction with the said main line and terminating by a junction with the said main line at a point in the said township of Warring- ton, at the north side of the Three Arch Bridge, situate south of and near to the high level station at Bank Quay ; (a) de % iation railway number 3. The diversion of the Warrington and Stockport railway by the construction of a deviation railway, commencing in the said township of Warrington by a junction with that railway, at the western abutment of the bridge of that railway over the river Mersey near Arpley station, and terminating in the said township of Latchford, at the point where that railway crosses Cross-lane. 9.—By clause 29 power is sought 1)317 the company to construct and maintain every description of subsidiary work which may be incidental to, or necessary or expedient in connection with the works authorized by the Bill, and particularly power to alter, vary, and reconstruct all or any of the bridges over the rivers Mersey and Irwell, and to substitute opening for fixed bridges, and to remove all bridges rendered unnecessary by the construction of sub- stituted bridge,: By clause 30 the works of the company may be so deviated as to raise the level of the water of the Canal and river near Warrington eight feet. By clause 31 the company are authorized to divert into the Canal and other works of the company, the waters of the Mersey, Irwell, Bollin, and other waters, and all the waters of the Mersey and Irwell navigation, and all other waters under their control, and to supersede and discontinue for the pur- poses of navigation so much of the present course or chan- nel of the saidrivers as may be rendered unnecessary by the construction of the proposed works. By clause 32, subject to the provisions in " The Railways Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845," and in Part I. (relating to the construction of a railway) of " The Railways Clauses Act, 1863," contained in reference to the crossing of roads on the level, the com- pany may,in the construction of the railwayacarry the same with a double line only across and on the level of the pub- lic highway numbered 3 on the deposited plans relating to the township of Latchford in the parish of Grappenall. 10.—Your petitioners submit that the effect of the powers sought by these and other clauses in the Bill, will be to vest lathe company all the waters of the river Mersey, and to enable them, if they think Et, to cease allowing any water to -flow down the present bed of the river, from Walton past Bank •Quay to Runcorn, and to enable them entirely to supersede and discontinue the navigation down the existing river to 'Runcorn; also to vest in the company the right to dredge the whole of the river, and to prevent the free use of the river from Warrington to Runcorn as heretofore. 11.—Various sewers and storm overflow-channels under the jurisdiction of your petitioners at and near Bank Quay, fall into the tidal river Mersey. The effect of the construc- tion of the proposed dam and sluices 21 chains east of Wal- ton Bridge, and the raising of the waters of the.canal, will be to prevent the flow of water down the river which at pre- sent exists, and in course of time will cause the river to silt up, and the sewers to become useless. Other sewers and storm overflow-channels under the jurisdiction of your petitioners empty themselves into the said tidal river Mersey above the proposed dam and sluices. The effect of , the construction of the proposed dam, and the raising of the water on the river and canal will be to convert the tidal river into dead water. The aforesaid dead water will thus become the dock of Warrington, into which the sewers will empty, and in process of time a deposit will tee formed which will be dangerous to health. And further, if the water in the river be raised by the works of the company above the outlet of such sewers they will be blocked or im- peded. 12.—A great part of the trade of Warrington is in classes of goods which are carried to and from Warrington and Liverpool in barges which use the existing waterway be- tween Runcorn and Warrington free of charge. The river Mersey, below the proposed dant and sluices, will, in pro.

div.head: cess of time, become silted up and dry, and the barges will accordingly be compelled to use the canal and pay the
div.p: cess of time, become silted up and dry, and the barges will accordingly be compelled to use the canal and pay the
dues.
13.—The wharves on the banks of the tidal river Mersey above the said dam and sluices will, When the river is con- nected with the canal, become part of the works of the corn-

pany, and o'aly approachable through the canal or from the proposed dock at LAtchford, and consequently will become subject Arrd liable to the canal dues and wharfage rates, and other 'privileges conferred upon the company by the Bill. 14.—The wharves also at Bank Quay and below the dam

5.-1 d sluices will be rendered valueless by the want of water in, and the silting up of the river as before mentioned, while they will be cut off by the dam from the other part of the river which passes through Warrington. The company take no powers by the Bill to take tolls from Runcorn to Bank Quay, and your petitioners, therefore, submit that although they take powers to dredge this portion of the river they do not intend to do so. _ .

15.—The company will be enabled to remove the existin stone bridge at Warrington and to substitute for it, if they think fit, an opening or swing bridge. The existing bridge is the first roadway across the river after quitting its mouth. It is situated in the borough of Warrington, connecting its Lancashire and Cheshire portions, and is the main highway between Lancashire and Cheshire, over which there is a continuous flow of traffic. Such an alteration, therefore, if

made, will seriously affect your petitioners, and will be a most dangerous impediment to the traffic passing over the said roadway. 16.—That by the above-recited powers the company will be enabled entirely to cut off the supply of water from the river at present used by the manufacturers. The well-water is not suitable for manufacturing purposes, and consequently the manufacturers use the river water in large quantities. Further, the proposed canal will cut through the Wilders- pool-causeway and the Knutsford-road, both of which roads it is proposed to carry over the canal by swing-bridges. Such mode of construction will materially prejudice and interfere with the large and increasing traffic on the said roads, and will be very injurious to the inhabitants of Warrington, and will greatly interfere with the sewers and gas mains of the Corporation. 17.—1 t is proposed by deviation Railway Number 3, as shown on the deposited plans, to carry the Low Level Rail- way in a tunnel under the proposed canal, and on the level across the Wilderspool-road. The said road is crossed on the level by the existing railway, and great inconvenience to the traffic, as well as danger to life, thereby arises, and the same has been the subject of an inquiry by the Board of Trade with the view of the abolition of the said level cross- ing. Your petitioners submit that no such level crossing should be re-enacted, but that any deviation as now pro- posed should have been so arranged as to get rid of the existing level croesing by carrying the said railway either under or over the said road. 18.—By-Part V. of the Bill and the schedules therein re- ferred to, various powers are proposed to be conferred do the company to demand and take dues in respect of every vessel using and entering the canal, and to demand and take certain rates in respect of all animals and goods which shall enter or leave the canal at its commencement near Runcorn, and be carried thereon in any vessel for any distance on the canal between the said commencement thereof, and a point situate 40 chains east of the entrance to Warrington Dock; and to demand and take certain wharfage rates, and to de- mand and take in respect of every ton of geods carried for any distance on the canal between its commencement near Runcorn and Hunt's Bank, but not entering or leaving the canal, any sum not exceeding three shillings and fourpence, and so proportionatly for every greater or lesser quantity of weight, and for other purposes. 19.—The proposed tolls, dues, and rates are unfair to your petitioners, and might and will seriously affect the trade of Warrington and the district. The whole of the dues to be charged as fixed by the bill, except the canal dues, are or may be so fixed by the company as to be the same both for Manchester and Warrington. There is nothing in the bill to prevent the company from putting the maximum toll on Warrington, and accepting a far less toll from Man- chester, and by that means making the rates to Manchester equal or less than to Warrington, and driving the carrying trade up the river, instead of its being put on the rails at Warrington. 20.—There are no provisions id the Bill with reference to barges trading between Liverpool and Warrington like those now existing, independently of the provisions and dues set out in the Bill relating to ships, though provisions are made for barges trading between Manchester and Runcorn, but not leaviog the canal. 21.—Under clause 61 of the Bill, as it at present stands, the company will have the exclusive right of loading and unloading all vessels not only in the canal or docks pro- posed to be made, but at the existing wharves and quays on the river Mersey between Wilderspool and the weir, and for charging for the use of the same as in the said clause pro- vided; and clause 109 gives power to the company to make bye-laws ftr regulating such user. 22.—Your petitioners also object to the said Bill on the ground that no limit of time is fixed for the completion of the said works, nor is there any provision contained therein making the formation of the proposed docks at Warrington compulsory. 23.—Your petitioners would further point out that the company seeks power under the Bill to acquire an enor- mous area of land in the neighbourhood of Warrington, amounting to two and a half miles in length, with an aver- age of a quarter of a mile in width, including the bed and channel of the river Mersey between Latchford Weir and Woolston, which your petitioners apprehend will be re- quired by the company for the purpose of depositing spoil, and your petitioners allege that they will be greatly injured tiaercb7. 24.—8 y part IX. of the Bill powers are proposed to be given to your petitioners amongst other local authorities to subscribe and contribute funds not exceeding one-fourth part of one year's rateable value of the borough towards the making and maintaining of the works by the Bill proposed to be authorised, and of taking and holding shares in the capital of the company proposed to be created and for other purposes. The same part of the Bill also provides that such local authority shall not dispose of or transfer any of the shares for which they may subscribe, and confers upon the local authority powers to borrow money on the security of the rates for the purpose bf such contribution, and provides for the discharge of the moneys so borrowed by means of sinking funds. 25.—8 y Clause 118 any local authority whose contribu- tion amounts to not less than two hundred and fifty thousand pounds may from time to time in respect of each sum of two hundred and fifty thousand pounds fully paid up by them nominate a member of their body to be a director of the company. Your petitioners object to such application of the borough funds as proposed as being incon- sistent with the purposes for which they are intended. 26.—Under the above recited pro vision, your petitioners would not be represented on the board of the proposed com- pany ; and your petitioners submit it is unfair that a local authority should not have the same power to dispose of its shares as any other shareholder. 27.—The Bill (part X.) contains powers to transfer the undertaking of the company to a body of trustees upon the application of certain local authorities (your petitioners among them) upon certain terms in the Bill set out. Your petitioners object to the said terms as being uncertain, and the liabilities proposed to be created are so vague that the benefits proposed to be conferred upon your petitioners by this portion of the Bill as wholly illusory. 28.—The details of the engineering of the works by the Bill proposed to be executed are defective and objectionable, and are inefficient to secure the objects sought to be attained, and the estimates of expense are insufficient. 29.—The preamble of the Bill is untrue, and cannot be substantiated by evidence. 30.—That if the Till do pass into law, other clauses and provisions ought to be inserted therein for the protection of your petitioners, and their property, rights and interests. Your petitioners therefore humbly pray your Honourable House that the Bill may not pass into law as it now stands, and that they may be heard by themselves, their counsel, agents, and witnesses before the Committee of your Honourable House to whom it may be referred, against the preamble of the same, and against all and every the clauses and provisions thereof which relate to or . affect their rights, property, and interests, and that in case your Honourable House should think fit to sanction the same, such clauses and provisions may be introduced therein for the protection of your petitioners, their pro- perty, rights, or interests, or that they may have such other relief in the premises as to your llonourable House shall seem meet. And your petitioners will ever pray, &c. JOHN RD. PICK lIERE, Deputy Mayor.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WARRINGTON SCHOOLMASTER.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WARRINGTON SCHOOLMASTER.

The members of the scholastic profession in Warrington, and the public generally, will hear with regret the announcement of the death of Mr. Thomas Gibson, master of Wycliffe day schools, Warrington, which event I took place quite unexpectedly yesterdty afternoon. With the object of visiting some relatives, Mr. Gibson left War- rington with his wife on Good Friday for Fallowfield, near Manchester, and:while there he complained:of being unwell. On Monday, it was deemed advisable to call in a medical gentleman, who found Mr. Gibson suffering from severe cold. Inflammation of the lung afterwards set in, but nothing serious was apprehended until Thursday, when ' the disease was aggravated by old complaints of a compli- cated character. However, yesterday morning an improve- ment was noticeable, but at noon there was a change for the worse, and he died at five o'clock in the afternoon at the early age of 33 years. The deceased gentleman served as a pupil teacher under Mr. E. Brewtnall at Warrington British Schools, and afterwards proceeded to Borough-road College, London, where he underwent the usual course of training. On leaving college he obtained an appointment at Waterloo, near Ashton-under-Lyne, and he subsequently removed to the latter town. Thence he went to Staley- bridge, and then to Lee•street school, Opens haw, where he remained 6years ; after which he obtained the mastership of Wycliffe school, which position he has oclupied for the last three years. Under his management the achool has steadily improved in every way, and recently it has been found necessary to increase the accommodation. It will he with great regret the managers lose the services_of Mr. Gib- son, who has brought the school to so flourishing a condi- tion, and that regret wilt be increased by the suddeness by which the loss has been occasioned. Much sympathy will be extended to the widow' and parents of the deceased vutler.an in their sad bereavement.

div.head: LOSING HARD-EARNED MONEY AT
div.p: LOSING HARD-EARNED MONEY AT
WARRINGTON.

Yesterday, at Warrington Police Court, before Captain Reynolds and Mr. Ziba Armitage, Patrick Farrell, Clothhall- yard, arid Joseph M.'Guire, Chrime's-yard, were charged with having stolen on the previous night from the person of James Malooney, a discharged soldier, about £l6 in gold and a silver medal.—The chief constable (Mr. Hunt) said that the prosecutor was discharged from his regiment on Tuesday, when he received about £l7 17s. He came from Manchester to Warrington by train on Wednesday about noon, and on leaving the station and going into Horsemarket- street he met with the two prisoners, and the three turned into a heerhouse near Crown-street. From there they went to several other beerhouses, and were drinking the whole afternoon. In the evening Farrell asked the prosecutor to go to his house and have tea with him, and he did so, and they afterwards went out and had more drink. P.C. Jones saw the three together near Farrell's house, and seeing that the prosecutor seemed a respectable man and apparently in possession of some money he advised him not to stay there. He replied that they had all been chums during the day and he would be all right. The three afterwards returned to Farrell's, and took with them a quantity of whisky. The prosecutor came to the police station very early on Thursday morning, and gave the information that his money and medal had been stolen. P.C. Jones and Sergeant Bowen went to Farrell's and were searching the house when Farrell gave them 3s or 4s and the medal, say- ing that prosecutor left it on the shelf. The search was proceeded with, and in Farrell's bed was found about 4s in copper. M'Guire's house was then searched, and M'Guire raked out of the ashes in the grate 4s and some coppers, and gave it to the officers saying that he put it in the grate when he went home drunk, so that his "old woman "would not feel in his pockets and get it, and that prosecutor gave it to him. Inquiry was made, and it was found that the three had had some fetuales with them from a common lodging house. There was no doubt he (the chief constable) thought that the money had been stolen, but the question • was by whom, because Farrell's was a common lodging house registered for 40 lodgers, and Farrell's mother, the prisoners, lodgers, and prosecutor had all been drinking to- gether.—The prosecutor, besides bearing out the Chief Con- stable's statement, said he felt stupefied when he left Far- rell's, and thought that something was put into the whiskey to make him so. He could not say positively who took the money and medal. In answer to Captain Reynolds he said be passed through the Zulu campaign and took part in some of the actions. He was now going back to Treland.—The Bench said they were sorry he bad lost his hard-earned money but it was his own fault for getting into bad com- pany. There was not sufficient evidence to convict the prisoners, and they would be bound over to appear when called upon.

THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION SANITARY COMMITTEE THE TREATMENT OF IVANURE AT ROCHDALE. The Borough Surveyor (14. r Longdin) has submitted to the chairman and members of the Sanitary Committee of the Warrington Corporation the following report:— "Gentlemen,—ln accordance with the resolution of the Committee of March 7th, "that a deputation of this Com- mittee (to consist of such members as can find it convenient to go), together with the borough surveyor and Mr. Din- widdie, visit the manure works at Rochdale on Tuesday next,' the following members of the committee went to Rochdale on March 3rd, 1883 :—Messrs. Monks, Barker, Dakin, Collin, and Sutton; the borough surveyor and manager of Longford depot. Since the last visit of the Committee, on August 18th, 1882, the works have been completed, and the following is a description of the prin- ciple now working at the depot :—The ashes are collected separately from the town in carts, which deliver themselves close to a horizontal sieve worked on the ' jigging ' prin- ciple. This sieve is fed by hand, and the fine ash which accrues from the process is removed to tips or given away to any person who wishes it. The rough cinders are wheeled and used at the furnaces for the purpose of evaporating the excreta and generating steam. The pails are collected by special vans and brought into a room set apart for washing and disinfecting, and taken from the vans and placed upon a flat platform, which is formed as a . hydraulic lift, and raised about ten feet, and then emptied . into wooden vats or ciscerns placed over the dryers. Separa- ting grids are fixed in these cisterns to prevent rags or other , 'heavy substances from being drawn into machines, and the vitriol which is requisite to be put into the excreta for the purpose of evaporation is here mixed. The dryers, flys in number, which combine furnace, boiler, and dryer, com- plete in one machine, are fixed on the ground level. The furnaces are fed at the front with the ashes previously named, and the product of combustion passes through an iron pipe from the back of furnace conducting the heat to the dryer, which is simply a wrought-iron cylinder revolv- ing round, having a fixed scraper on the inside. Bale plates are fixed in the dryer opposite the iron pipe, to prevent any flame from entering the dryer, and to distribute the heat through the pail contents as much as possible. An iron ipipe leads from the end of dryer to a large waste or draw- off pipe, which is connected, at a considerable distance from the machines, to a "Root's Blower," which draws the waste beat and vapour, formed by the process of evaporation, through a large upright plate condenser, and thence to the chimney. The condenser is fed by about 6,000 gallons of water per hour, pumped from the river, which is inclose proximity to the works. The dryers receive the excreta from the cisterns before described, which is let into the machines by a trough or spout. Each machine takes a charge of 31 tons, and occupies 10 hours to reduce the same into a lump manure containing from 25 to 30 per cent of moisture. The machines empty the lump manare into a pit formed underneath, which manure is wheeled away and placed on the floor of a room heated by the passage of the pipe leading to condensor before- named. After remaining on this floor from 18 to 20 hour', it can be thrown into a machine, which grinds it into powder containing from 13 to 17 per cent of moisture, and ready for being put into bags for sale. At the time your deputa- tion was present four of the machines were in full work, which were being turned by a 14 nominal horse-power engine, which was stated to be amply sufficient for all the five machines. Your deputation were informed that suffi- cient ashes were collected, not only for evaporating the excreta, but for all purposes required in carrying on the works. Your deputation were also informed that ten men were sufficient to work the whole of the lye machines. Your deputation paid special attention to the smells arising from the works, and with the exception of the room in which the vans and pales are washed, and the the room over dryers where the storage cisterns are— which were considered to be defective in structural arrange- ments--A0 particular smell was discernable. The smoke, &c., after passing through condenser into flue leading to chimney was examined and a slight smell was here noticed, although not of such a character as to create a nuisance ; still the chairman of the Rochdale Sanitary Committee (Alderman Taylor) and their manager (Mr. Haresceugh) stated they would not be satisfied until the slightest smell was overcome, and for that purpose they were engaged put- ting up a boiler, through the fire of which the smoke, Arc., would be consumed before passing into chimney. Your deputation cannot but think that the mode of treatment adopted at Rochdale bids fair in getting over the dificulty experienced in disposing of town's refuse at a minimum of cost.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.—THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT, 1878. Notice is Hereby Given, that the Local Authority of this Borough has granted a Licence ta JOSEPH TAYLOR. of the Norton Arms Hotel, to hold a Public Sale of Animals, Fat and Store, at the Norton Arms Hotel, in this Borough, on Monday, the Second day of April next, subject to the following con- dition No animal brought to such sale shall be moved therefrom unless and until the same has been inspected by the Inspector of the Local Authority, who will attend such sale. The Pig Market, Town Hill, will be open on Wednesday next for the sale of both fat and store pigs. No licence will be necessary for the movement of animals in, or ihto, or from this Borough if the movement is from or into a district not infected with Foot-and-Mouth Disease and within the county of Lancaster or Chester. Dated this Thirtieth day of March, 1883: wkr. HY. BROOK, Town Clerk.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. (2423.) Infected Districts Matkets and Fairs Order of 1883.—At the COUNCIL CHAMBER, WHITEHALL, the 22nd day of MARCH, 1883. By Her Majesty's Most Hot ourable Privy Council. Present : Lord President. Chancellor of the Exchequer. The Lords and others of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Counc.l, by virtue and in exercise of the powers In them vested under The Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1878, and of every other power enabling them in this behalf, do order, and it is hereby ordered, as follows : SHORT TITLE.-1. This Order may be cited as The Infected Districts Markets and Fairs Order of 1883. COMMENCEMENT.-2, This Order shall commence and take effect from and immediately after the thirty-first day of March, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-three. EXTENT.-3. This Order does not extend to—(i.) Foreign animals wharves; and (ii.) Areas for the time being declared by the Privy Council to be Areas infected with foot-and-mouth disease (for which Areas proviiion is made, as regards public. , and private sales, by The Foot-and-Mouth Diseases No. 2 Order of 1881, and The Foot-and-Mouth Disease No. 2 Order of 1881, Amendment); and (iii.) Areas for the time being declared by the Privy Council to be Areas infected with swine fever (for which Areas provision is made, AS regards public and private sales, by The Swine Fever Order of 1882); aud (iv.) The Metro- polis (provision being made for the metropolis, as regards public and private sales, by The Metropolis (Foot-and-Mouth Disease) No. 2 Order of 1881, and The Metropolis (Foot-and- Mouth Disease) No. 2 Order of 1881 Amendment No. 3). INTERPRETATION.-4, In this Order—Animals means cattle (that is, bulls, cows, oxen, heifer s, and calves), and sheep, and swine. Fat animals means animals intended for slaughter. Store animals means animals other than fat animals. Public sale includes a market or fair, and any sale, whether conducted by auction or not, which is open to the public, whether on pay- ment of entrance money or other payment or not, whether it is held in a public place or not, and whether animals of different owners are exposed thereat or not; and includes also an exhibi- tion. Private sale means any sale other than a public sale. Foot-and-Mouth Disease Infected Area means an area for the: time being declared by the Privy Council to be an area in- fected with foot-and-mouth disease. Foot-and-Mouth Disease Infected Place means a place for the time being declared by a Local Authority or by the Privy Council to be a place infected with foot-and-mouth disease, Expose means expose for sale or in any manner put up or cffer for sale, or exhibit at an exhi- bition. Farm or premises includes two or more adjoining farms or premises in the same occupation. Other terms have the same meaning as in The Animals Order. PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SALES.-5. No public or private sale of an animal or anima, fat or store, shall be held in the DistEct of any Local Authority in England or Wales or Scotland in which there is a Foot-and-Mouth Disease Infected Area or a Foot-and-Mouth Disease Infected Place except as expressly authotised by this Order. PUBLIC OR PRIVATE SALES OF FAT OR STORE ANIMALS BY LICENCE OF LOCAL AUTHORITY.-6. (a.) A public or private sac ef animals, fat or store, may be held with a licence of the Lccal Authority. (8.) A licence of a Local Authority for a public or private sale of fat or store animals under this Article shall be signed by the clerk of the Local Authority, by special: direction of the Local Authority, and shall give notice of the conditions (if any) which the Local Authority may deem it expedient to impose as the conditions on which the licence is granted, and shall be granted to the person entitled to hold the sale (as owner of a market, or as an auctioneer, or otherwise), and shall specify the'place where the sale is to be held, and may authorise the holding of periodical sales on stated days for a time limited, not exceeding one month, but may be renewed from time to time, and shall be published in such a manner as the Local Authority consider best fitted to insure publicity for the same. (c.) If the Privy Council are of opinion, with respect to any licence of a Local Authority for a public or private sale of fat or store animals under this Article, that the holding of the public or private sale thereby licensed is inexpedient, or that the licence is objec- tionable in any particular, and direct the revocation thereof, the same shalt thereupon cease to operate. PUBLIC OR PRIVATE SALES OF FAT OR STORE ANIMALS WITHOUT LICENCE OF LOCAL AUTH@RITY.— 7. A public or private sale of an animal or animals, fat or store, may be held without a licence of the Local Authority, in any case where the sale is held in accordance with the following condi;ions (namely) :—(i ) That the sale is held on a fat m or premises not in a Foot-and-Mouth Disease infected place; (ii.) That ?lo animal on the farm or premises is infected with Foot-and- Mouth Disease (iii.) That the animal or each animal exposed at the sale has been on the farm or ptemises not less than fourteen clear days immediately before the day on which the sale is held. SALES BY LICENCE OF PRIVY COUNCIL.-8. Without preju- dice to the foregoing provisions and in addition thereto, a public or private sale of an animal or animals, fat or store, may be held in any circumstances, with a licence of the Privy Council. OFFENCES.-9. If a public or private sale of an animal or animals, fat or store is held in contravention of this Order or of the conditions of a licence of a Local Authority or of the Privy Council thereunder, the person or company holding the sale, and the occupier of the place or farm or premises where the sale is held, and the owner or consignee of each animal exposed thereat, and the person exposing the same thereat, and the auctioneer, if any, or other person conducting the sae, and the person, if any taking entrance money or other payment for admission thereto, and the purchaser thereat of any such last-mentioned person or such purchaser knowing the sale to be held in contravention as aforesaid, shall, each according to and in respect of his or their own acts and defaults be deemed guilty of an offence against the Act of 1878. 0. L. PEEL. THOMAS BREW'S, Town Clerk.
